DAKOTA NEWS.
WASHINGTON, Feb. 11. The following resolutions were handed the president by the south eastern Dakota delegation yesterday:

Whereas, It is the earnest desire of the people of the Territory of Dakota residing south of the forty-sixth parallel that such part of said Territory should be formed into a State and admitted into the Union; and whereas, N. G Ordway, the present governor, has at sunday times and in divers ways, through self-sought press interviews, his annual report to the secretary of the interior and his letter to the president of the United States, possessed the people thereof as responsible and the legislature as mercury, and that an alarming financial and political condition exists therein; and whereas, by such representations the said Ordway has grossly defamed the people of the said Territory, and has greatly damaged the material interests of the same, has left his post of duty at the capitol of the Territory to give his entire time and attention to opposing admission whle pretending to favor 1; therefore be it

Resolved, That we, the delegates appointed by the convention of 500 members, represent all of the old counties comprising the proposed new State of Dakota, most urgently and respectfully recommend his immediate removal; and be it further

Resolved, That this delegation go as a body to the president of the United States and ask the removal of the governor of Dakota Territory as a measure of communities to the people of said Territory,

B. T. CAMPELL, Chairman.

EUGENE HUNTINGTON, Secretary.

Feb. 9, 1882.

The delegation, numbering about seventy members, called upon the president, and after formally presenting the matter for his consideration, retired with the understanding that he would meet a committee to-day. The committee, consisting of Maj. Kellam, chairman, Maj. Washburne, Messrs. Taylor, Cook and Sterling, called on the president to-day and had a full and satisfactory hearing.

THANKING PETTIGREW.

At a meeting of the delegates from North Dakota the following resolution was unanimously adopted:

Resolved, That the thanks of Northern Dakota are due and hereby tendered the Hon. R. F Pettigrew for his valuable aid in presenting the claims of that section of Dakota to a separate Territorial government, and for the uniform kindness and courtesy shown by him to the delegation.

Resolved, further, That this preamble and resolution be signed by the chairman and secretary of the delegation and that a copy thereof be presented to Mr. Pettigrew.

A. H. BARNES, Chairman,

F. H. ADAMS, Secretary.

THE ENABLING ACT.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 11. The sub-committee of the house committee on Territories have agreed to report to the full committee on Tuesday next in favor of the proposition to admit as a State all that portion of Dakota lying south of the forty-sixth parallel of latitude: the northern portion to constitute a new Territory of Dakota. The sub-committee will prepare a substitute for the pending bill, provid-

the northern portion to constitute a new Territory of Dakota. The sub-committee will prepare a substitute for the pending bill, providing for the necessary machinery of government, etc.

Joseph Budd, in jail at Yankton for the murder of C. A. Borst, four years ago has been released on his own recognizance, pending the arrival of two important witnesses.

A negro barber broke into the residence of Mrs. Merrill of Watertown and attempted to rape her, but her cries brought asistance and the negro fled. A posse of citizens are after him and if caught will be dealt with in a summary inner.

It is intimated that Strang of Pennsylvania will succeed John B. Raymond as marshal of Dakota.

The noted character and so-called heroine of the Black Hills and frontier, Calamity Jane, has arrived in Bismarck.

A very large citizens' meeting was held at Deadwood to discuss the question of bonding the counties of the Hills to aid the railroad company first constructing a railroad to the Hills. Much enthusiasm prevailed. The sentiment was in favor of building from the Northern Pacific at Cheveune, which latter city voted $400,000 for the same purpose. A committee of fifteen was appointed to procure a line of action.

A delegation from southeastern Dakota waited upon the president last Friday, and asked for the removal of Gov. Ordway.

At Sioux Falls, a dwelling upon Phillips avenue, owned by Mrs. Schuntzeler and occupied by Edward Burns, was burned. Loss, $600; insured for $150.

Yankton Press: The Milwaukee road is making preparations to extend south beyond Ashton in the early spring, to connect at Huron with its Jim River branch from Yankton north. The Northwestern is also building westward from Watertown through Clark county, and will probably connect with its Ordway branch at Redfield, though, of course, nothing is definitely known relative to the movements of the road west of Clark Center, aside from the survey to Redfield.

Emigration to the James River Valley via the Hastings & Dakota division of the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul, has already commenced, the new settlers are daily arriving from Michigan, Wisconsin and Iowa. The great majority appear to be intelligent and in very comfortable circumstances—just the kind to make the Jim River prairies blossom beautifully.

A Washington special says that the proposition to establish a new land district in Dakota, with office at Jamestown, has every prospect of success.

Alexander H. Stevens says he will support measures for the division and admission of Dakota. He takes a broad and statismanlike view of the question.

In sinking a well on the tarm of Mr. Moore, twelve miles from Wahpeton, at the depth of 175 feet was struck a vein of water which thruws a full round stream twenty feet in the air, forming, as it wore, the finest artesian well in the great northwest.

A crazy fireman on the Northern Pacific freight train, near Alsop, recently, overpowered the engineer and undertook to run the train to suit his own idea of speed—about a mile a minute. The engineer finally succeeded in stopping the train just in time to save a collision, but had his coat and vest torn off by the maniac. As soon as the train was stopped the lunatic started across the prairie and has not since been seen.

Wm. A Moore has sold his paper, the Ordway (Dak.) Times, to Messrs. Elliott & Howard.

Ole Oleson Tol of Flandrau was kicked by a horse on Wednesday and died the following day.

Lawrence county has a debt of $550,000, which costs 10 per cent. interest.

Dell Rapids hopes to have 1,000 inhabitants before the end of the year.

The body of Wild Bill, who was killed by Jack McCall at Deadwood, Black Hills, in 1876, was buried in the old cemetery at that place and two years afterward removed to the new burial grounds further out of town. Upon removing the coffin lid his remains were found solitified, with fea-ca

tures as perfect as the day upon which the funer. occurred.

A reporter of the Fargo Argus interviewed Hon. J. W. Fisher, who came in from Casselton, regarding the Callins-Slingsby case, which has been creating some excitement there. Mr. Fisher states that the preliminary examination closed in the presence of a large audience, and that Justice Lawrence's decision that these was no cause of action met with such universal approval that Slingsby was carried from the hails of justice to his residence on the shoulders of the people. The impression prevails that some one desirous of securing the position of postmaster, which Mr. Slingsby has filled for some time past, originated the scandal, hoping for a change. The verdict of Justice Lawrence seems to meet the general approval of the people of Casselton.

### Stabbing Affair—Carriage Accident—A Wife-Beater in Court.

LOS ANGELES, August 221.—An altercation occurred at Santa Monica Saturday between G. Scammon, of this city, and W. H. Gayner, of Santa Monica, in which the former gave the latter a few gashes with a knife upon the leg and face. None of the wounds are of a serious character. Scammon was arrested and conducted to the office of Justice Boyce, who released him on bail to appear for examination on a charge of assault with a deadly weapon.

Sunday afternoon Max Newmark and wife, of Compton, were out enjoying a ride on the roads, above Old Santa Monica, leading to the bee ranches. They were accompanied by Mrs. Mallette, Mrs. Dillon and Miss Carpenter. While driving along about 6 P.M. the buggy was suddenly overturned and all were thrown to the ground. They were all badly scratched and bruised, but the saddest part of the whole affair was the injuries received by Mrs. Mallette. Her left arm was broken and her jaw badly fractured.

In the trial of Groben for wife-beating yesterday for yesterday Mrs. Groben denied all the charges she has ever made against her husband, and contradicted herself in many ways. The jury failed to agree, six standing for acquittal and six for conviction.

Santa Rosa Races.

SANTA ROSA, August 221.—The fourth annual meeting of the Sonoma Agricultural Park Association opened at the grounds today, to continue through the remainder of the week. The races are exclusively for trotters and pacers, no entries for running horses having offered. The attendance to-day was fair, the largest portion being from San Francisco and other places. the largest portion being from San Francisco and other places. First came a trotting race for two-year-olds, free for all, mile heats, best two in three, for a purse of $200—$120 to the first, $60 to the second, $20 to the third. Ideal, Clara Patterson and Mayday started, two being withdrawn. The first was a dead heat between Ideal and Mayday in 2:30, Clara distanced. Ideal took the next two heats in 3:05 and 3:04. Mayday was the favorite in the pools. Then came the trotting race free for all that had never beaten 2:35, mile heats, best three in five, for a purse of $400—$240 to the first, $120 to the second, $40 to the third. Johnny Boss and Ralph started. Boss was the favorite. Boes and Ralph broke very badly in going around the first turn, and Johnny won the heat and race in 2:33, distancing the two others. Thursday will be the big day. An extra train will run to accommodate San Francisco, and take them home that night.

Serious Runaway Accident.

MERGED, August 22d.—An Italian fruit and vegetable peddler from the Badger Flat settlement, on the West Side, named Antonio, met with a serious accident here about 11 o'clock this morning. He had disposed of his load and started home, and after passing the El Capitan Hotel the hit came out of the mouth of one of his horses, when the team commenced to run. Not knowing what was the matter, Antonio pulled hard upon the lines, causing the team to run in a circle, and finally the horses broke across the railroad track, and on striking the rails threw the unfortunate man out, his head striking the rail of the track and tearing his scalp from the skull. He now lies at the Eagle Hotel in a precarious condition, though his skull does not seem to be fractured.

Result of Carelessly Handling a Pistol.

SMARTSVILLE, August 22d.—While Gus Moore was engaged in loading a pistol in the presence of his wife and children to-day, it was accidentally discharged, one bullet entering his thigh, inflicting a severe wound. Two others exploded a large can of powder, setting fire to his clothes and burning him and a six-year-old boy very severely.

Tragedy in Tulare County.

VISALIA, August 22d.—Ben Harris (colored) about 1 o'clock shot and mortally wounded his wife a mile north of town, killed a step-daughter aged 14 years, and struck in the forehead another step-daughter aged 10, but the child had hold of the handle of the ax and was too close to receive more than a slight wound in the forehead. He made his escape before the news reached town. Twenty or thirty men are on his trail and he may be caught before morning.

School-House Burned—Fire in a Show-
Window.

FRESNO, August 22d.—The public school-
house at the California Lumber Company's mill was destroyed by fire on the 17th. The fire is supposed to have been set by one of the students—a half-breed Indian girl.

A lamp exploded in the show-window of Maxe & Faber's store, in the Denahoe block, last evening, and destroyed the contents of the window before it was extinguished. The flames gained such headway that at one time it was thought a general conflagration would ensue. The loss is about $100.

Suicide of a Lunatic.

NAPA, August 22d.—George Alexander, aged 35 years, a patient at the Iosane Asylum, last night committed suicide by cutting his throat with a butcher knife.

Robbery on the Highway.

ORLAND, August 22d.—At about 8 o'clock last night the brewery-man of Germantown, while on his way from Riceville to this place, was knocked out of his wagon and robbed of twenty-eight dollars in money. There is no clue to the robbers, but they are supposed to have been tramps.

Sentence of the Tumor Fraud.

SAN DIEGO, August 22d.—Mrs. Dr. Patterson, the spiritualistic "tumor snatcher," was yesterday sentenced to pay a fine of $225 and serve six months in the County Jail.

A Fair Chance of Life.

FRESNO, August 22d.—Hensley, who was shot on Friday by Walter Brown, has so far rallied that his recovery is very probable. Brown was released on bail.

Sentence of a Forger.

NEVADA, August 22d.—In the Superior Court to-day Fred, Hinckley, who pleaded guilty Saturday to a charge of forgery, was sentenced to three years' imprisonment in the State Prison at Folsom.

Mono County Republicans.

BODIE, August 22d.—The Republican County Convention met to-day and elected the following delegates to the State Convention: M. P. Wiggen, H. Z. Osborne, N. S. Warren, James E. Goodall, T. A. Stephens, John Lynch. The following county ticket was nominated: Sheriff, James Showers; County Clerk, H. E. Battin; Assessor, J. B. Marshall; Treasurer, W. T. Elliott; Superintendent of Public Instruction, Mrs. C. W. Sullivan. A committee was appointed to confer with Inyo county relative to Assemblies.

PACIFIC COAST.
A Fall and Hurt.
A Fall and Hurt.
Pork Townsend, August 23.—A man named Doyle, second mate on the steamer Mississippi, fell from between decks to the lower hold of that vessel while discharging freight here, and was badly injured. He was taken to the Marine Hospital for treatment.

The Queen.
SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 23.—The steamer Queen of the Pacific will discharge at dan Louis Obispo about seven hundred tons of railroad iron. She is expected to arrive here about the 30th inst.

Murdered Three.
VISALIA, Cala., Aug. 23.—B. F. Harris, a colored man, living near here, shot and mortally wounded his wife, killed a step-daughter 14 years old, and seriously wounded another step-daughter, aged 10, with an axe. Harris escaped before rows of the tragedy reached town. Thirty men are in hot pursuit of the murderer.

Political Platform.
TUCSON, Aug. 23.—The following is a synopsis of the Republican platform adopted today at the Republican Territorial Convention: It declares allegiance to the national Republican platform of 1880; holds that all railroad and other corporations should be subject to the people through the Legislature; declares in favor of maintaining free public instruction; holds appropriations for the support of hostile Indians is a great wrong, and that hostile tribes should not be kept, fed and supported by the public treasury, and is in favor of disearning them; it declares against Chinese immigration and a free system of public offices; it claims that reorganization of the judicial system is necessary; demands that the Territorial and Federal Legislature should be used to discourage mining litigation, and to render mining titles more secure; declares in favor of free and unlimited coinage of silver upon the same terms and under the same regulations as gold.

FREESNO, Aug. 23.—Ben. Harris, the negro who murdered his wife and children near Visalia yesterday afternoon, and is now supposed to be making his way north along the foothills, is armed with a shotgun.

A man killed.

SAN DIEGO, Cal., Aug. 23.—News was received by the Sheriff this morning of the murder of Dan. B. Argailar on Monday, near his home in Guaty Valley, about fifty miles from this city. There was a gunshot wound in the right side, and another in the head. The body was found lying near the forks of the roads. Deceased is an old resident of the county, and highly respected.

Funeral Services.

SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 23.—The funeral of the late B. B. Redding took place this afternoon at the First Congregational Church. A large delegation was present from the Central Pacific Railroad Company's offices, the Academy of Sciences, and Regents of the State University. The services were attended by a very large number of friends and acquaintances of the deceased.

Wheat and Barley.

Wheat is firmer and more in demand, at $1.68@1.70; barley, feed, is firmer, at $1.28@1.30 for spot, and $1.02@1.02% for August.

The Kewanee (Ill.) bank-robber has been captured.
The Cliff House at Newport, R. I., was burned Friday night.
The Atlantic and Pacific has reached a point 365 miles west of Albuquerque.
There were thirty-three new cases of yellow fever at Brownsville Saturday.
The Republicans of the Second Illinois District have nominated J. R. Boies for Congress.
Coker, the negro, who outraged and murdered a white woman at Montgomery, Ala., has been lynched.
San Angelos and Ben Ficklin, Tex., are under water. Great damage has been done to property, and at least forty lives have been lost.
The house of Lyman Ware, at Walpole Plains, Mass., was burned Friday night. Two young men, George L. Ware and Calvin Gay, were burned to death.
Mrs. Maggie Copeland was brutally murdered Saturday near Kewanee, Ill., by some person unknown, who entered the house, knocked her down with a board, shot her twice through the body and crushed in her head with a club.
The regular passenger train leaving Saratoga, N. Y., at 8:30 Saturday afternoon was run into by the local train between Waterford and Callston. A few passengers were injured by the concussion, including Ten Eyck, the oarsman.
A propeller was burned Tuesday night abreast of North Fox island, Lake Michigan. All hands were saved. She was an old vessel, plying between Chicago and Buffalo, in the grain trade. The loss is estimated at $25,000; insurance unknown.
General Singleton publishes a letter to the voters of the Twelfth Illinois Congressional District, explaining and vindicating his independent candidacy, but though tacitly indorsed by the Greenback and Republican conventions, he makes no allusion to them, or any promises as to his independent action in Congress. The letter is rather directed to a vindication of his Democracy in bolting the regular nomination.
A member of the Chinese Legation visited the State Department at Washington Saturday and informed Acting Secretary Davis that a party of Chinese play-actors from Panama had been denied permission to land at San Francisco. Secretary Davis called upon Secretary Folger in reference to the matter, and the result was that Secretary Folger
Palamis had been denied permission to land at San Francisco. Secretary Davis called upon Secretary Folger in reference to the matter, and the result was that Secretary Folger telegraphed the Collector of Customs at San Francisco that the department did not regard play-actors as laborers within the meaning of the Chinese Act, and suggested that the facts in the case might bring it within the late decision of Judge Field that the law did not apply to Chinese who had shipped before the passage of the act.

FOREIGN.

In a single province of the Philippine islands 4,000 have died of cholera.

A decisive battle is expected to take place at Zagazig. The Egyptians lost 4,000 men in the recent battle. It is reported that Arabi is losing ground in the interior. Two thousand Albanians have been enlisted for service in hospitals. De Lesseps still thinks Arabi is a patriot, and prophesies British disaster. Dufferin adheres to his policy that Turkish troops shall only land at Rosetta, Damietta and Aboukir. General Wolseley has applied for more troops.

PACIFIC COAST.

Three lepers have been found in Los Angeles.

There is no truth in the report of a revolution in Sonora.

Burns, Deputy Sheriff of Pascal, N. M., was shot at Silver City Saturday.

Thomas Williams was killed and three other miners were badly wounded by a cave in a Grass Valley mine Saturday.

The City Marshal of Nevada City has issued a notice to several hangers on at houses of bad repute to leave town on Monday or suffer the consequences. Among those thus notified are two or three parties who have been employed as piano-players.

The negro Harris, who murdered his family on Tuesday last, was found two and a half miles north of Visalia Saturday, at noon, and while attempting to escape he was shot by John Dice fatally. He had come to the house where he committed the murders during the night and was tracked to the place of rendezvous and killed. He will be buried in grave.

A dispatch from San Rafael says: The reported prize fight at Saucelito is a hoax. The only foundation for such a report is that two antiquated citizens of that burg named Chas, Oram and George Emerson, who have spent most of their time in drinking and standing the saloons off for their gin, were yesterday prevailed upon by a prominent member of the Saucelito Lying Club to put on the gloves and have a friendly set-to for the drinks.

Two daughters of Farmer Wm. A. King were drowned while bathing near St. Paul, Minn., on the 19th.

SEVERAL trainmen were injured by a collision on the Pennsylvania Central, near Bristol, Pa., on the 20th.

Some practical jokers told a young man named Edward Waterman, at Milwaukee, Wis., that the water off the breakwater was fourteen feet deep, inducing him to dive. The water being but three feet, the diver's neck was broken and death ensued immediately.

An Ohio & Mississippi express train broke in two, near Olney, Ill., the other night, and when the engine was reversed the detached sleepers dashed into the day coach and demolished it. J. R. Challen, aged 10, was killed; Miss B. Reynolds, of Vincennes, Ind., was seriously injured and several others were cut and bruised.

A PARTY of imported miners sent to extinguish the fire in the Astor mine, near Lonaconing, Md., were attacked by a large body of strikers and driven back to their barracks. Firearms were used freely on both sides, but so far as learned no one was injured.

JAMES BIRD, a cooper, who had just separated from his wife, sought her at the residence of her sister, in Gratiot, Wis., on the 21st, and after saying they ought at least to be friends drew a revolver and shot her twice, inflicting serious wounds. He then turned the weapon on himself, with probably fatal effect.

C. W. WARD, colored, was hanged at San Antonia, Texas, Aug. 21, for a criminal assault upon Dora Ellerman, a young German girl.

The bodies of three unknown men, supposed to have been murdered, were found in a skiff floating down the river near Uniontown, Ky., on the 21st.

The body of an unknown man killed by the cars near Boston, Mass., is believed to be that of Peter La Grassa, once a celebrated operatic tenor.

JAMES McINTYRE, of Bradford, Pa., a State Senator, was drowned while bathing in the surf at West Brighton, N. Y., the other day.

An informal meeting of the Cabinet was held at President Arthur's house in New York on the 21st. All the members, except Secretary Teller and Postmaster-General Howe, were present. There was no business transacted, and the session was more of a social one than otherwise. The cause of the meeting, as explained by Secretary Folger and Attorney-General Brewster, was that as Secretaries Lincoln, Chandler and Folger and the President were in New York, Secretary Frelinghuysen in Newark and Attorney-General Brewster at Long Branch, it was thought best to meet and inquire whether anything in any of the departments required joint action. Nothing of this nature came before the meeting.

An enterprising individual named B. D. Ply, stationed at Boody, Ill., has been sending out circulars to Western farmers offering for sale a new variety of wheat so superior in quality that he is willing to trust the farmers until they have sown and gathered the grain, and then if it does not yield a third more than other kinds of wheat, he asks no pay. In carrying out this benevolent scheme he finds it necessary to call upon his beneficiaries to send by mail $1 to prepay the express charges on the large bags of seed wheat. The dollar has, in many cases, been sent, but no wheat came, and the victims have complained to the Post-office Department, which can do nothing but direct the return to the senders of all money orders and registered letters, having no power to interfere with his ordinary sealed letters.

In Choctaw County, Ala., the other day, a mob hanged a negro named Jack Turner, who was charged with being the ringleader of a plot to murder white people.

CHARLES McMAHON, a wealthy farmer residing near Mount Pulaski, Ill., and two of his laborers, named John Carlock and Solomon Malheny, were literally butchered by unknown men, the other night, the crime remaining undiscovered for two days. The house was thoroughly ransacked for valuables.

Two sections of a circus train crashed together near New Burnside, Ill., on the 20th. Four men were killed in a car containing eighty sleeping showmen, and at least twelve others were seriously injured.

FOUR enlisted men of the Ninth Infantry, stationed at Fort Omaha, Nebr., went on a spree the other day and amused themselves by robbing citizen of $6. This proved so easy a task that the team of Mr. Woolsey was stopped on the highway with a demand for money. The reply was a bullet which killed Emanuel K. Shrader. His companions, Dawson, Flintwell, and McDonald, are in jail.

An express on the Boston, Concord & Montreal Railroad went down an embankment near Woo dville, N. H., on the 21st. By a miracle, nobody was seriously injured, though several were severely hurt and the cars and locomotive were badly damaged. Train-wreckers had fastened a chain to the rails.

RIOTERS disturbed a church festival in Cleveland, Ohio, on the 21st. Knives, pistols and clubs were freely used. Moses Gooley was shot and killed, a woman was fatally stabbed, and several persons were seriously wounded.

OFFICIAL advices from Brownsville, Texas, report thirty-five new cases of yellow fever and one death on the 21st.

The Mayor and fifty-five Councilmen of Reading, Pa., have been arrested on an indictment for not keeping the streets clean.

A STAGE was robbed of $5,000 near Globe, Ariz., on the 20th. Andrew Hall, the messenger, was killed.

A BROKEN rail wrecked a Wabash freight train, near Logansport, Ind., the other night. J. A. Depler and Harris Lin-

A BOILER explosion demolished a saw-mill at Sullivan, Ind., the other afternoon. Irvin Bailey, George Morris, and George Inglehart were fatally injured.

The Maryland Knights of Labor have ordered the Cumberland miners to resume work on the best terms they can make. The strikers at Wilkesbarre, Pa., have accepted former rates. Fifteen hundred looms are in operation at the Harmony Mills, Cohoes, N. Y.

A SUDDEN rise in the Rio Grande carried away part of the Mexican National bridge at Laredo and swept off some rails of the International road.

ROBERT AIKEN, a clerk, was fatally shot by a hunter named Gibbon, at Rock Creek, Albany County, Wyo., the other evening. The murderer was informally hanged.

JAMES SUMMERS, a brakeman or the Kentucky Central, was instantly killed while coupling cars near Paris on the 23d. The cause was a projecting timber, crushing his head against a box-car in front.

GEORGE P. KING was killed and his sister, Ella, probably fatally injured by a runaway horse near Freeman, Ill., on the 22d.

Two children of Henry Butler, of Bonnieville, Ky., quarreled about an apple the other day. Hayes, aged six years, savagely attacked his sister Retta, aged 8, with a knife, inflicting wounds which will probably cause her death.

A DISPATCH from Henrietta, Texas, says Bessie Gordon and Jennie Smith, young ladies, were drowned in the Little Wichita the other evening.

THE Adirondack Hotel, the Nolette House, and thirty stores and dwellings on Main street, Reeseville, N. Y., burned on the 23d. Loss, $100,000. The iron works at Syracuse, N. Y., were damaged to the extent of $200,000 on the 22d. Three hundred men were thrown out of work.

BEN HARRIS, a negro living near Visualia, Cal., killed his wife and one stepdaughter and seriously injured another, Aug. 23. A party of lynchers went after the murderer.

RYMER, who fatally stabbed Wm. McGarvey at Fort Lyon, Colo., was taken from jail at West Las Animas on the night of the 20th and hanged by a mob of masked men, supposed to be soldiers from the fort.

PROF. G. BROWN, of El Paso, Texas, was fatally stabbed in an encounter with a man named Bostwick, father of a pupil whom he had punished.

PACIFIC COAST.
San Francisco, August 26.—John Caddington, associated since 1863 with Will S. Green, in conducting the Colusa Sun, died of consumption at Oakland to-day. He was a native of Fishkill, N. Y., aged 43.

San Francisco, August 26.—A Visalia dispatch says Ben Harris, the negro who murdered his family last Thursday, was found near town to-day and in attempting to escape he was shot dead.

San Francisco, August 29.—A Red Bluff dispatch says: The Sierra lumber company's planning mill, sash and door factory burned at six a.m. Also the dry house and a large amount of lumber. The loss is very heavy.

San Francisco, Cal., August 26.—The Republican primaries here to-day were hotly contested. There were several tickets in the field and a large vote polled, all parties apparently taking a hand. Reports from the interior, so far as received this evening, show that the county conventions are very generally disposed to enforce the Sunday law.

El Paso, August 26.—In the habeas corpus case of the Texas Pacific conductor, W. A. Baird, for the rape of Mary Meade, Judge Fulvey to-day rendered his decision, which was virtually an affirmation of that of Justice Johnson in the preliminary examination. The prisoner was remanded to jail without bail. Great interest has been taken in this case, and the railroad companies, together with the Pullman Car Company, have prosecuted the case most vigorously, though the defendant had an able counsel. The defense has appealed to the Supreme Court.

San Francisco, August 26.—Louis A. Garnett and John Hewston, Jr., have each brought a label suit in the sum of $100,000 against F. F. Low, president of the Anglo-California bank, on the ground that on the day of the failure of the Bank of California the defendant said that during the preceding night the bullion in the San Francisco Refinery, under the charge of Garnett and Hewston, and belonging to depositors, to the value of $600,000 or $700,000, was feloniously taken to the mint and sold and that W. C. Ralston, President of the Bank of California, was also Vice-President of the refinery, of which Garnett was Manager and Hewston Superintendent, and that most of the bullion belonged to Flood and O'Brien or to mining companies which they controlled.
GUAYMAS, August 26.—Three hundred more troops have just arrived on the transportation steamer, Mexico, and will immediately be sent to the district of Sahuaripa to act in conjunction with a large force under Gen. Reyes, who is now operating there. This makes the federal force in the State including the three hundred impressed prisoners, over one thousand. The National Guard in the field is upward of five hundred. A courier is expected daily from the scenes of the late depredations which are on the Rio Chico in the Alamos and Sahuaripa district.

—Twelve Chinamen were landed at New York, Monday, by a steamer from Havana. The fact was learned, on inquiry, that the anti-Chinese immigration law, passed by Congress May 6, does not go into effect until August 5.

—In the United States House, the bill to place General Grant on the retired list of the army, with the rank and pay of General, was referred to the Committee on Military Affairs, where it will rest until next Winter, at least.

—The Secretary of the Interior decides the Desert Land Act requires more than mere conducting of water upon land to which title is sought. Irrigation must thoroughly prepare the land for the production of an agricultural crop.

—The Utica (N. Y.) Observer says: There are very few men in Congress, irrespective of parties, who will not confess that Kentucky leads all other States in the ability, eloquence and general brilliancy of her Congressional representation.

—South Carolina democrats have nominated the following ticket: For Governor, Hugh S. Thompson; for Treasurer, S. P. Richardson; for Supt. Education; Rev. Ellison Capers; for Adjutant and Inspector General, Gen. A. M. Manigault.

—Although the war ended seventeen years ago, the republican party is determined to keep up the war taxes in time of peace, as, rice, 105 per cent.; window-glass, 80 per cent.; hollow-ware, 82 per cent.; woolen goods, from 58 to 140 per cent., etc.

—A movement has been set on foot for an investigation of the affairs of the Soldiers' Home at Hampton, Va. Among the charges brought against the Superintendent is that of his issuing wooden chips being only receivable at the Home store and beer saloon, where exorbitant prices are charged.

—The National Mining Exposition opened at Denver Tuesday. Nearly every Western State is represented. Military from Leadville and other towns of the State participated in the opening exercises. The city is crowded with strangers. Hon. William D. Kelley, of Pensylvania, made the opening address.

Before learning of the action of the two Houses in passing the River and Harbor Bill over the President's veto, a large number of Chicago business men sent the President a dispatch, congratulating him on his firm and decided course in refusing his assent to the measure, which they regarded as dangerous legislation.

Wednesday, as a freight train was passing through Walton, Ky., John Richy came out of a saloon and fired two shots from a revolver at the conductor and two brakeman sitting on top of the caboose. One of the balls struck John R. Carson, one of the brakemen, in the head inflicting a fatal wound. Richy was arrested.
—In Monroe county, this State, Bish Emberton and Dick Speakman went to the residence of Mr. Garrett, during his absence in Tennessee, and brutally outraged his wife. Garrett's father summoned the neighbors and captured the ravishers. They were identified by their victim, and started for the Barren county jail under guard, but were overtaken by a mob and hung.

—The following is the ticket selected by the Indiana democrats in convention at Indianopolis Wednesday: For Secretary of State, Wm. D. Myers; for Auditor, Jas. H. Rice; for State Treasurer, Jno. J. Cooper; for Attorney General, Hon. Francis T. Hord; for Clerk of Supreme Court, S. C. Sheerin; for Supt. Public Instruction, Jno. W. Halcombe; for Supreme Judge, Geo. J. Howk.

—In the British House of Lords, Monday, amendments to the effect that a landlord could refuse his consent to tenants applying for relief under the bill, in cases where he believed in the tenant's ability to pay, and that if a tenant who had taken advantage of the Arrears Bill, subsequently sold his farm, the landlord should be able to recover out of the sum of the tenant right the amount he had been deprived of by the action of the bill.

—The President's veto of the River and Harbor Bill availed nothing, since both houses Wednesday passed the aggregation of jobbery over his veto and the bill is a law. The appropriations for the Mississippi river and the Potomac flats were among the items which have the stamp of legitimacy. The greater portion of the enormous draft on the Treasury presents a sickening array of unmitigated jobbery, which is a disgrace to the Fortv-seventh Congress.

—There is very little prospect for the pardon of Sergeant Mason, the would-be assassin of Guiteau, during the term of the present administration, unless the President should act contrary to the advice of the Attorney General. Mr. Brewster says that Mason's conduct was not only in violation of law, but prejudicial to good discipline, which is the main element of strength in the army. The Attorney General has no intention of recommending Mason's pardon.

CRIMES AND CABALITIES.
An
An attempt was made to assassinate a police magistrate in Frederickton, N. B., the other morning. Sergeant Vandyne was shot in the arm while arresting a suspected person named Lee.

AMELIA COOK, aged 24, daughter of a shrewtie (La.) merchant, died suddenly the other day from the effects of too much morphine.

ROBERT ROCK was killed and John McLester was seriously injured by the explosion of a boiler at Gosport, Ind., Aug. 1.

E. B. WHEELER and Walter Preston, prominent young attorneys at Seymour, Texas, quarreled about the ownership of a book the other day. Pistols were resorted to and Preston was killed.

In a free fight at McKinney, Texas, the other night, one negro was shot dead and others were wounded. A Cherokee half-breed named Joe led the shooters and managed to escape.

JAMES BROWN, a farmer, was killed by lightning near Belknap, Iowa, Aug. 1.

J. W. CLOYDE, the colored route agent in jail at Charleston, S. C., on a charge of robbing the mails, killed himself the other night.

In an altercation between Detective Wm. Walsh and J. Healy, at New Orleans, Aug. 1, the former was fatally shot. Healy says he acted in self-defense.

FOUR chirus elephants escaped from their keepers in Troy, N. Y., Aug. 2. Patrick Ryan and wife were knocked down, the former receiving fatal injuries. Several other persons were hurt. One of the animals charged a bloom of red-hot iron in a rolling-mill.

BISHOP EMBERTON and Richard Speakman, who so brutally assaulted Mrs. J. B. Garrett, of Tompkinsville, Ky., a few days ago, were lynched by a mob, Aug. 1, while on the way to Glasgow under a guard of fifteen men.

As a freight train was passing through Walton, Ky., Aug. 1, John Richy fired two shots from a revolver at the conductor and two brakemen sitting on the top of the caboose. One of the balls struck John R. Carson, brakeman, in the head, inflicting a fatal wound. Richy was arrested.

The engine and mail car of a Union Pacific train went through a burned bridge spanning Granite Creek, between Glen Elder and Cawker City, Kans., Aug. 3. Britton Craft, engineer, and C. McGee, fireman, were fatally injured and died soon after. Mahaffy, express messenger, and Wentworth and Chamberlain, mail agents, were hurt, but not dangerously. The passenger coaches remained on the track. There is a curve and cut near the bridge, and the engineer could not see the fire in time to stop the train.

W. H. Yeates was hanged at Chatham, Va., Aug. 4, for the murder of P. E. Adkerson. Two negroes mounted the scaffold in Florida on the same day: Merrick Jackson, at Fernandina, and Harrison Carter, at Jacksville.

At Indianapolis, the other evening, two colored boys, Charles Bly and James Jones, engaged in a friendly sparring match. Bly was struck in the stomach and expired before medical aid could be secured.

There was a fight between rustlers and citizens in Phoenix, Cal., the other day. Three cowboys were captured, one killed and one badly wounded. As the prisoners were being taken an attempt was made to lynch them. Officers came to the rescue and removed them to the jail.

A WILD coal train collided with cars standing on the track near Oil City, Pa., Aug. 4. Six miners were killed and a number seriously injured.

Mrs. Ford, Martin Johnson, Wm. Bosum, and John Fehrerman were drowned in South Park Lake, Chicago, Aug. 4. A pleasure boat upset.

bob-wilson-memphis-1882-10-01.A1:
A BLACK SHOOTER.
A Young Negro Thief Shoots a Well-Known Grocer with Probably Fatal Effect.
The Criminal Captured After a Long Chase by Captain Hackett and Officer Jackson.
Last night in the neighborhood of 9 o'clock an event occurred which will in all likelihood furnish a first-class tragedy. Mr. Frank B. Russell, who keeps the large grocery on the corner of Hernando and Vance, was the possible victim. Night before last, burglaries broke into the grocery and stole some lard, hama, cigars, etc. Mr. Russell was consequently on the alert to get some clue to the thief. Last night about 9 o'clock a negro by the name of Robert Wilson was seen by Mr. Russell directly in front of the grocery making way with a bucket of lard, which he had obtained in the rear of the store. The negro, when he saw that Mr. Russell had discovered him, started away in a full run. The grocer hurriedly seized his pistol and started after him. The thief had only run a short distance when Russell fired, striking him in the calf of the leg and inflicting a flesh wound. The negro sumbled and fell; but before he could rise and run Russell reached him and took him prisoner.

The negro seemed to be pretty painfully wounded; and it is probable that he tried to enhance his condition so as to throw his capturer off his guard. At any rate Mr. Russell took him into the drug store of W.B. Safford, 189 Hernando store, to have his wound dressed. Arrived here, Russell indiscreetly laid his pistol on the counter to attend to the negro's wounds. The latter, however, had been shamming. His wound was not at all what he had made it out to be. Hardly had the weapon been placed upon the counter ere he seized it. Russell seeing his movement grappled with him, and a scuffle ensued, in the course of which the grocer was shot twice. The first shot took effect in his abdomen and the second in the left breast. The negro disengaged himself from Mr. Russell, who fell to the floor exhausted. The murderer took to his heels and rapidly ran away in the darkness of the night. No one pursued him at the time, as the dangerous condition of the wounded man monopolized the attention of the druggist. Dr.F.L. Sim was quickly sent for, and word was telephoned to the police station of the occurrence. Capt. Hackett and Chief Davis were soon on the scene. The chief telegraphed to Charlie Saltmarsh for a horse, which was sent him, and he and the captain started off on the trail of the negro. When last heard from the latter was out on Rayburn avenue, and the chief was in hot pursuit. Owing to the fact that he was wounded, his escape is very improbable.

The wounds received by Mr. Russell were thought by Dr. Sim to be fatal. The wounded man was carried to his residence where everything was done to relieve him. His wife and children were very much unnerved.

LATEST DETAILS.

About 1 o'clock this morning Capt. Hackett and Officer Jackson brought in a negro lad of nineteen, named Robert Wilson, together with a negro named Wm. Hunt. An APPEAL reporter met Capt. Hackett at the stationhouse, and from him obtained an account of the capture.

"When I went down there," said the captain, "I sent Chastaine and Plummer out immediately to overhaul the houses in the neighborhood. I thought that if Wilson was dangerously wounded he would be hiding in the neighborhood. Finding out that he had fled, we went to Fort Pickering, searched there and on Rayburn avenue, but could find no trace. I met a friend who told me that Wilson's woman was at church. I went after her, and she took me to the house on Pontotoc, between Main and Front, where Wilson lives. We went in and found him in bed. Under the bed were two pistols, which we brought with us."

One of the pistols is a self-cocking Colt, from which one bullet was out. This is the pistol that belonged to Russell. The other pistol, which is much smaller, is a Colt new thirty-two caliber; four out of its five barrels were empty. The pistols shed a different light on the story, and show that Wilson was himself armed and that he shot Russell with his own pistol, and probably picked up the pistol from the counter from motives of self-protection.

An examination of the darkey at the stationhouse showed that he had been wounded as the officers expected. Finding himself cornered, he confessed that he was stealing some lard and that a man shot him in the rear. This, of course, fixes the crime on him. Wm. Hunt, who was brought in with him by the officers, is a "pal" of his. They are both regular thieves, and there is no question but that they are the parties who robbed Russell the night before. At last accounts the wounded man was dying.

THE precarious condition of Mr. Frank B. Russell, the Vance street grocer, renders it more than probable that within a few hours he will be no more. Indeed, his spirit may already have left its earthly tenement for the brighter world. Slain by the merciless hand of a thievish, bloodthirsty villain, who went into Mr. Russell's grocery to rob, and prepared to kill, the soundrel now languishes in the city prison, trembles with fear lest an outraged people should take his case in hand and make short shrift of it. Too many of this class roam at large for the good of the community. Every few days it becomes necessary to detail some rascally work of the despicable class, to which Wilson be longs. THE MURDERER.
Death of Mr. Russell and a Mob Demand for Wilson the Murderer.
About seven o'clock yesterday evening death came to the relief of Mr. Frank B. Russell. A post mortem examination made by Drs. Sims and Rogers showed that the ball which caused his death had entered the bowels and severed the intestines in half a dozen places, making recovery an absolute impossibility from the moment the ball entered. When the news of his death spread about the neighborhood a crowd began gathering and an hour after the sidewalk in front of the house on Hernando street near Vance was lined with a hundred or more men, whose manner boded no good for the vile scoundrel, to whom the catastrophe was due.

Between 1 and 2 o'clock this morning about two hundred persons collected in front of the county jail, and a number of them, who were masked, advanced to the gate and demanded the keys. The jailer, Mr. William Quinn, refused to hand them over, and after a short while spent in parley the crowd dispersed for want of a leader. The movement had been desultory and wholly unorganized, and for this reason did not succeed. A crowd who collected Saturday night, with the same purpose in view, concluded it would be unwise to hang the fellow, as Mr. Russell's wounds had not then ended his life.

It is a lucky thing for the murderer that he was protected by the strong walls of the jail, for, had he been allowed to remain in the insecure stationhouse, his carcass would by this time adorn a lamp post.

JUDGE LYNCH.

CHARLOTTEVILLE, Va., Oct. 2.—James Rhodes, the murderer of the Massie family, was taken out of jail last night by a body of armed men and hung to a tree. He confessed that he was Rhodes, and said his mother and brother Lee did not do any of the killing.

CHARLOTTEVILLE, Va., Oct. 2.—The lynchers of James Rhodes, last evening, numbered about forty. It is thought they had a hundred or more confederates in town. They compelled the jailor to surrender the keys of the jail, and the guards were overpowered. Rhodes on discovering their object gave a loud cry, heard at a consider able distance. A crowd of citizens followed the lynchers. They were halted by guards on the highway about fifty yards from the tree on which Rhodes was hanged. He admitted he was James Rhodes, and said that his brother in jail and his mother took no part in the murder. He begged for fifteen minutes, promising to tell about the murder. The lynchers seemed to fear interference, and urged the execution. The attorney for the commonwealth made an appeal to have the law take its course, but was warned off on peril of his life. In 1877 Rhodes, a boy then, attempted to poison his mother and all the family. He fled to Tennessee, where, in the same year he committed three felonies for which he was convicted. He escaped the penitentiary in December, 1881. Besides murdering the Massies in March last, he is charged with arson and robbery committed in East Tennessee. His body was cut down this morning by order of the commonwealth's attorney. A grand jury is ordered for to-morrow to investigate. This is county court day and the excitement is great.

LACKED THE NECESSARY SAND.

MEMPHIS, Tenn., Oct. 2.—At a late hour last night a crowd of 250 went to the county jail and demanded Bob. Wilson, a negro who Thursday night shot Frank Russell, who died from the effects last night. The jailor refused to comply with the demands of the mob. The crowd loitered about the jail for an hour, but made no demonstration further than mentioned. They evidently were in need of a leader. No more trouble is anticipated, as the jail is a strong one and the officers are on the alert.

Owen Sound, Sept. 12.—The Tug Ann Long arrived here this a. m., having on board the following bodies of those lost off the ill-fated steamer Asia: John McDougal, purser; F. H. RAILROAD ACCIDENTS.

MEMPHIS, TENN., Oct. 2.—The west bound passenger train on the Memphis & Charleston road met with an accident last night near Madison, Ala., 203 miles west of Memphis. One passenger coach and a sleeper were thrown from the track, and several passengers received injuries. The sleeping car conductor is reported to have a leg broken. Mr. and Mrs. Sam. Tate, of Little Rock, were slightly injured; also, Clarence P. Hunt, of this city. A broken rail caused the accident. The train was delayed 3 hours.

ATLANTA, 2 p. m.—Western and Atlantic passenger train this morning struck Alice Simmons and her son, aged 6 years, killing her instantly and knocking the boy a distance of fifty feet. The boy cannot recover.

LAWYER'S FEUD.

St. Louis, Oct. 2.—W. H. Clapton, a well known attorney and Democratic politician, attempted to cowhide ex-United States Senator Jewett and his partner, Edward C. Smith, lawyers, in their office between one and two o'clock this afternoon. Clapton attacked Jewett while the latter was talking with a lady client, struck him in the face, and while attempting to repeat the blow, Smith was struck. A pistol was then drawn, but before damage was done the parties were separated. The reason for the assault was that this morning Jewett filed a petition in the court of appeals preferring charges against Clapton and asking for his disbarment. The feud grew out of some old suits over property in which all the parties were interested as attorneys. Each side charge the other with underhand practices.

A STOUT ROPE
In Store for Robert Wilson, the Negro Who Murdered Frank Russell, on Vance Street.
Judge Horrigan Overrules the Motion for a New Trial and Sentences Him to Hang.
The motion for a new trial in the case of the State as. Robert Wilson was argued before Judge Horrigan, in the Criminal Court, yesterday, by Col. Richardson and Mr. J. M. Harris; the culprit's attorney. It will be remembered that Wilson was tried last Monday in the Criminal Court for murdering Mr. Frank B. Russell on the 28th day of September last, and convicted of murder in the first degree. The jury, which was composed of nine white men and three colored men, was out only about thirty minutes. The two grounds raised on for a new trial by his counsel and presented to the court yesterday were (1) misconduct on the part of the jury trying his cause; and (2) that the evidence was not sufficient to warrant a conviction.

AS TO THE FIRST GROUND
the jury were summoned back and examined separately, and the examination disclosed no misconduct on their part, each testifying that he had rendered his verdict on the law and the evidence, and that it accorded with his conscience. That the first ballot in the jury-room resulted in eleven for conviction of murder in the first degree, and one, who said he was not fully agreed as to whether the judge charged the jury that Russell had a right to arrest Wilson; but after the dissenting juror had the charge of the Court on this point, he voted also for murder in the first degree. As to the second ground, Judge Horrigan said that he was perfectly satisfied that the evidence was full and amply sufficient to sustain the verdict of the jury; that he regarded this as

A TERRIBLE MURDER
and one that deserved the severest penalty of the law. That the defendant Wilson, as disclosed by the evidence, first robbed the store of deceased on the night before the murder, and on the night of the murder had returned to the deceased's place of business to get a part of the goods that he was unable to carry away on the night of the robbery. He had gotten a bucket of lard, and was leaving with it, thus committing a second larceny and felony, when discovered by Russell, who arrested him and carried him into the drug store to send for a policeman. While waiting for the arrival of the police, the defendant

CONCEIVED THE IDEA
of escaping even if he had to take the life of his captor to accomplish his desire. This Mr. Russell (who legally had him under arrest, and had over him all the authority that the sherriff would have had he arrested him) tried to prevent, and the defendant premeditatedly and deliberately drew a pistol and shot him, inflicting wounds of which he died; that in all civil-d lands a murder deliberately, premeditatedly and deliberately drew a pistol and shot him, inflicting wounds of which he died; that in all civilis-lands a murder deliberately, premeditatedly perpetrated by a felon under arrest upon his jailer, was held to be of the most aggravated character, for it was striking at the very foundation of justice, and that to take this case he saw

NOTHING IN IT
to warrant a new trial, and he thereupon asked that Wilson be brought "around." Wilson, up to this time, had occupied a seat between his counsel. He is a rather "chunky," heavy-set man, and would weigh about 130 pounds, well built and has the appearance of being strong and active. He left his seat and walked around in front of the judge, but evidently showed signs of being very nervous, and that he fully realized his situation. The Court then asked him

WHAT HE HAD TO SAY
why sentence of death should not be passed upon him, and he remarked that he did not want to be hung. The Court remarked that he had had able counsel, who had defended him with much ability, and that a fair trial had been given him, and thereupon pronounced the sentence of death—to be executed on February 3d next. He will appeal to the April term of the Supreme Court, which will delay his execution until about June, next year.

There are many bad characters in town. In fact, we have as many
There are many bad characters in town. In fact we have as many hoodlums here now as we had three years ago, when we found it necessary to hang two of them by lynch law. It seems that there are many who sympathize with the miscreants who were arrested yesterday. To all such we say—and we are backed up by all the law abiding citizens of Phoenix—that the sooner they make themselves scarce, the better for their worthless carcasses. No more hoodlums will be tolerated in our town, and the men referred to will do well to leave pretty shortly, for they are known and watched. It will only be a few more days until this matter will be carefully looked after by the authorities, and should they fail, the citizens themselves will take care of it. The saloons are filled with men who do nothing for their living, and yet have money to spend. How do they get it? No one knows. Probably by "rolling" some poor drunk who happens to have money in his pocket, or by some other devilry. We endorse the action of our city Marshal in yesterday's fuss, and congratulate ourselves that we were so fortunate as to have such an officer. If Tombstone or Calabasas have any more cowboys to spare let them send them to Phoenix and we will take charge of them.

While the present state of public excitement lasts we omit saying much about the matter, and merely give an outline of the facts.

After careering through the back streets, shooting their pistols and alarming the populace generally, they came down the main street and commenced riding on the sidewalks, pulling pistols on citizens, riding into saloons, and abusing everyone they met. During the short period while they were having their innocent fun, they did not cease to discharge their pistols in all directions, not omitting to shoot into private houses. Henry Garfias, our brave Marshal, being soon notified of the fact, hurriedly called a posse consisting of W. O. O'Neill, Manuel Garcia and H. McDonald, and started to arrest them. The desperados, who were several blocks distant when they noticed their pursuers, wheeled and charged down the street, while Garfias and his brave posse calmly awaited the attack. The foremost of the ruffians opened fire, and a returning shot from Garfias broke his right hand, causing his pistol to drop to the ground. Then commenced a regular fusilade, and the cow boys broke and ran, closely pursued by the posse and returning shot for shot as they ran. On Monroe street one of them fell from his horse and died soon after, having been shot through the head and lungs. The two others kept on until they saw it was impossible to escape when they abandoned their horses and took to the bush, where they were soon captured and marched up and lodged in jail. This has been the first attempt made by the cow boys to "take in" Phoenix, and is very likely to be the last.

The communities in the southern counties have been standing this kind of thing and letting the ruffians get away with them, but up here in Salt River Valley we simple-minded farming folk do not understand these matters properly, and perhaps some may think we were hasty in shooting men who endanger the lives of our wives and daughters and friends while "having a little fun." Such men are dangerous members in any community, and the only safe way is to use the well-known receipt for making "good Indians." Of course there are many men here, of a certain class, who sympathize with these marauders—for Phoenix is not entirely cleansed yet—and we have only to say that even the sympathizers and upholders of such men are not wanted in this peaceful community. To Mr. Henry Garfias and the few men who followed and stood so bravely by him, too much credit can not be given; and we must all feel thankful that during so much promiscuous shooting in crowded streets, no one was hurt, though it is not the fault of the cow-boys that twenty men, women and children are not corpses to day.

FOUR NEGROES KILLED.
Riot at a Political Meeting to Advance the Candidacy of Col. Cash, the Duellist.
LANCASTER, S. C., Sept. 28.—A political meeting was held here yesterday and was addressed by Col. Cash, the Independent and Republican candidate for Congress, who was a short time ago tried for the murder of Judge Shannon, whom he killed in a duel. About the close of the meeting a difficulty arose at the stand between a white Democrat and a colored man, which resulted in the former being wounded in the head by a blow from a stick or a stone. At this time two or three pistol shots were fired near the stand, but no one was hurt. Soon after this a large procession of colored men on horseback came upon the streets, one of the number having a large pistol buckled to his waist. The negro pointed the pistol at a white man and said: "There is the d——d rascal who did the shooting." The white man gave him the lie, and the colored man drew his pistol and fired at the former. Immediately several shots were fired by white men and the colored man fell dead. A number of shots were then fired by white and colored men, and three other colored men were killed and many wounded. The authorities soon succeeded in restoring quiet, which now prevails. It is believed that the trouble is over.

THE MASSACRE.
Seven Negroes Killed and Twenty Wounded—Further Details of the Fight. New York, Oct. 2.—A Richmond dispatch says: Private information received here is to the effect that the political riot at Lancaster, S. C., on Thursday, was much more serious than was represented in the meagre dispatch published the next day. That stated that the number killed was four, and a few wounded. If now turns out that there were seven persons killed and some twenty-one wounded. Col. Cash, who was to address the meeting, had to lock himself up to escape the fury of the whites. A mounted force rode into town and fired over the heads of the rioting whites on the negroes who were engaged with them, killing and wounding the latter. All the stores in the town were closed, and every man was out armed to the teeth. A large quantity of firearms was also sold that day. It is stated, somewhat in justification of the massacre, that the negroes had threatened to burn the town and murder the white people, and that the strongest evidences of the purpose were found in not only their actions but in the material and documents in their possession.

Eurther Details—Narrow Escape of Mr. D. J. Carter, Editor of the Ledger—Negroes Threaten to Renew the Trouble—Cash Keeps his Room Throughout the Riot.

LANCASTER, September 28.—The roit of yesterday originated thus: Col. Cash, after a very turbulent and noisy procession through the streets, was addressing a crowd of about 700 negroes. Mr. Carter, editor of the Ledger, had taken position on the stand as reporter for his paper, and Cash was proxie in his abuse of the Legislature and charged that the planters were cheating the negroes of their earnings.

The negroes were drinking at the stand and were wrought up to high pitch. Cash, it is said, would turn around to Carter and make repeated remarks that he would not vote for him, but his sympathizer. Carter then asked Cash to allow him to reply. Cash said certainly, and remarked that he should have respectful hearing. Carter attempted to reply, but the negroes would not hear him. Cash asked them to be quiet, but it did no good, and Carter and the negroes were getting into a wrankle. Cash left the stand and went direct to his room at the hotel. The negroes
asked them to be quiet, but it did no good, and Carter and the negroes were getting into a wrankle. Cash left the stand and went direct to his room at the hotel. The negroes were dridking and they had a jug of whisky near the stand.

Carter being promised both by Cash and the county chairman a reply still tried to speak, but the negroes crowded so upon the stand that the stand broke down. Thereby being greatly infuriated the crowd took hold of Carter and dragged him off the stand, and he would have been killed had it not been for Albert Clinton and Ed. Saddler and others.

The word came up town that Carter had been shot, but he had only been struck and had not been shot. About this time a drunken negro was misbehaving on Main street and the town authorities ordered his arrest. His friends tried to rescue him from the sheriff and he was resisting arrest himself, but after a struggle the sheriff without hurting him had him carried to jail.

Then the negroes hearing of this sent a procession of about two, hundred, headed by William Crockett. Crockett reined up and, without inquiring what was the matter, commenced cursing a white man, charging him with shooting and, from his horse, fired upon this man, and then there were a half dozen shots returned, and the fight then commenced in the Main street and lasted for a quarter of an hour, when the same was quelled by the pencible citizens of the town and country. Four or five negroes, Crockett included, were killed and several wounded.

Everything was quiet last night and all to day, but conflicting rumors are reported that the negroes are threatening to renew the trouble. The whites are on the alert and will in prudence keep down trouble. The whites are united.

Col. Cash remained in his room from the beginning of the trouble until he left this morning on the train for Chester.

[Special Dispatch to the Greenville Daily News.]
[Special Dispatch to the Greenville Daily News.]
Columbia, September 28.

News has reached here of a terrible political riot at Lancaster, yesterday (Wednesday) afternoon. It seems that Col. E. B. C. Cash, Independent candidate for Congress, held a meeting and addressed a crowd composed largely of negroes, in his usual style. After the speaking was over a difficulty occurred between one of the white men present and a negro and the latter was shot. Much excitement ensued, but quiet was restored for a time. Soon afterwards a crowd of negroes marched up and one of them selected and pointed out a white man, saying: "There's the d—d scoundrel who did the shooting." The white man earnestly protested his innocence, but the negroes refused to listen, and began an attack upon him. Pistols were immediately drawn and a regular pitched battle took place, lasting a few moments, during which many men were knocked over on both sides. An examination of the field showed that four colored men were killed. There was the wildest excitement for a time, but by the active exertions of officers and citizens quiet was permanently restored.

Home and Democrat. CHARLOTTE, N. C. Correspondence of the Home and Democrat
Editor Home and Democrat:—I have been very much gratified by the assurances of Democratic success in the pending North Carolina election, not only furnished by the State papers which are kindly sent to me by a number of Editors (a favor which I highly appreciate), but also by the many North Carolina merchants whom I have seen within the past few weeks. They all concur in the opinion that Liberalism, which at one time threatened disaster, is dead, and that it rather helped than hurt the Democratic cause. And very naturally. For the "sore-heads" who left the Democratic party to become Liberals, all wanted the offices, though they count as one in a thousand as compared with the Republican party from which they expected to get office. This naturally disgusted the latter party. And so it turns out that they "left their party for their party's good."

An illustration of the moral tone of politics and politicians in these parts is furnished by a remark of Mr. Pierre C. Van Wyck, superintendent of the U.S. assay office, and a member of the Republican State Committee and State Convention at Saratoga, that nominated candidates for Governor, &c. Mr. French, a leading Republican and Commissioner of Parks, appeared and claimed a seat and vote as a member of the committee by virtue of a forged telegram appointing French a proxy for Robertson. When Robertson heard of this he pronounced the telegram a forgery. But in the meantime French took a seat and helped to nominate Folger as the Republican candidate for Governor. Now all this is characteristic of the "grand old party of moral ideas," but it is not all. The papers having represented Mr. Van Wyck as saying, in regard to the forged telegram, that "while he had nothing to do with it, yet if it had been necessary to gain a point by such means he would not have hesitated to do it," a reporter of the World went to Mr. Van. Wyck and asked him if he desired to contradict the report. He replied, "I have no recollection of having made such a remark and I am sure I did not. I could not have made it. It certainly would have been unwise for me to do so." Only "unwise," nothing more. Mr. Van Wyck had no idea that it would be vile, as well as unwise, and the papers appear to regard it in the same light as he, for they make no comment, doubtless considering his denial and the reason for it all right.

Forgery seems to be the order of the day with the party. Not only did Commissioner French obtain a seat by a forged telegram, but W. J. Montaguye also obtained a seat upon a like forged telegram. Both of them voted for Folger, and but for their votes it is said Cornell would have been nominated. This verifies my opinion that Cornell was rascal enough to suit the party if he had not been cheated by some of the other rascals.

But it is surprising as it is gratifying to find that very many Republicans, and even Republican papers, openly avow their disgust and detestation of such fraud and forgery, and their determination not to vote the Republican ticket. The Brooklyn Young Republican Club, the leading organization of the party in that city, adopted resolutions to that effect after discussion, by an overwhelming majority. This State will be Democratic next month by an immense majority.

A new wrinkle in the matrimonial line has just been developed. A gentleman at the fashionable Windsor Hotel inquires of the Sun as follows: "If a lady agrees to become the wife of a man for five years, and signs legal papers to that effect, can she hold the man after the five years?" And the Sun very properly replies, that "No lady can agree to become the wife of a man for five years or for any other limited time. Matrimony is a contract which is always for life." Yes, always except in this section where divorces are getting to be almost as common as marriages. But I rather wonder that the "gentleman" didn't inquire whether he could hold the "lady" for the full term of the five years for which she had agreed.

The Riot at Lancaster S. C.

On the 27th ult., at a political gathering at Lancaster, an unfortunate difficulty occurred between white and colored men, resulting in the killing of four colored men and the wounding of others. Four of the wounded colored men have since died making eight deaths by the sad affair. We give the following particulars:

"Eye-witnesses of the riot in Lancaster report the following full particulars of the event: Several hundred negroes gathered in Lancaster on the 27th ult., according to advertisement, to a political meeting at which speeches were to be made by T. Hendrix McLane, the Greenback candidate for Governor, and Col. E. B. C. Cash, independent candidate for Congress. McLane failing to arrive, the meeting was organized in a grove about a quarter of a mile from town, F. A. Clinton, colored, presiding. Cash was introduced at 12 o'clock, and spoke about an hour and a half, making, it is said, a conservative address. At the conclusion of Cash's speech, the chairman invited a reply by Mr. D. J. Carter, editor of the Lancaster Ledger. He accepted, and in the course of his remarks was insolently interrupted by several colored men, who denounced him as a liar. The remarks were re-asserted, when an infuriated mob of drunken negroes rushed upon the stand, tearing it down and dragging the speaker off, together with Messrs. W. C. Moore, J. Quay Dunovant and John Vaughn, the only white Democrats present. Clinton and several other colored men interfered, and protected the whites, and finally rescued them, after they had been beaten with clubs and shot at.

Clinton received a slight pistol wound in the nose from the mob, who fired the only shots. Quiet being restored, it was reported that a row was in progress up town, whereupon the crowd repaired thither, under great excitement. The negroes were mounted and reached main street, where an effort was being made to arrest Hamp Mabley, who was drunk and disorderly.

During the melee Mr. J. Quay Dunovant had come up and was standing in the street opposite Twitty & Conner's store, where the excited negro horsemen rode up, headed by Bill Crockett, pointing out Dunovant and cursing him as the d—d scoundrel who started the row at the stand. He fired his pistol at him, the ball striking a memorandum book and glancing off without harm. Crockett was immediately shot dead from his saddle and firing began indiscriminately on both sides. Two other negroes, Tom Cunningham and Nathan Cureton, were killed outright and twenty or thirty wounded, at which discomfiture the mob fled precipitately, leaving behind their three dead comrades, two dead mules and two mortally wounded men. We learn that four of the wounded have since died, making seven killed. Order being restored, Coroner Beldon held an inquest over the bodies, and it was found that they came to their deaths at the hands of parties unknown to the jury. And have they not learned by mournful experience that the men who excite them to bring about these conflicts are never in the fight, but always "retire to their room," or some other place of safety, as soon as the row begins, leaving the deluded colored men to be shot at like targets, and shot down by men who would infinitely prefer to take them by the hand, in all kindness of heart, and unite with them in the noble effort of preserving the peace and secure prosperity and good will among all classes?

We supposed it had been proved, to the satisfaction of the most ignorant as well as the most turbulant colored man in the State, that in a conflict of arms between the white and colored races, irrespective of the number on either side, the colored race is always defeated by the more resolute, brave and cool anglo saxon.

The white man of the South is far from seeking any difficulty with the colored man. He has persistently tried to avoid it; and there would be no difficulty between them if the prejudices of the latter were not excited by the inflammatory teachings of political demagogues who, through the negro vote, are willing to sacrifice the dignity of their race, the honor peace and prosperity of the State, to secure for themselves the emoluments of office.

If the negroes will not be convinced by what we say, let them read the following, and then seriously ask themselves if the Greenbackers are not using them as targets to be shot at, while they "retire to their rooms" or stand looking on, leaving the colored men to do the fighting and get killed or put in jail?

RIOT AT LANCASTER

LANCASTER, September 28.—The riot of yesterday originated thus: Col. Cash, after a very turbulent and noisy procession through the streets, was addressing a crowd of about 700 negroes. Mr. Carter, editor of the Ledger, had taken his position on the stand as reporter for his paper, and Cash was profuse in his abuse of the Legislature and charged that the planters and farmers were cheating the negroes out of their earnings.

The negroes were drinking at the stand and were wrought up to a high pitch. Cash, it is said, would turn around to Carter and make repeated remarks that he, although he would not vote for him, was his sympathizer. Carter then asked Cash to allow him to reply. Cash said certainly, and remarked that he should have a respectful hearing. Carter attempted to reply, but the negroes would not hear him. Cash asked them to be quiet, but it did no good, and Carter and the negroes getting into a wrangle, Cash left the stand and went direct to his room at the hotel. The negroes were drinking and they had a jug of whiskey near the stand.

Carter being promised both by Cash and the county chairman a reply, still tried to speak but the negroes cowed so upon the stand that the stand broke down. Thereby being greatly infuriated the crowd took hold of Carter and dragged him off the stand, and he would have been killed had it not been for Albert Clinton and Ed. Saddler and others.

Afterwards a large number of negroes mounted on horses and armed with pistols rode through the streets of Lancaster. A negro named Crockett with a pistol buckled around him headed the procession, and on passing a street corner where a white man was standing, said "There is the d__d rascal who did the firing." The white man told him that he lied, whereupon Crockett pulled out his pistol and fired at the white man, the ball narrowly missing his head and passing through the coat of another white man who was standing by. Three our four shots were fired at Crockett, who fell from his horses dead. The firing then became general, and three more negroes were killed and six wounded. The negroes then rode into another part of the town and halted. Serious fears were entertained that they would renew the attack, and to prevent further bloodshed the Intendant of Lancaster sent to Chester for aid. The disturbance was, however, quieted down without the use of the military. It is not known whether there were any casualties among the whites. Col. Cash remained in his room from the beginning of the trouble until he left this morning on the train for Chester.

The following are the names of those killed on the spot, viz: William Crockett, Thomas Cunningham and Nathan Cureton, and Mack Mobley died the next day from his wounds. The following were fearfully but not fatally injured: Ransom Brown, Joseph Foster and William Cureton. About eight or ten were slightly wounded. The wounds of the whites were very slight. There were two or three mules killed outright and several wounded.

The wife of Mack Mobley testified before the inquest that Mack stated before he died that the white people were not to blame for the trouble; that the blacks had brought it all on themselves, and it is said many others of the colored people say the same thing, and some say that the colored women are largely responsible for the trouble. But who will not believe that the speaking together with the whiskey had much to do with the affair?

KIOT IN SENECA CITY. — Senca City. September 25—on Saturday night, the 23d, a large crowd of negroes had congregated with a few white Greenbackers in front of the bar room run by the Greenback nominee for State Treasurer, W. H. Stanton. Some of the negroes became boisterous, using profane and vulgar language, when the marshal of the place, Mr. W. B. Dickson, attempted to hush it up, whereupon some twenty-five or thirty negroes rushed upon him with sticks and clubs, infiltrating a serious wound in the head. Mr. Dickson fought manfully, knocking down two with his club. Mr. William Hamilton started to his assistance, but was met by a brickbat over the eye from one of the crowd. There were several white Greenbackers near by, but they did not offer any assistance. It is thought that the thing was "cut and dried" No indignation meeting has been held, but the good citizens are fully aroused. Two negroes, Henry Perry and Sam Roberson, have been arrested and lodged in the calaboose. Some of the good citizens in the surrounding country say that the little nest of Greenbackers here have injured the reputation of Seneca City
