A Boom at Charlotte. CHARLOTTE, N. C., Oct. 6.—Information received here to-day from Lancaster, N. C., is to the effect that there are fears of another riot. The white people of the town have been considerably alarmed the past few days over the surly and threatening behavior of the negroes, and they have deemed it necessary to picket the town to-night, as they fear that the negroes will make an attempt to burn the place. Armed men patrolled the streets all last night, but the negroes, if they entertained any intention to burn the town, made no attempt to carry it out. The number of deaths resulting from the riot has increased to twelve in all, four more of the wounded negroes having died on Saturday and Sunday last. In the fight twenty-eight negroes were wounded and seven mules were killed. Many of the inhabitants, white and colored, move about fully armed, and should there be another outbreak the loss of life will greatly exceed that in the recent affair. Benny Thinks He'll Get There.
New York, Oct 6.—Gen. Butler, who was in town to-day, was the centre of a group of democratic politicians at Fifth avenue hotel, anxious to ascertain from him how things were looking in Massachusetts. The general seems to entertain no doubt of his election, whatever other doubts he may have. Just now, he says, men are of very little account down there, but principles are everything; and, as this campaign is to be fought out on that basis, principles will win. The antimonopoly feeling, he further declares, is very strong in the Bay state, and no man that sets himself up to resist, be he republican or democrat, has the slightest chance of success. He also predicts that anti-monopoly will be the winning card in the next presidential election.

Freight Train Telescoped.

PITTSBURG, Pa., Oct.—This morning at an early hour, while the first section of a freight train was standing at Linden station, a few miles from the city on the Baltimore & Ohio railroad, it was run into by the second section of the train, injuring Conductor Ruffner and Brakeman Sanders, who were in the caboose of the first section, and slightly hurting Brakeman Cline of the second section. The caboose and two freight cars of the first section were badly broken, and engine of second section was slightly damaged. The accident was caused by a failure of Flagman Devine to go back a proper distance, and on account of the dense fog. Sanders has since died, and Conductor Ruffner will lose a leg. Cline will recover.

Bergh's Latest "Kick."

NEW YORK, Oct. 6.—Mr. Henry Bergh has appeared in a new role, and it is one in which he will no doubt have the sympathy of that portion of the public that frequent places of amusement. The great humanitarian now wants human animals in thetheatres protected. He has addressed several letters to the inspector of public buildings complaining that the aisles in the Fifth Avenue and Standard theatres are not wide enough for safety in the event of fire or panic. Mr. Bergh's complaints have had the desired effect, and the necessary alterations of the theatres mentioned have been undertaken.

Mrs. Scoville Astonished.

CHICAGO, Oct. 6.—Mrs. Scoville, sister of Guiteau, was interviewed as to the poisoned bouquet. She says the statement of Chemist Tilden surprises her. The bouquet was bought at her request by John Guiteau, and was not in her hands, being carried by Miss Chevalier, secretary of the society for the protection of the insane, who handed it to a son of Warden Crocker. Lawyer Reed was in the cell at the time he took the bouquet. She is sure there could have been no poison when given him. If poisoned at all she says it was done by some crank of the Mason kind.

A Deadly Quarrel.

St. Louis, Oct. 6.—The Republican's Carlville, Ill., special says: James Field, a boarding boss at a contractor's camp on the Burlington & Ohio railroad, two miles from that place, attacked Willis McVickers to-day, firing two or three shots at him, wounding him in the arm. McVickers then returned the fire, striking him in the breast and killing him immediately. McVickers surrendered and is now in the Carlinville jail. The affair grew out of a quarrel between the men about some horses.

Frank James Locked Up.

JEFFERSON CITY, Oct 6.—There was no examination of James to day. He will be locked up in jail to-night, and possibly his examination will be held on Saturday. CHICAGO, Oct. 6.—Frank James spent last

week in this city, sleeping at night at the Sherman house, under the assumed name of Pratt, and consulting with friends from Missouri with reference to his surrender. One of the United States marshals here became aware of his presence and served out a warrant before a United States commissioner charging James with robbing the United States mails. For some unknown reason, however, the deputy made no effort to arrest his man. James left for Missouri Monday morning. Previous to coming here he was in Cleveland.

He Gulled the Grangers.

Chicago, Oct. 6.—James E. Morse was arrested here on complaint of a bank at St. Johns, Mich. He is agent for the Porter manufacturing company, Syracuse, N. Y., which manufactures agrilcultural implements and sends machinery to farmers on time, taking their notes. It is alleged that Morse, as agent, forged and passed off duplicates of notes taken, to the amount of $6,000 or $7,000. It seems the bank bought some of these alleged forged notes.

Killed His Father-in-Law.

MILWAUKEE, Oct. 6.—A special to the Republican-Sentmel says a murder was committed at Sextonville, a small town seventy-seven miles south of Richland, central Wisconsin, last night, which causes great excitement. Arthur Van Dusen, a young man, killed his stepfather, named Dougherty, by shooting him twice. An altercation arose from family difficulties. Dougherty had threatened the life of the young man and drew a revolver on him. The son was quicker than his father. Van Dusen gave himself up. Public sentiment is in his favor.

Stephens' March Through Georgia.

AUGUSTA, Ga., Oct. 6.—Thirteen counties give Stephens 10,694 majority. Three other counties to hear from will make it 12,000. Stephens' majority in the state will be 60,000. Stephens to-day sent the governor his resignation of the office of congressman of the Eighth Georgia district. An election to fill the vacancy was ordered for November 7. Gastrell, the defeated candidate for governor, will contest the election—not with any hope of getting in, but to show up the frauds and intimidations of the election.

Parished in The Flames.

BAXTER SPRINGS, Kas., Oct. 6.—A fire this morning destroyed the residence of Mr. Rosencraz, at Lowell, four miles west from here, and two of his daughters, aged 7 and 13, perished in the flames. The oldest had succeeded in getting out of the building with her mother, when she rushed back for her sister, and had dragged her through the smoke to the head of the stairs, when the floor fell with a crash and both were pitched headlong into the burning mass below. Both were burned nearly to ashes.

Hazelton Still on the Track.

MILWAUKEE, Oct. 6.—It was to-day definitely settled that George Hazelton shall remain on the track in the contest for congressional honors in the Third district. At a meeting of Hazelton delegates, held in Dodgeville to-day, it was deoided by a vote of twenty to two not to allow Hazelton to withdraw, but that he should stay in the field as the regular nominee of the party in the Third district.

Raymond, of this city, causes the property of Edward Russel and other proprietors of a mercantile agency, to be attached in the sum of $75,000, which sum Raymond claims that he was damaged by the false and malicious reports as to his credit, published by the defendant, causing his failure and ruining his prospects.

A Fatality at Omaha.

Omaha, Neb., Oct. 6.—Four men were caught in a caving trench to-day, and one named Wm. McGaw, was instantly killed.

The Bloody Shirt as a Campaign Banner.

It cannot be charged against the Republicans that they have raised the "bloody shirt" this year as a campaign banner. All questions relating to Southern politics have been ignored or left to the Southern people to settle for themselves. The Republicans of the Eastern States have had their hands full in the effort to adjust factional dissensions. The Republicans in the Western States have been sufficiently embarrassed by the various phases of the liquor question, which has been introduced as a disturbing element. There was some pretense in Mr. Hubbell's circular that the assessments levied by the Congressional Committee would be used mainly to galvanize the Republican party of the South into new life, but there have been no evidences that the money has been employed for that purpose. The fight against the Bourbons in the South has been abandoned to the Greenbackers, the Readjusters and other independent movements organized partly to gain protection for Republican voters under some new name and partly to enable disgusted Democrats to join in anti-Bourbon demonstrations. There has been no effort made in any part of the country to rally voters for the Republican party on the ground of the intolerance, fraud and violence of the Southern Democrats. Yet there has been no lack of Southern outrage, which cannot, under the circumstances, be charged to Republican invention. It became notorious that in certain parts of Arkansas, at the late election in that State, notably in and about Helena, the old bulldozing methods were revived. The polling places were seized, the negro voters driven off, and the ballot-boxes turned over to the Bourbon managers. In Alabama not long since the old story of a threatened massacre by the blacks was set in circulation as preliminary to the hanging of a negro who had made himself politically obnoxious to the Bourbons, and in order to terrify the blacks into silence and inactivity. And now comes trustworthy advices from South Carolina to the effect that the Red Shirts are again on the war-path, and that Greenback and Independent meetings will not be tolerated any more than Republican meetings were formerly. A few days ago a Greenback meeting at Winnsboro was broken up, and Mr. McLane, the Greenback candidate for Governor, who is described as "an inoffensive and respectable gentleman," barely escaped with his life after being shamefully maltreated. Within a week a more bloody affair occurred at Lancaster, where Colonel Cash, a former Confederate and a typical Southron, was holding a meeting as an Independent candidate for Congress to protest against the bad faith the Bourbons had displayed in their dealings with the negroes. Cash was not attacked personally, as that might have been dangerous to some of the Red Shirts; but when he and his immediate friends had quit the ground there was an onslaught upon the negroes. The blacks withdrew, as they always do in such cases, and went off to a distant part of the town, where they remained several hours in the hope that the bulldozers would disperse and permit them to return to their homes in peace. But the Red Shirts were not willing to forego so excellent an opportunity for "killing negroes;" so they lay in wait, renewed the attack, shot six negroes dead and wounded eighteen others, most of whom are expected to die. Not a single white man was hurt. This account reads very much like those which came North every day or two a few years ago when the Southern Bourbons sought to justify themselves by the plea that they were engaged in throwing off "carpet-bag rule." In some respects the recent bulldozing is the most outrageous ever perpetrated. "Home rule" is now thoroughly established all over the South. The opposition to the Bourbons is led in the main by Southern Democrats and ex-Confederates who have tired of the dictation and injustice of the men in power. But it is evidently the purpose of the ruling party in South Carolina and other Southern States not to tolerate the negro in politics, no matter who his sponsors may be. One of the most discouraging features of the recent South Carolina outrages is that the Charleston News and Courier, which formerly affected to condemn the Red-Shirt system, is said to have actually applauded the Winnsboro bulldozers and thereby promoted the Lancaster massacre. In the "bloody shirt" shall become a factor in the pending Congressional campaign, it will be because the Southern bulldozers force it upon the North by outrages which no civilized people could afford to ignore.—Chicago Tribune.

An astronomical observatory has lately been erected by the Italian Government on Mount Etna, above Catanta, which is the highest inhabited building in Europe, as it beats the St. Bernard Hospice by over 1,000 feet. It has two stories, with spacious balconies, and has been built on a cone near the summit of the mountain. The observatory will not be touched by any eruptions, as the lava always flows down on the further side of the volcano. Chicago Journal.

It was an English school girl who defined a water shed as "a mountain like a cave by which the water flows." And it was another who said that "Moses and Aaron disobeyed God by doing good to other people instead of to their parents, and for this act of disobedience their mother put them in an ark of bulrushes at the battle of the Nile."

POLITICAL MURDERS.
A LETTER FROM SECRETARY CHANDLER.
To the Editor of The Tribune.

SIR: It is claimed by THE TRIBUNE that the issue in the elections of 1882 at the North is that of "Machine Rule" and "Reform," and that the Republican party, to destroy the one and accomplish the other, ought to split itself into two pieces and give the Democratic party control of the two principal States of the North.

But what is THE TRIBUNE's plan for the South? What does it propose to do to secure a free vote and an honest count in Lancaster County, South Carolina? The Vth Congressional District has a population of 67,168 colored persons to 54,140 white. Its colored voters are at least 12,669 to 11,805 white voters. Lancaster County has a population of 8,968 colored to 7,935 whites; and its colored voters are at least 1,700 against 1,600 whites.

Let the Republicans of the North look to see what the Republican vote of Lancaster County will be on the 7th of November. If it is not entirely suppressed it will not be for lack of political murders. On October 27, 1882, E. B. C. Cash, Independent candidate for Congress, addressed a meeting at Lancaster Court House. A light resulted, and in broad daylight William Crockett, Thomas Cunningham, Nathan Cureton and Mack Mobley, colored Republicans, were shot dead. The Coroner's jury found that Mack Mobley came to his death by gun-shot wounds inflicted by some person or persons unknown to the jury. Of course the Democrats claim that the bloodthirsty negroes began the affray. This is shown by the fact that no white man is proved or claimed to have been injured; and yet The Lancaster Review of October 4 says: "The whites deplore the necessity which caused so much blood to be shed, but believe that the prompt resistance on the part of the white men was the only thing that prevented a general massacre."

A significant fact is that the murdered Crockett was a witness to the lynching in August of Daniel Blakney, a colored boy falsely charged with crime. Since the murders of October 27 the whites of Lancaster County have organized military companies. The same Review says: "A military company was organized last Friday night for the purpose of keeping the peace. The name of this company is the Lancaster Greys." Are these illegal military companies organized to prevent the murder of more negroes at Lancaster Court House, or to murder more, if necessary, to make the county Democratic? The various companies drill in the country districts in the day-time and in Lemon's Hall at the Court House at night with State arms sent them by Governor Hagood; and moderate Democrats state that the disturbance of the 27th was organized when it was found that Colonel Cash was to address the colored people, and that the object of the military demonstrations is to break down the colored majority in the county.

All these are facts which cannot be successfully disputed. Are they of importance to Northern Republicans or not? Are Northern Republican Congressional Districts to be turned over to Democrats to promote "Reform," while Southern districts are to be carried by Democratic false counting, intimidation and murder, and the National House of Representatives again placed in Southern Democratic control? Cannot some of the denunciation of Northern Republicans be turned upon Southern murderers? At all events will not THE TRIBUNE notify the country to watch and see the real purpose of the unpunished assassination at Lancaster Court House, South Carolina, on October 27, 1882, of the martyred William Crockett, Thomas Cunningham, Nathan Cureton and Mack Nobley? Their blood cries from the ground to Northern Republicans.

Washington, Oct. 31, 1882. W. E. CHANDLER.

[THE TRIBUNE has been in this field before the Secretary. He need not turn further back in his file than THE TRIBUNE of yesterday for an illustration.—We hope, however, that the Secretary's statement of facts at the South is less open to the suspicion of partisan one-sidedness than his statement of THE TRIBUNE's position at the North.—Ed.]

A MURDER CASE.
Trial of John Lyons for Complicity in the Killing of Richard McCoy.
Progressing is the trial of John Lyons in the District Court on a charge of complicity in the killing of Dick McCoy in LaSalle county. Dolly Durand testified for the state as follows:

"When we got to Altito pasture a fellow came up on a dun horse and Jim Wright said he was a spy. He said he wanted to buy cattle. He was told he had no time to buy cattle, and we arrested him and took his gun. He had laid down and we put a guard over him. Some cattle men were in the pen, when others came up. The man in front went to take down the bars we had laid up. As the man went to lean forward, James Wright and brother shot him, and then defendant fired. I ran, and saw Pedro Lopez and Garza run, too. We ran across the river and saddled up and came on home. About thirty shots were fired. Had been employed to drive cattle out of the pasture. I took no part in the fighting. Jim Wright said to stick together or all would get killed. I went up from the river because James Wright told me to, and I was afraid to refuse. The man shot was just across the pen about twenty yards. James Wright seemed to be the leader of a party."

Wm. Dunn asseverated: "I am sheriff of Guadalupe county, and was during May, 1881. I knew Richard McCoy. He was my deputy in 1881. A bunch of cattle was stolen and I placed him on trail. The owner had given me a power of attorney. I furnished it to McCoy."

Wiley Moore stated: "On the 16th of May, 1881, I went to Jim Wright's cattle pen to buy cattle. I found fourteen or fifteen men there. I rode up to the pen, and when in about ten steps of it ten or twelve men presented guns at me. I told them I was all right. They said if I was all right to ride around—that I might belong to the other party. I rode around and got down. They took my gun out of the scabbard and then took me into the pen, when I told them what I had come for. I told them I wanted to go. They said no, and made me lay down, and gave a Mexican a six-shooter and told him to guard me, and if I made any brake to shoot me. While there a man rode up and they shot him. He went backwards off his horse. I laid there, and while the shooting was going on the Mexican guarding me threw down his pistol and ran off with two others. I afterwards told them again I wanted to go, and they said if I didn't dry up they would pitch me into the river. A woman interceded for me and they let me go. I left without my horse. They said to say nothing of the killing. I do not know them.

Following is a part of John Y. Bell's testimony: "We went to Mr. Wright's ranch to look at some cattle we heard were there. We were thirteen in all. We had been informed at a meeting of our association that there were four or five hundred head of cattle in the Altito pasture which belonged to the association. We found two or three hundred head and thought we would drive them into the ranch, Some of them belonged to our association.

"When near the pen we saw the gap was up, and Dick McCoy rode off through the cattle to the pen. Alf Talk and myself rode around to the side of the cattle. When very close to the pen I heard three or four shots, and then a perfect volley—something like a hundred shots. I did not see McCoy at the time of the shooting. I saw him next morning. He was dead. I saw several cattle belonging to our party—one belonging to my brother. The brands on these animals had been disfigured by burning out or adding to."

Lee Floyd testified: "In April I knew Jas. Wright had thirty head of my cattle in Altito pasture and others belonging to neighbors. In May we started for the pasture. I first notified the sheriff who was sick; also the district attorney. I got a search warrant to search Altito pasture. I learned of Judge Pleasants of the range. I met with Richard McCoy at Pleasanton. I met Walker Tally and Sergt. McNally too. We started to Altito pasture where we believed the cattle were. We did not search the pasture for two reasons. One was that the sheriff was not there and the other that the cattle had been moved down the river. I arrested two or three men in order to make sure of the arrest of James Wright, but I could not make a case against them for handling and herding my cattle. We went on two or three miles towards James Wright's and saw some of my cattle with the brands on them blotched. We soon heard a gun shot. We took it to be a signal. We went up to Mrs. Anderson's camp and struck camp for the night. The next morning we gathered our cattle. That day we rounded up and drove the cattle toward the pen. McCoy was ahead of the cattle on the right point. John Bell, Alf Tumlinson, John Doudelstadt and others were there. McCoy rode up to open the gate. Then the firing was commenced. I found him dead the next morning."

"In May, 1881," testified John McNally, "I was a ranger, and in LaSalle county. I went with others to Altito pasture to arrest some persons if we could find them. We had papers for J. P. Wright. A warrant was handed me in Pleasanton; it was from Gonzales county. Trying to execute the capias I went to James Wright's ranche, but did not then find him. We camped there that night. The next day we gathered a bunch of cattle. About sun-down we drove the cattle off to a pen, and I was off some distance and heard the shooting. The capias was directed to the officers of Atascosa county or to any member of the frontier troops. On the 15th of May I went to the house of Wright. I saw there two or three ladies and children. I had no papers but I arrested several persons and kept them prisoners two or three days. I did it to keep them from carrying news. I think there were 18 in our crowd."

Walker Tolly said he went with McNally from Atascosa county. "A warrant for James P. Wright was given to me by officers of Atascosa county. I turned it over to McNally. We were lying in the shade at the river when we heard a gun or pistol fired. A lady came down to the bank of the river and talked to some one on the opposite side. McCoy and I went down the river and met two boys who were in a flat. One of the boys made a peculiar noise when he saw us. We followed the trail of the lady and came to some boys herding sheep, where we saw her again. She spoke to us and we to her. I told Mc. to ask her who she had been speaking to and she said 'Watkins.' A horse was tied near by and she said it was Watkins' horse. She then went to the house. I was not present when the shooting was done. It was understood that Mc. was going along to hunt cattle supposed to have been stolen."

Unimportant testimony was given by Steves Tullis and Chris. McCoy for the state, and Henry Boone for the defence. Witness for the defence is now being examined.

ON THE STAND.
Witnesses Testifying for the Defense in the McCoy Murder Case.
"I acted as an officer in the arrest of some parties who were charged with the killing of Dick McCoy. Joe Sheely and myself went down on the Atascosa. We had agreed to meet Capt Oglesby at old man Long's. They did not get there at the time we expected them. We waited till daylight next morning, and they did not come, when Joe Sheely and myself went to old man Garza's, and arrested Pedro Garza. Joe Sheely sent me to old man Ingle's and I arrested a man named Jose Hernandez. I then turned Pedro Garza and Louis Hernandez over to Joe Sheely. I then went to Dolly Durand's and arrested him. We arrested him on suspicion of killing Dick McCoy. I told him I wanted him to go along with me. I made a promise that I would try and get him out of his troubles, and would not indict him on this charge. His troubles were that he was indicted in this county for horse-stealing. I do not know that he was indicted in other county than this. I was authorized to make this proposition. We had him under guard from about daylight in the morning until dark. I know Pablo Lopez. I do not know what propositions were made to him. He was arrested in San Marcos by Joe Sheely. He was taken out to Cotulla. We held him, Pedro Garza and Dolly Durand under guard until the grand jury met in Fort Ewell. The reason why they were held under guard was on account of the danger of Dolly Durand and Pedro Garza running away. We held them them until they went before the grand jury—keeping them in the brush near near Fort Ewell."

The testimony of Tom Scott, mentioned in the Light yesterday, was to the effect that Dolly Durand was bribed to run away by Buck Lyons, Joe McMahon, John Butler, George Gleason, Alfred Alee, and Joe Tumlinson, the sheriff of Dimmitt county. "Gleason," said Scott, "asked if Oglesby had not promised to pay him for swearing every day against John Lyons, and if Oglesby had not
Gleason wanted to talk to Dolly, and said he would pay me, He told me if I gave the thing away he would fix me. He said the crowd would make it all right with me. George told me he had the money ready for Dolly at any time. We did nothing on Friday. On Thursday Gleason reappeared to me and Dolly. Then he called Dolly off and talked to him awhile. Then he came to me and told me he would drop it and have nothing more to do with Dolly Durand; that he was an officer, and it did not pay him to get into it. George Gleason and I and Dolly were sitting in a dark place. Dolly showed me a $2.50 gold piece which he said Gleason gave him. Joe Tumlinson promised Dolly Durand some money to leave last Saturday. This was at the Alazan creek, on the other side of the International depot. Joe told Dolly that he would give him $200 to leave and bring a horse for him to leave on Monday. Dolly then said if you will have the horse here by three o'clock I will leave, otherwise I will give myself up to Captain Oglesby. Dolly Durand first sent me to Tumlinson to borrow $25 to get out of town, but I did not go. They wanted him to come up and say that John Lyons was not at the murder. George Gleason told me that he would give money if he (Dolly) would come up and swear that John Lyons was not the murderer. Dolly said he could not swear to this because he had told Capt. Oglesby that John Lyons was there. I was running backwards and forwards taking messages. I have not seen Pablo Lopez. I do not know that he has left. They wanted him to leave and go to Mexico, and he refused to go. Joe Tumlinson gave Pablo some nickels. Joe McMahon gave Pablo $1 one night to dance with. Dolly told them he was unarmed and had to answer questions. Pablo Lopez said he had told nothing but the truth in this case and refused to leave his state, but wanted to remain in it. It was Monday that Dolly asked me to go to Joe Tumlinson for $25. He said the arrangements for him to leave for Mexico had been made out in Atascosa before this court commenced. It was a verk dark place on one of the streets of this city where Gleason met us."

Joe Tumlinson testified that he knew nothing of the alleged talk with Scott. Said he: "On Friday evening last I went out on business with Buck Lyons, Alfred Alee, Dolly Durand and George Gleason. We went out of town and had a talk with Dolly Durand. We asked Durand to make a clean statement of why he testified for the state in this case. He said that Capt. Oglesby and Joe Sheely promised him to keep him from trouble in this case if he would testify for the state. Durand then said he would not turn state's evidence till Gleason would promise to reward him. Durand said further that he now wanted to leave; that he wanted Mr. Joe McMahon to help him to leave. McMahon told him he could not assist him; that he wanted him to go back and make a fair statement. I never heard any reward offered. I never paid Durand any money nor saw any money paid to him by any one. I never heard any conversation with Tom Scott."

Buck Lyons, Alfred Alee and Joe McMahon corroborated Tumlinson's story, and Lyons and McMahon swore that Dolly Durand told them Capt. Oglesby paid him $30 a month to stay and testify for the state.

A large crowd was about the federal court building, in which the district court is sitting, all morning. The troubles which arose yesterday have not yet been settled to the entire satisfaction of the persons concerned. and other rencontres may occur. The report of them in the LIGHT last evening was incorrect in several particulars, as a result of misinformation. Mr. W. S. Hall was not on the witness stand, as stated, and had no controversy with Joe Shely. The gentleman who did have was Alfred Alee, a witness in the case. Appended is a statement he made to a reporter to-day:

"Myself and Mr. Joe Tumlinson, sheriff of Dimmitt county, walked upstairs together, into the hall. Sam Newton and Joe Shely were talking, and I asked Mr. Shely if he didn't tell a certain man at Cotulla that for the sum of $2,000 he would furnish evidence to convict all of these boys indicted in the LaSalle murder case. He said it was a lie. I told him a responsible man said he did say it. Then he gave it the lie, and I gave him the lie. During this talk Sergt. Charley McKinney drew his pistol partly out of the scabbard, supposably on me, and then Major Teel called me off down stairs. While Major Teel and I were talking I heard that Capt. Oglesby and Sergt. McKinney had hold of Tumlinson. I came back up stairs to Tumlinson with my pistol. Capt. McCall, while I was talking to Tumlinson, came out and asked for my pistol, and I gave it to him. No one had asked me for my pistol before that. I state this because I heard this morning that a report was in circulation to the effect that I had refused to part with my weapons. My object in asking Sheely this question was he had been helping the state in the case, and if he would acknowledge this I thought it would be of benefit to the defense."

This morning Mr. Alee pleaded guilty of carrying a revolver, and was fined $25 by Justice Anton Adam. It is said that Mr. Alee had authority to carry the weapon, but did not want to be troubled with a trial. Joe Tumlinson and Sergeant McKinney, too, were fined to-day by Recorder Anderson, each in the sum of $5. Tumlinson was charged with using insulting language, to which he pleaded not guilty, and McKinney with striking Tumlinson.
At half-past 2 o'clock this afternoon the jury had not announced a verdict.

LATER—We learn just as going to press that the jury has returned a verdict of "not guilty."

dolly-durand-1882-10.A6:
MURDERED ASLEEP!
Dolly Durand Shot and Killed.
Dolly Durand had been shot and killed. On inquiry it was found that on Saturday Dolly Durand was out a few miles from the ranch on the Ingle settlement, in company with a man named Jim, tending horses. At night, whilst Dolly and his companion were sleeping out, some persons stole upon them and shot Durand in the neck, breaking it, and killing him instantly; but, as if to make sure of their foul work, they riddled his body with bullets, firing so close that the clothes were set on fire. The man who was with him jumped up and ran. Several shots were fired at him, but he escaped unhurt. Dolly Durand, it is said, was en route for San Antonio, and it is supposed that he has been killed, either as a revenge for the evidence he gave for the state in the McCoy murder trial, or to prevent him giving further evidence.
dolly-durand-1882-10.A8:
San Antonio.
SAN ANTONIO, October 2.—Information was received here to-day of the killing of Dolly Durand, who was the main witness in the case against John Lyons, recently tried here. Durand was asleep in the woods at 1 o'clock at night, when a party of six men rode up and literally riddled him with bullets. One of the shots broke his neck. Durand was a notorious thief, and was believed to have been the murderer of Dick McCoy, as he turned state's witness to swear the lives of others away. He was undoubtedly killed an account of his testifying against Lyons.

frank-fisher-galion-1882-04-30.A7:
THE MINNEAPOLIS PLAN.
A Negro Ravisher in Ohio Hung by Indignant Citizens on the Spot Where His Terrible Crime Was Committed—Louisville Furnishes Another Victim.

CLEVELAND, Ohio, April 30.—A Galion dispatch says: The negro ravisher Fisher, was captured at five o'clock this morning at Frederickstown, Knox county, by two officers, just as he was leaving this place afoot. Fisher denied his name but was recognized, arrested and taken in a carriage to Galion, where he was put in an iron cage in the city prison about noon, arrangements being made to send him to a jail in some neighboring county to prevent threatened lynching, but at 3 o'clock a large crowd of determined people unmasked, went boldly up to the city hall prison and demanded the surrender of the negro to them. The officers refused and Mayor Underwood and others made speeches to the excited throng, counseling that the law be permitted to take its course, but to no purpose.

The mob forced the doors of the prison, broke down the iron cage and dragged the negro into the street with fierce shouts. Meanwhile a delegation accompanied by physicians who had been pressed into the service, drove to the house of the victim of the negro's lust to ascertain whether the girl, Barbara Rettie, was morally and physically able to confront and identify the prisoner. She told the physician she could as she had often seen him chopping wood near her home. This being reported to the crowd the negro was marched to her home, preceded by men carrying a rope, and surrounded by a howling rabble. When Barbara saw the cowering wretch, she exclaimed: "That is the man," and fainted.

The noose was then thrown over the negro's head and he was dragged to a tree at the rear of the lot. Somebody suggested the scene of the rape was the fittest place to strangle him. This was the view of all, and Fisher was taken to the spot, when he was told that his time had come to die. He protested his innocence to the last, but the blood still perceptible on his clothing was evidence of guilt, as well as the girl's statement, and he was quickly strung up, when the crowd quietly dispersed.
frank-fisher-galion-1882-04-30.A9:
A Black Flend Lynched.
CLEVELAND, April 30.—Frank Fisher, a negro, who ravished a 13-year-old girl, on Friday, was lynched at Galion, at 4 o'clock this afternoon, by a mob of about two hundred men. Fisher made no resistance, and while hanging squirmed but once. He choked to death.

CINCINNATI, April 30.—The Commercial's special from Galion says: Frank Fisher, arrested near Fredericktown, this morning, was jailed at Galion at 3 o'clock p.m. Locomotives whistled and fire bells rang, when over 2,000 people rushed to the jail and broke it open; negroes joined in the mob and a negro broke open the cell. Fisher was dragged out and taken to the bedside of his victim, Barbara Rettig, who recognized him as the person who had outraged her. A crowd of 4,000 then took him to the scene of his crime, gave him time to pray and hanged him. He declared his innocence to the last. Many people in Galion condemn this method of proceeding.

The town of Gualalleysville, in Arizona, just over the New Mexico line, was burned and completely destroyed Tuesday evening by Indians. Thirty-five white people were killed. Citizen Indians attacked the American Mining Camp, at Bacuahi, Sonora, April 20, killing Messrs. Lowery, Ray and Rickey. Three others made their escape.

A MAIL pouch on board one of the New York elevated railroad trains, exploded with a loud noise and much smoke a few days ago. Examination disclosed an infernal machine addressed to Cyrus W. Field, and another of the same character addressed to W. H. Vanderbilt. The premature discharge is supposed to have been caused by the jolting of the train.

The Utah Constitutional Convention has adopted a Constitution, and provided for its submission to the people May 22. No provision is made respecting polygamy. It was discussed at length in committee, but left for Congress to take the initiative. The instrument is liberal to mining interests, provides for public schools, and secularizes public instruction.

1 FRANK FISHER, colored, guilty of committing a vile assault on a German girl aged thirteen, at Galion, Ohio, was arrested Sunday at Frederickstown, Knox County, and returned to Galion prison. A mob took the prisonor out and, after he had been recognized by the girl, hanged him. The scene—in Ohio, by an unmasked mob, in broad daylight, and on Sunday—was unusual.

WILLIAM and Bradford Courts, disreputable characters, were hanged by a mob at Brookville, Braken County, Ky., on the 27th for killing James Smith at a log-rolling. At Lake City, Colorado, George Betts and Jim Brown were lynched for killing Sheriff Campbell while attempting to arrest them. An Indian murderer was lynched on Stormy Creek, west of Colusa, California. A good record for one day.

emony was conducted with great pomp, Archbishop of Canterbury officiating as chief clergyman. The bridemaids were eight in number. The Prince of Wales and the Duke of Connaught acted as "best men." GENERAL IGNATIEFF publishes a communication denying that anti-Jewish disturbances are the result of a want of action on the part of the Government, and declaring that serious disorders have occurred only at Balta, where the Jews were in fault, as they began demonstrations in revenge for an insult to a Jew by a Christian child. General Ignatieff states that elsewhere disorders have been averted through energetic measures of the authorities, which will be continued.

The most sensational point of the three days' examination of ex-Secretary Blaine at Washington was reached on the 27th, when the witness told Mr. Belmont, who was examining him, that his construction of one of his instructions to Minister Hurbut was untruthful, and Mr. Belmont told Mr. Blaine (reserving his reply to this assault on his veracity for private communication), that he believed him to be a bully and a coward. Blaine struck the table with his fist and cried, "The insolence of the young man is astounding."

A DISPATCH from Moscow says: A man named Koboseff Bogdanowitch recently submitted to the authorities a plan for the illumination of the Kremlin with the electric light. Inquiries were instituted, and it was discovered that the intention was to blow up the whole Kremlin during the festivities attending the corporation of the Czar. At the man's residence there were found a number of peasants' caps, the crowns of which were filled with explosive material. It is supposed these caps were intended to be thrown into the air in greeting to the Czar, and that, on falling to the ground, their contents would explode with the effect of bombs. Bodganowitsch and 300 Nihilists were arrested.

frank-fisher-galion-1882-04-30.A21:
JUDGE LYNCH ACES.
JUDGE LYNCH ACTS.
The Black Brute Who Outraged a Child at Galion Hanged by the People.
GALION, O., May 1.—Last Friday as Barbara Rettig, a German girl, thirteen years of age, was returning home from a neighbor's house, she was assaulted by Frank Fisher, a burly negro, dragged into the woods, repeatedly and brutally outraged, and left in an insensible condition. When she returned to consciousness and dragged herself home and told her story, there was intense excitement, and searching parties were immediately organized to look for the black beast and capture him if possible. Yesterday morning a negro answering to the girl's description was arrested in Frederickstown, Knox county, and brought here and lodged in jail. Immediately a crowd began to gather, and ominous threats of lynching were heard. The fire bells were sounded, whistles blown, and the people began to gather around the jail. The officers in charge of the jail were unprepared for an assault, and tried to induce the mob to leave. The Mayor also addressed the mob, advising order and counseling them to let the law take its course. All pleadings were vain. A rush was made, the jail doors forced, the prisoner's cell broken into, and the hapless wretch dragged out, howling and begging for mercy. The people seemed frenzied with fury, and the prisoner was dragged along the street, kicked, choked, and pelted with stones at every step. The negro was taken to the home of the injured girl and taken into her presence as she lay suffering the most intense pain, and unable to move. She was asked if the prisoner was the man who misused her, and she said, without hesitation, that he was the man. There was other and conclusive evidence against him, and he was told that his time had come to die. He was taken from the house and followed by a howling mob of at least two thousand people, dragged to the woods where his foul crime was committed, and bidden to make his peace with God, for his time was short. The scene was horrible. Fisher, with distorted face, shrieked for mercy and protested his innocence. He was told he could have five minutes to pray, but all the more he writhled and twisted and asked for mercy. To the very last he delared his innocence. When the five minutes were expired the hands of the shrieking wretch were pinioned, a rope was placed around his neck and the other end thrown over the limb of a tree. There was a moment's pause, and a pitiful scream of the victim was stifled as the rope was pulled up and he swung writhing in mid air. The crowd stood by until the last convulsive struggles were over, and then disappeared, leaving the body hanging, and where it remained all night. There are but few people who condemn the deed, however lawless, and the general sentiment is that it was well done.
frank-fisher-galion-1882-04-30.A24:
LYNCHED.
Frank Fisher Taken From the Gallon Jail and Hanged.

GALION, Ohio, April 30, 1882.

This has been the most exciting day in the history of the city and county. Frank Fisher, the negro who so horribly outraged the little German girl, Barbara Rettig, aged only thirteen years, in the woods, where he had been chopping wood last Friday noon, and who escaped, was captured about five o'clock this morning at Fredericktown, Knox County, by Officers T. J. Wurts and W. H. W. Nichols, of this city. The arrest was made just as the negro was about to leave Fredericktown on foot. He was first accosted by Officer Wurts, who asked him whether his name was Frank Fisher. "No, sah, that is not my name, sah," he replied, but Officer Nichols knew him, and after a few more questions, among which was asked why he had left Galion, he replied that he had got tired of chopping wood and thought he would skip. The officers, of course, arrested him, and at once started with him in a carriage, accompanied by two Fredericktown officers, for this city, arriving here at 11:30 this morning. The prisoner was at once taken to the jail in the City Hall and confined in one of the heavy iron cages, and the Mayor and city officers were laying plans to take him to the county jail at Bucyrus, or some other jail in some neighboring county, fearing that the loud threats of lynching would be carried out if Fisher would remain in the City Hall cell. Their fears were well founded, for the news of Fisher's capture spread through the city and the neighboring town like wild-fire, and at three o'clock this afternoon a large crowd of determined men boldly, defiantly and unmasked, with hammers, crowbars and other implements, and a huge and significant loop-rope, presented themselves before the entrance of the City Hall prison and demanded that Frank Fisher, the negro rapist, be surrendered into their hands. The officers of course refused. Then ensued a terrible scene of strife. The handful of officers were powerless, and the speeches of Mayor Underwood, G. M. Zeigler and others, who begged the excited crowd to let the law take its course and deal with the prisoner whose blood they sought, were unavailing and unheeded. With their implements of destruction they forced open the doors as though they were paper, broke open the iron cage that contained the guilty, trembling wretch, and grasping him with a dozen hands, as in a vise, they pulled him out into the street with a defiant shout. Previous to this, however, a delegation accompanied by a physician, whom they had pressed into service, drove furiously down to the residence of the victim of the negro's lust to ascertain whether she was in a proper mental and physical condition to see the negro for identification. The physician states to your correspondent that he asked her whether she knew the negro who had caused her misery. She replied yes, that she had often seen him while he was chopping wood near their home, and described his appearance. Being asked whether she could identify him, she replied she could. The delegation being satisfied reported at the City Hall, and then the scene that has been described was enacted. With hoots, yells and cheers, the crowd, preceded by some men and boys, bearing the fatal rope, marched with the frightened negro to the Rettig residence, at the foot of South Market Street, just south of the city limits, and took the black beast into the presence of Barbara Rettig, the little girl whom he had so horribly outraged. As soon as her eyes fell upon the cowardly and cowering wretch before her, she exclaimed: "That is the man who did it," and soon fainted with the terrible recollections.

The crowd threw the rope over the negro's head and dragged him to a tree in the rear of the lot, but some one suggested the woods—the scene of his terrible crime—hard by as the fit place to expiate his crime, and to the woods where he had been but a few pays ago chopping wood Frank Fisher was dragged and told that his time to die had come. He protested his innocence to the last, but the blood stains upon his clothing and the girl's evidence, coupled with numerous lies to the officers, was enough to condemn him in the minds of the infuriated and desperate crowd; and hang him they would, for a trial by law would only send him to the penitentiary and cheat the gallows of as black-hearted a demon as ever trod the earth. But they let him pray for a short time. He said in his prayer, "O Lord, take care of me. I know that I am going to die, but I have many friends." The balance of his appeal was drowned by the cries of the crowd to string him up. His hands were tied behind his back, his feet pinioned, a handkerchief placed over his face, a steady pull was given on the rope, the end made fast to a stump, and at 4:10 the soul of Frank Fisher, the negro rapist, was sent to answer for his crime before a higher court than that of Crawford County; and at this writing (9 p. m.) his body still dangles in mid-air. It is estimated that at least two thousand people, men, women and children, among whom was your correspondent, witnessed the execution by Judge Lynch. A large number of people from Bucyrus, Mt. Gilead, Crestline and other neighboring towns witnessed the ghastly spectacle. We should have stated that while the negro was being taken by the crowd a fire alarm sounded, and the lynchers thought it a ruse to get them to disperse; but the alarm was genuine, a frame house on South Market Street, on the line of march to the woods, having caught fire. The lynching of Frank Fisher, in broad daylight, upon Sunday, by unmasked men, was one of the boldest affairs that has ever transpired in this county. While the affair is to be regretted the crime was such that he has not a particle of sympathy from any one who has heard the particulars of the crime for which he has so dearly paid with his life. The Coroner of the county has been notified and may yet to-night hold an inquest and render a verdict. There is some talk of having the leading lynchers indicted by the grand jury, but it would not be safe to attempt that at present.

gus-knight-barlow-1882-09-11.A1:
SPEEDY VENGEANCE.!
A Negro Fiend Lynched in Thomas County.
BARTOW, GA., September. 12.—Gus Knight, a mulatto living on Judge Tarver's plantation, overcame and committed a most heinous crime upon the person of a very highly respectable young married lady, living about four miles south of Bartow, about ten o'clock yesterday morning. He was afterward captured, identified and confessed the crime at a preliminary hearing.

The lady when attacked had a helpless baque in her arms, and the brute chased her around the house and yard, and overcame her in a fainting fit. At night the two constables on guard were overpowered by a mob, and the negro was taken off and summarily disposed of.

Gainesville Southron: "Last Saturday night about eight o'clock, one of the severest storms we have ever seen in this section struck us from the east. The rain fell nearly constantly and the wind increased in fury, until at about 6 o'clock Sunday morning it culminated in a perfect gale, unroofing a part of the Arlington Hotel, damaging it greatly, and blowing down trees and fences. All day Sunday the rain came down, whirled into every crevice in the east side of all buildings, filling houses, stores and everything else with water. All in all, it was the severest rain storm in this country for nearly twenty years, and more damage has been done."

The Oconee Monitor has this in reference to the late cyclone: "The storm last Saturday night lasted ten hours with great fury, blowing down timber and sweeping corn and cotton to the ground, as if a log had rolled over it, burying it in the mud. The wind was accompanied by incessant rain all Saturday night, and the rain still continued all day Sunday, overflowing all the bottom lands, and in some localities covering the fine corn completely in water. Messrs. Cochran, L. Fambrough, Giles, and many others have lost their entire crops of corn and nearly all their cotton. Cotton fields look like they had been visited by heavy frost. The damage to Oconee county alone, will be perhaps not less than fifty thousand dollars."

The following details we find in the Louisville News and Farmer of the lynching of the negro Knight, who had committed a horrible outrage upon the person of a respectable married lady in Jefferson county: "On Monday morning last, a few miles beyond the Central Railroad, in this county, a negro boy by the name of Gus Knight went up to a house in the neighborhood, and seeing the lady with her child in her arms (the husband being absent), he called to her and told her to come to the gate. She at once became frightened and ran. He pursued her, and told her resistance on her part was useless, as he would carry out his purposes or kill her. He accomplished his hellish crime, and went to work at Donovan & Perkins' mill not far off. A party of justly infuriated citizens found him about five o'clock in the eveing. He confessed everything, giving the details, and said he did not know what possessed him to do it. He was carried out, the report of a number of guns was heard, and it is not likely Gus Knight will appear again in his usual avocation and walks of life."

The marble quarry at Long Swamp creek, Pickens county, is attracting attention. A recent visitor says of it: "The quarry is situated about three miles from one of the depots of the Marietta and North Georgia Railroad, on Long Swamp creek. We spent a day and two nights with the owner of this quarry who lives in sight of it. He showed us the quarry and we think with a proper amount of capital (the more in the bounds of reason the better) to work it, a vast fortune may be realized. The small mountain or large hill in which the marble is imbedded is on this creek, and in places the creek is very near the base. At one point the marble covers the bottom of the creek. At this point a perpendicular measurement—judging by the eye—to the top of the hill would be one hundred and fifty or two hundred feet. The marble in sight at this point is very imposing and abundant. How deep it goes no one can tell. It crops out only in places at the base and up the sides of the hill, much of which is covered with rich soil, the accumulation of ages gone by. This marble hill and fifty acres of land are offered for sale. Twenty or more acres of this land (some of it bordering the creek) is rich enough for gardens without fertilizers."

Atlanta Constitution, 15th: "Yesterday afternoon the incoming passenger train on the Western and Atlantic Railroad ran over Mr. W. H. Meigs, of this city, and inflicted injuries which caused his death about six o'clock in the evening. Mr. Meigs was a printer, and for the past six years worked for Elsas, May & Co. Yesterday his employers suspended business on account of it being Jewish New Year, and Mr. Meigs gladly accepted the holiday. About ten o'clock he left home in fine spirits and repaired to the home of his daughter, in the western portion of the city, where he remained until about one o'clock, when he started for his home. His route was shortened by traveling the railroad track, and his journey was half finished when the accident occurred. Just before reaching the Forsyth street crossing he heard an engine coming up behind him, and looking back saw a switch engine approaching at a rapid rate. When this engine was first seen it was close upon him, and Mr. Meigs jumped from the track without looking back, and in doing so jumped directly in front of the engine drawing the passenger train, which was on an adjacent track. As his feet struck the ground Mr. Meigs discovered his new danger, and tried to save himself, but was not quick enough. The engine struck him with such force that he was knocked down, but in falling he managed to throw his body clear of the track and escaped instant death, but the wheels of the engine passed over both legs, crushing them to splinters. The accident was witnessed by many persons, who ran to the injured man's assistance, and by whom he was placed on a stretch.

DOMESTIC.

The wheat crop report of the Department of Agriculture this month says: The result of the spring wheat harvest is in close accordance with the indications of the August report. The quality is good and the yield above the average. The general condition of winter and spring wheat when harvested is represented by 160. The average is rarely attained. Since the harvest, in parts of the winter wheat region, especially Michigan and Indiana, some millions of bushels have been lost by sprouting in the stack. There has also been some loss of spring wheat from the same cause in Wisconsin and other States. The Ohio Valley has nearly as large a product as in 1879. Ohio, Indiana and Illinois have apparently secured about 142,000,000 bushels. The South has increased both her acreage and the yield per acre. The aggregate of winter wheat, as indicated by the returns, is about 380,000,000 of bushels, of spring wheat about 140,000,000, or 520,000,000 in all. The threshing test may slightly modify these figures. The first threshing generally exceeded expectations, but the latter threshing has in many places been disappointing. It is quite certain that the per capita supply of wheat will not be quite so large as in 1879 or 1880. The average condition of potatoes in August was 101, but it has fallen in September to 92. Last year the decline during August was from 92 to 70, and it continued in a greater ratio till harvest. The prospect now is favorable for a crop of not less than 150,000,000 bushels, from the present outlook. The decline has been heaviest in New England and New York. Prospects are improved in Maryland and Virginia, have been well maintained in the Ohio Valley and the lake region, and has not materially changed west of the Mississippi. Only Wisconsin and Kansas of the Western States fail to show averages of 100 or higher. Maine stands the lowest, at 65.

Four persons were killed by a tornado in Winsted, Mass., on the 14th.

The finances of Milwaukee are reported to be in a very muddled condition.

A DISPATCH from Knoxville, Tenn., September 14, says: "A terrible tragedy was enacted this afternoon at Sweetwater, forty miles west of Knoxville, in which two men were killed. Sheriff W. T. Cates and Deputy Sheriff John Conway, of Chattanooga, Hamilton County, had in custody three prisoners to bring to Knoxville to the Supreme Court. Two prisoners—John Taylor and Sam Carter—under sentence for murder, were chained together. The other prisoner, a negro, was chained to a seat. When the train stopped at Sweetwater station three men entered the car. One was a brother of the prisoner Taylor, and entered the car from the rear, while the other two entered at the front. Taylor's brother approached Deputy Conway from behind, placed a pistol to the back of his head, and blew his brains out. He then took the keys from Conway's pocket and unlocked the prisoners. Taylor and the latter secured the Deputy's pistol. At this instant Sheriff Cates rushed at the men, firing at them and the prisoner. As he fired the prisoner Taylor shot him through the bowels, and the other two shot him in the breast, the Sheriff falling dead. Prisoner Taylor was slightly wounded in the arm, and Carter slightly wounded in the legs. The three rescuers were not hurt. Taylor, with his three rescuers, jumped on the engine and compelled the engineer to pull out, with a pistol at his head. They made him put on more steam and forced him to run twenty miles to Leneir, through three towns without stopping. At Lenoir the four men jumped from the engine and secured horses which were waiting for them and all escaped. The prisoner Carter and the negro came to Knoxville without guard, and surrendered to the Sheriff of Knox County. Conway's dead body was brought to Knoxville, Cates' body was left at Sweetwater, being thrown from the car platform by the rescuers. The gang boarded the train at Sweetwater, but the killing was done at Philadelphia, a station eight miles east of Sweetwater. The Sheriff of London County is following the gang, but has no hope of overtaking them. They are making for the mountains of North Carolina. Five thousand dollars reward is offered for the arrest of the Taylors. The sum will be increased."

JAMES TRACY, a Chicago murderer, and Samuel Reddin, of Mound City, Illinois, were hanged on the 15th inst., and a negro at Bartow, Georgia, and one at Charleston, South Carolina, were hanged by mobs on the same day.

Tinkis and Mary Ann Morrison, supposed to be the only survivors of the wreck of the steamer Asia, arrived here. Tinkis reports he boarded the Asia near Owne Sound, in company with J. P. Tinkis and H. A Shocking Crime.

THREE WHITE ROUGHS ARRESTED FOR OUTRAGING A COLORED WOMAN.

One of the most audacious cases of rape which has occurred in this city for a long time was perpetrated early yesterday morning by three white men on a colored woman in the northeast portion of the city. About 2 o'clock Sunday morning Henrietta Robinson, a colored woman, 43 years old, who lives in South Washington, but who had lost her way in going home from the house of a friend, was hailed by some white men standing by the track of the Baltimore and Ohio road, corner of F street and Delaware avenue n. e., and asked where she was going; she replied that she was going home if she could find her way there—that she had been lost. They replied that they could show her. She said she thought not, and asked if they knew where she lived. They replied yes, and at once took hold of her and led her to a large vacant square, between North Capitol street and the railroad track and Delaware avenue and G and E streets, and when about the center of the square threw her down, when she commenced to scream. One of the ruffians placed his hand over her mouth and, holding her to the ground, he accomplished his purpose. She kept up her screams when she could wrench their hands from her mouth, and a gentleman hearing the outcry hastily dressed himself and ran to Lieut. Austin's station and quickly recited what he had heard and suspected. Lieut. Austin at once sent a squad of men, who approached the place indicated and caught Maurice Connors with the woman and took them both to the station-house, where the woman was scarcely able to stand from exhaustion and lameness. She said, by direction of Connors, the other two men had gone for a bottle of whiskey and were to return and have a night of it. The police then returned to the place, just in time to catch the other two men, named Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds, who were also arrested and all locked up on the charge of rape. Connors is a bad character, and has been often arrested by the police, and has given them much trouble in various cases of assault upon them and in attempts to rescue prisoners from them. He is 26 years old. Officer Kaucher arrested him. McNulty is 23 years old and some years ago was convicted of rape and sentenced to ten years in state's prison, but was pardoned out after serving two or three years.
this afternoon the prisoners were called up out of the cells and charged with feloniously outraging Henrietta Robinson. They pleaded "not guilty," through their counsel, Mr. W. P. Williamson. Mrs. Robinson testified she is 43 years old and lives in "Frogtown." just south of the Capitol. She positively identified the defendants. She testified that she left home Saturday evening to visit her brother and on leaving his house after dark, and not being well acquainted with the streets, she wandered around until nearly 2 o'clock yesterday morning, when she passed the defendants, who were standing talking in "Swampoodle." Connors asked her where she was going and said he would take her home. They then caught hold of her and dragged her to a vacant square, on which there is no building except a barn. They dragged her to the rear of the barn and forcibly threw her to the ground. She struggled and screamed to make them release her, but Connors put his hand over her mouth and the others held her while Connors accomplished his purpose. The others did not. Connors sent them after some whisky, and before they returned the officers arrived and took Connors into custody. A colored woman named Eben Branch testified that she lives in the neighborhood of this lot, and at an early hour Sunday morning she heard a woman scream, and on going to the window, saw three men drag a woman to the cow shed, and throw her to the ground. Eliza Bracket, a white woman, corroborated the statement of the preceding witness. Policemen Prather and Kaucher testified that they were notified of the occurrence, and on arriving at the place found Conners setting on the ground holding the woman. He took them both to the stationhouse, and was then told by the woman that there were two other men who had left the place to get a bottle of whisky and return to make a night of it. The officers returned to the spot and concealed themselves in the shadow of the cow shed, and shortly McNulty and Reynolds returned, and were put under arrest, and identified by the woman. The court heard no testimony for the defense.

HELD IN $3,000 BONDS.

The case was sent to the grand jury, and the defendants were committed in default of $3,000 ball each. Conners was arrested with a crowd of others some years ago on a charge of outraging Miss Maggie Cheeny in this neighborhood. He could not be identified, and finally got off. McNulty was also with Tom Fitz, who killed Drager in his own store, at the corner of 21 and G streets, several years ago.

Alleged Attempt to Bribe a Witness.
A MATTER WHICH WAS CALLED TO JUDGE SNELL'S ATTENTION THIS MORNING.

Prosecuting Attorney Moore called Judge Snell's attention this morning to a determined effort on the part of some parties to "fix" a witness in a rape case. He said that the colored woman Henrietta Robinson, who was brutally outraged in "Swampoodle" on the 4th of this month by Maurice Conners, Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds, has been approached by certain individuals in the interest of the defendants, who are now in jail under $3,000 bonds awaiting the action of the grand jury. Lieut. Kelly, of the Swampoodle precinct, stated to the court that he had learned that persons working in the interest of the prisoners had raised money to get the prosecuting witness out of town, and he deemed it his duty to take her into custody under these circumstances. Mrs. Robinson, who was present, was told by the court if he sent her to jail as a witness she would receive $1.25 per day as witness fees. She said she had a family, and it would be inconvenient for her to go to jail. She said she would appear whenever called on, and no offer that could be made to her would induce her to leave the city. The court said he thought she was an honest woman, and he did not want to compel her to suffer the hardship of being sent to jail, and he would take her personal bonds for her appearance. She was notified by Judge Snell and Mr. Moore to have any one arrested who attempted to bribe her, and they would be punished to the extent of the law.

The Potomac Archers.
THE CONTEST YESTERDAY WITH THE SANDY SPRING CLUB.

"Regular archer's weather" was the verdict passed by the Potomacs as they met yesterday morning for their trip to Sandy Spring. Arriving at mid-day at the residence of Mr. Francis Miller, where the targets had been set out, and having lunched and renewed many pleasant friendships with the resident bowmen, bows were strung and soon the merry thud of the arrows rang out the music so dear to the followers of Robb Hood. The best scores of the day were made by Mr. Al Brooke and Miss Debbie Brooke, of the Sandy Spring club. In the team contest at the American round the Potomacs led, the score being—Sandy Spring, Al Brooke, 393; Miss Debbie Brooke, 292; C. F. Brooke, 196; H. H. Miller, 172; total, 1,053. Potomacs—L. Maxson, 366; W. A. Bartlett, 334; F. O. Maxson, 272; A. Johnson, 254; total, 1,226. Columbia round: Sandy Spring—Mrs. C. F. Brooke, 231; Mrs. Al Brooke, 140; total 371. Potomacs—Mrs. W. A. Bartlett, 198; Mrs. Butcher, 165; total, 363—victory resting with the Sandy Spring ladies. Individual scores at the Columbia round were—Miss Van Doren, 152; Miss Freeland, 150; Miss Morse, 145; Miss Conn, 140; Miss Burnside, 103. At the American round—Mr. Minnix, 206; Mr. Paret, 108. The scores made by the last three are very good, these members having but recently joined the club. At sundown the Potomacs bade farewell to their friends, and with lingering regret that the happy day was past wended their way home. TRIAL FOR RAPE. Connors, McNulty, and Reynolds Convicted.
In the criminal court Wednesday Maurice Connors, Patrick McNulty, and James Reynolds, all white, were tried for having committed a rape on Henrietta Robinson, a colored woman, on the 3d of last September. Messrs. H. H. Wells, jr., and Charles Pelham appeared for the defendants and Mr. Charles S. Moore for the government. The colored woman testified that she lived in South Washington, and on the night in question she lost her way, when a young man offered to show her the way home; that he took her to a cow-shed, and, being joined by others, they outraged her. Other testimony was heard to the effect that one of the men went off for whisky, leaving the largest man with her; that Officers Prather and Kaucher found this man with the woman, and took both to the station house, and, going back, the two others came up to them and said they were looking for a young man, and they took them to the station, where the woman identified them. Connors testified to having had improper relations with the woman, but it was with her consent. The other defendants swore they had not committed the offense charged against them and denied using any violence to the woman. The jury, after being out a short time, found Connors guilty as indicted and the other two guilty of being accessories before the fact. Mr. Wells asked the usual four days in which to file a motion for a new trial.

A MODEST REQUEST
To Have Accessories to a Rape Released on Personal Bonds.
Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds were arraigned in the Criminal Court this morning on an indictment charging them with being accessories before the fact to a rape on Henrietta Robinson on the 3d of September last, and both pleaded not guilty. Maurice Connors was convicted as principal in the above offense, and is now serving a ten years' sentence in the penitentiary.

Mr. H. H. Wells, jr., asked that McNulty be admitted to bail on his personal recognizance to appear when wanted.

His Honor thought that a cool request. Here was a man indicted as accessory before the fact to rape, and the Court was requested to release him on his personal recognizance.

Mr. Charles Pelham said that there was no case here and the Court knew it. The case would never be called for trial, and he thought the District Attorney would enter a nolle pros. The men could never be tried on the charge, and they should be restored to their liberty.

His Honor said that if the counsel pressed him to speak he would say that there was a case and a good one against the defendants, and he would fix ball at $1,000 in each case.

A Pair of Accessories Plead Not Guilty- The Court Record.
ACCESSORIES HELD.

In the criminal court Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds were arraigned for being accessories, before the fact, to a rape committed by Maurice Connors, and pleaded not guilty. They were indicted as principals and convicted under the indictments of being accessories before the fact, the punishment being the same for both offenses, but owing to this technicality the sentence was set aside and a new indictment found. Mr. H. H. Wells, jr., counsel for McNulty, asked that his client be released on personal bonds. The court thought the request was a decidedly cool one. Mr. Charles Pelham, on behalf of Reynolds, said there was no case and the court knew it. The case would never be tried, and a nolle pros. would be entered. Judge Wylie said now that counsel had pressed him, he would say that there was a good case, and he would hold the defendants in $1,000 bonds each.

Saturday evening, last N

On Saturday evening last Nannie Carr, the ward of R. S. Parker, living in Union township, about twelve miles down the river, went to Parker's schoolhouse to sweep it out and arrange for religious services on Sunday. While there Jim Sanders, a negro boy of this city, crept into the building and seized her from behind, throwing her to the floor. She screamed twice, and then became unconscious. Her screams attracted the attention of Wm. Pinson, who ran to the building and looked in the window. Sanders saw him and escaped, Pinson shooting at him once. He made his way to this city, and was arrested at two o'clock yesterday afternoon by Chief of Police Counts at the corner of Main and Eighth streets. The Chief turned him over to Deputy Constable Carter Walls and a posse of men, who took him down to Union and delivered him to Magistrate McAllister. This officer placed him in charge of Constable Monroe Bowen. He was lodged in a small house near the mill. At 10 o'clock last night a body of masked men broke into the house, overpowered the guards, and riddled Sanders with bullets, killing him instantly.

Deputy Sheriff Botsford and Coroner Woolford left for the scene of the trouble at 10 o'clock this forenoon.

Magistrate McAllister, who is in town, told our reporter he feared a collision between the whites and blacks, but we anticipate no trouble of that character.

A Negro Attempts an Outrage, and is Lynched by a Mob. Special to The Times Democrat.

LITTLE ROCK, May 29. In the vicinity of Parker's store, 10 miles south of this place, there occurred last night a terrible tragedy, the victim being a negro boy named James Sanders, who on Saturday attempted to outrage Miss Nannie Carr, The young lady was sweeping out the church and school-house on the eve of the day named, when she heard a noise and looking up, saw Sanders before her and with a gun on his shoulder. He asked for a drink, and when told that there was none in the building, he sprang forward and caught Miss Carr in his arms. A desperate struggle followed, the young girl fighting fiercely to preserve her honor. She screamed loudly, when Sanders seized her by the throat saying that he would kill her if she made another outcry. She gasped and struggled, pulling her assailant toward the door. A man named Penson happened to pass by, and hearing the noise came toward the house. Sanders saw him, and jumping out of window, fled. Sanders was arrested in this city yesterday, taken to the scene of his attempted crime and lodged in a frame building, preparatory to having a hearing. About midnight the rude building was surrounded by a number of masked men, who overpowered the guards, broke down the door and riddled Sanders with bullets.

There is great excitement in the vicinity, the colored people being especially incensed. The coroner held an inquest to-day. To-night the excitement is reported still running high, and many predict that there will be further bloodshed.

Little Rock Gazette: "While sweeping out Parker's schoolhouse, in Union township, last Saturday evening, Miss Nancie Carr was indecently attacked by a colored youth named Jim Sanders. saturday while Miss Nannie
Last Saturday, while Miss Nannie Carr was cleaning out a church in what is known as Parker's settlement, near Little Rock, Ark., she was assaulted by a negro boy named Jim Sanders. Her shrieks attracted the attention of a man who chanced to be passing along the roadside, and Sanders fled, the man shooting at him, but without effect, as he disappeared. Sanders was arrested next day, taken to the scene of his attempted crime, and placed in a frame building, preparatory to the preliminary examination. At a late hour that night a mob broke into the house and shot the prisoner to death, literally riddling him with bullets. The matter has created intense feeling in the neighborhood, and when the inquest was held next day threats were made of further trouble. A great many colored people live in the vicinity, nearly all of whom are very bitter regarding the shooting of Sanders. The mob was composed of masked men, but it is said some were recognized, and will likely be indicted. The negroes are terribly worked up about it.

A NEGRO MURDERER KILLED.
CHARLOTTE, N. C., Dec. 7.—Joseph Ross, the negro who murdered F. N. McDowell at Camden on last Thanksgiving Day, was killed on Wednesday night at Ivey's Mill, on the Catawba River, in Lancaster County, S. C., by ferryman Alonzo Hunter. Ross was fleeing from a party in pursuit of him, who were close behind. He asked the ferryman to take him across the river. Hunter recognized Ross and tried to arrest him. Ross resisted and Hunter shot him. Before dying the negro confessed to having murdered McDowell, and also to having murdered Robert Hennegan, in Mecklenburg County, in this State, two years ago.

Here it was that they struck a hot trail. Ross had passed there a short time before, and with this information the party hurried on. At a negro cabin, a little distance further, they found several children, who told them that a man answeriag to their description had stopped there a short time before and asked for a piece of bread, which they gave him, and getting a chunk from the fire, he had gone in the direction of Ivy's mill.
