He caught the ramrod and drew it out, but before he could make his enslaught Mr. Huntley fired, and Ross fell to the floor soon in the back, just above the thigh. He was tied securely and Mr. Huntley went out to call in the men, who he had were near. When they all arrived at the scene, the negro was placed in a wagon and carried to the old Hagan house where a bed of straw was prepared for him. Upon this he was laid next to the gathered crowd, he proceeded to make his confession. At 5 o'clock in the morning, he died. He was shot at 6:00 the previous evening.

THE TERRIBLE CONFESSION.

One of the party drew out paper and ink and seated himself beside the dying negro to take down his last words, being a confession, told in a broken voice, of two savage murders which he had committed and for which he was soon to account before the Judge of all: He was suffering considerable pain and talked with considerable difficulty. He first confessed to the murder of Mr. F. N. McDowell, at Camden, and then told of the murder of the old negro Bob Hennegan, in this county, two years ago. His brother-in-law, he said, helped him to kill Mr. McDowell. He did the killing, but his brother dragged the body away, threw it in a dater and covered it with brush. He stated in detail that on the morning of last Thanksgiving day, Mr. McDowell rode up to his cabin and asked for him. "I was not in the house at the time, but soon came up and found Mr. McDowell standing by his horse, buckling the saddle girth. He said, 'hello, Joe, what's the matter with you?' I did not answer him, but went in the door and hind his back, picked up my axe and as he was bent down at the saddle, I knocked him in the head. I did not hit
ohind his back, picked up my axe and as he was bent down at the saddle, I knocked him in the head. I did not hit him but once, but that lick broke his skull all to pieces. My brother then charged the body to a ditch near by, threw it in and covered it with brush, and then came back and scraped up the blood from the ground." Ross then fled, came towards Charlotte, dodged about from place to place until he got to ivy's mill. This place, he said, was where he conceived himself after he had killed Bob Hennegan. It is... wild, rugged piece of country, and sale hiding place, and but for the party accidentally discovering his trail, he might now be hiding there in perfect safety.

The negro continuing his confession told how he waylaid Bob Hennegan, in this county abo't two years ago and with the assistance of two negroes, Marshall Baxter and El Harriss, beat his head to a pup and threw the lifeless body in the creek. El Harriss, he said, had more to do with it than Baxter did. Harriss, it will be remembered, turned State's evidence and was released. Baxter was tried and hung. Ross escaped and from that day to this has succeeded in outwitting the officers in their every effort to capture him.

WHY HE KILLED MCDOWELL.

Ross said he killed Mr. McDowell because that gentleman, for whom he had been working, had jailed him for selling mortgaged property. It seems that Tom Wilson, a brother of the murderer was living on Mr. C. J. McDowell's farm, and and to this brother's house Joe Ross came about a year ago, and hired himself out to work for Mr. McDowell, giving a mortgage on some hogs, etc., for money drawn. When settling time came, the mortgaged property was not forthcoming, and Ross was sent to jail. The manetied man, Mr. F. N. McDowell, went to his brother, Mr. C. J. McDowell, and arranged to take Ross out of jail, on Ross promising that he would work for the former. Ross was glad to accept these terms and was put to work on Mr. Fred McDowell's farm. He soon married and took the name of Joe Wilson. In a settlement with Mr. F. N. McDowell, he was again found minus the mortgaged property and was sent to jail, but was soon taken out on promise that he would
joe-ross-1882-12-06.A12:
go to work. He had been out of jail but a short time when he foomed the conclusion to repay Mr. McDowell's kindness by murdering him. It was on a bright and peaceful Thanksgiving morning, when the victim of his hate, thinking of no harm and fearing no evil, rode up to his cabin door and was cruelly stricken down with an axe. The murdered man was a wealthy and most highly esteemed citizen of Camden, and the indignation which his brutal murder aroused may well be imagined. Three hundred citizens put out in search of the murderer with the determination not to return home without his body, dead or alive, and they carried it back dead.

AN OBJECT OF TERROR.

Joe Ross, from the time he killed Bob Hennegan, became an object of terror among the colored people of this county. He was frequently reported as having been seen going about with women's clothes on, and so great was the fear in which the colored people in this city held him, that often at night they would call for the police to accompany them to their houses, and once inside their own doors they would draw the bolt and keep everything securely fastened until sun up. Although the officers of the law made daily raids in search of Ross and kept the most diligent outlook, he could never be caught, and after a time the remembrance of the desperado and his shocking deed, gradually faded from the public mind, only to be revived by the startling events of the past few days.

The Governor offered a reward of $200 for Ross' body, which has never been recalled, and which, we suppose, still holds good and will be drawn by Ferryman Huntley. Ross' brother Tom was with the party hunting for him and was one among the first to arrive at the ferry house where the desperado lay wounded. He at once recognized the man as his brother Joe and exclaimed: "They've got you at last." The dead negro's body was placed in a wagon and carried to Lancaster, thence to Camden, the scene of the murder, to be delivered to the brother of the murdered man.—Charlotte Observer.
joe-ross-1882-12-06.A15:
The Murder of a Murderer.
Rock Hill, December 7.—Joe Ross, the murderer of Mr. McDowell, near Camden, was killed last night near Fort Mill by a ferryman who became engaged in an encounter with him because the ferryman refused to put him across the river. The Camden gentlemen on the hunt for him were about to catch him and he was trying to elude them by crossing the river. They had posted the ferryman.—Charleston News and Courier.
joe-ross-1882-12-06.A17:
End of the Notorious Joe Ross.
About a year ago a colored man, who called himself Joe Wilson, went to Camden, S. C., and hired to work for Mr. F. N. McDowell, a highly esteemed and wealthy citizen of that place. They had some difficulty about a business transaction, and the negro resolved to murder Mr. McDowell, and on thanksgiving day, Mr. McDowell rode over to the negro's house, when he got off his horse, and while in the act of stooping to arrange the saddle girth, Wilson took an ax and brutally murdered him. Wilson immediately fled, after concealing the body. Three hundred citizens started in pursuit determined to capture the murderer, and went to the house of his brother to learn any particulars, when he informed them that Joe, Wilson was none other than the notorious Joe Ross, one of the murderers of Bob Hennegan, in this county, two years ago, and for whom a reward of $200 was offered by the Governor. After an unsuccessful search in the vicinity of Charlotte, as it was rumored he had been here, the pursuing party returned to South Carolina, and on entering Lancaster county ascertained that a man answering their description had passed there and gone in the direction of Ivy's Mill. Ross was now hemmed in by the Catawba River, and realizing that the ferry was his only chance of escape, went to the ferryman's house and asked to be carried over. Mr. Huntley knew Ross, and asked him to have a seat at the fire, and as Ross sat down Mr. Huntley picked up his musket and told Ross to consider himself under arrest. The negro sprang and attempted to grasp the gun, but failed, when Mr. Huntley fired and Ross fell mortally wounded. The pursuing party soon arrived, and among them was the brother of Ross, who, when he saw him, exclaimed "they've got you at last." The negro was carried to an unoccupied house and placed on a bed of straw, and gave those around him an account of his fearful crimes. He fully realized he had but a short time to live, and he suffered terribly, and his confession was given in a broken voice. He told of the horrible murder of Mr. McDowell, and of the negro Bob Hennegan, with the assistance of Baxter, who was hung, and Ed. Harris, who turned State's evidence and was released. Ross was shot at 6:30 in the evening and died the next morning at 3 o'clock. His body was carried to Camden and delivered to his brother. Thus ends the career of a desperate murderer.

He was tied securely and Mr. Huntley went out to call in the men, who he had were near. When they all arrived at the scene, the negro was placed in a wagon and carried to the old Hagan house where a bed of straw was prepared for him. Upon this he was laid next to the gathered crowd, he proceeded to make his confession. At 5 o'clock in the morning, he died. He was shot at 6:00 the previous evening.

THE TERRIBLE CONFESSION.

One of the party drew out paper and ink and seated himself beside the dying negro to take down his last words, being a confession, told in a broken voice, of two savage murders which he had committed and for which he was soon to account before the Judge of all: He was suffering considerable pain and talked with considerable difficulty. He first confessed to the murder of Mr. F. N. McDowell, at Camden, and then told of the murder of the old negro Bob Hennegan, in this county, two years ago. His brother-in-law, he said, helped him to kill Mr. McDowell. He did the killing, but his brother dragged the body away, threw it in a dater and covered it with brush. He stated in detail that on the morning of last Thanksgiving day, Mr. McDowell rode up to his cabin and asked for him. "I was not in the house at the time, but soon came up and found Mr. McDowell standing by his horse, buckling the saddle girth. He said, 'hello, Joe, what's the matter with you?' I did not answer him, but went in the door and hind his back, picked up my axe and as he was bent down at the saddle, I knocked him in the head. I did not hit
ohind his back, picked up my axe and as he was bent down at the saddle, I knocked him in the head. I did not hit him but once, but that lick broke his skull all to pieces. My brother then charged the body to a ditch near by, threw it in and covered it with brush, and then came back and scraped up the blood from the ground." Ross then fled, came towards Charlotte, dodged about from place to place until he got to ivy's mill. This place, he said, was where he conceived himself after he had killed Bob Hennegan. It is... wild, rugged piece of country, and sale hiding place, and but for the party accidentally discovering his trail, he might now be hiding there in perfect safety.

The negro continuing his confession told how he waylaid Bob Hennegan, in this county abo't two years ago and with the assistance of two negroes, Marshall Baxter and El Harriss, beat his head to a pup and threw the lifeless body in the creek. El Harriss, he said, had more to do with it than Baxter did. Harriss, it will be remembered, turned State's evidence and was released. Baxter was tried and hung. Ross escaped and from that day to this has succeeded in outwitting the officers in their every effort to capture him.

WHY HE KILLED MCDOWELL.

Ross said he killed Mr. McDowell because that gentleman, for whom he had been working, had jailed him for selling mortgaged property. It seems that Tom Wilson, a brother of the murderer was living on Mr. C. J. McDowell's farm, and and to this brother's house Joe Ross came about a year ago, and hired himself out to work for Mr. McDowell, giving a mortgage on some hogs, etc., for money drawn. When settling time came, the mortgaged property was not forthcoming, and Ross was sent to jail. The manetied man, Mr. F. N. McDowell, went to his brother, Mr. C. J. McDowell, and arranged to take Ross out of jail, on Ross promising that he would work for the former. Ross was glad to accept these terms and was put to work on Mr. Fred McDowell's farm. He soon married and took the name of Joe Wilson. In a settlement with Mr. F. N. McDowell, he was again found minus the mortgaged property and was sent to jail, but was soon taken out on promise that he would

go to work. He had been out of jail but a short time when he foomed the conclusion to repay Mr. McDowell's kindness by murdering him. It was on a bright and peaceful Thanksgiving morning, when the victim of his hate, thinking of no harm and fearing no evil, rode up to his cabin door and was cruelly stricken down with an axe. The murdered man was a wealthy and most highly esteemed citizen of Camden, and the indignation which his brutal murder aroused may well be imagined. Three hundred citizens put out in search of the murderer with the determination not to return home without his body, dead or alive, and they carried it back dead.

AN OBJECT OF TERROR.

Joe Ross, from the time he killed Bob Hennegan, became an object of terror among the colored people of this county. He was frequently reported as having been seen going about with women's clothes on, and so great was the fear in which the colored people in this city held him, that often at night they would call for the police to accompany them to their houses, and once inside their own doors they would draw the bolt and keep everything securely fastened until sun up. Although the officers of the law made daily raids in search of Ross and kept the most diligent outlook, he could never be caught, and after a time the remembrance of the desperado and his shocking deed, gradually faded from the public mind, only to be revived by the startling events of the past few days.

The Governor offered a reward of $200 for Ross' body, which has never been recalled, and which, we suppose, still holds good and will be drawn by Ferryman Huntley. Ross' brother Tom was with the party hunting for him and was one among the first to arrive at the ferry house where the desperado lay wounded. He at once recognized the man as his brother Joe and exclaimed: "They've got you at last." The dead negro's body was placed in a wagon and carried to Lancaster, thence to Camden, the scene of the murder, to be delivered to the brother of the murdered man.—Charlotte Observer.

The Murder of a Murderer.
Rock Hill, December 7.—Joe Ross, the murderer of Mr. McDowell, near Camden, was killed last night near Fort Mill by a ferryman who became engaged in an encounter with him because the ferryman refused to put him across the river. The Camden gentlemen on the hunt for him were about to catch him and he was trying to elude them by crossing the river. They had posted the ferryman.—Charleston News and Courier.

A WHITE GIRL ASSAULTED BY A NEGRO.
Rock Hill, S. C., June 11.—This morning Alice McDowell, a white girl of fifteen years, while out with a party of children hunting for plums, was seized and assaulted by John Johnson, colored, age seventeen years. Her companions fled and gave the alarm. Johnson was caught and has confessed the crime. He will probably be lynched.

The Scoville Family Troubles.
WIFE HAVING A BILL FOR DIVORCE PREPAY
Mr. Scoville and his wife, while in Milwaukee on Saturday, to arrange for the repurchase of some property, which had been foreclosed under a mortgage, had a bitter quarrel in the presence of the lawyer. He accused her of having surrendered herself to the control of a Chicago news bureau, which she denied. Mrs. Scoville intimated that they had a similar row on the boat from Chicago, and that Scoville had threatened to jump overboard. While Mr. Scoville was arranging about the property, his wife was engaged with a lawyer in drawing up a bill for divorce, to be filed in the circuit court at Waukesha. She alleges a failure to support her as a cause for divorce. He will resist the divorce, not but that he desires a separation, but he objected to her procuring a divorce on that ground. He says she has no ground for a divorce from him, while he has cause for a divorce from her. The quarrel is described as a most unseemly one. Scoville spoke without apparent excitement, but with force and earnestness. Mrs. Scoville had more fire, sarcasm and bitterness in her repartees. Scoville believes that Guiteau will be hanged. Mrs. Scoville is again preparing to give public lectures.

Cardinal McCaleb and the Irish bishops have issued an address promising their support to the people in a peaceful agitation in securing their rights, but condemning illegal courses, especially secret societies.

Alice McDowell, a white girl of 15 years, yesterday at Rock Hill, N.C., while hunting for plums with other children, was seized and outraged by John Johnson, colored, aged 17.

The Egyptian Crisis.

OBJECT OF THE ALEXANDRIA RIOTERS.

LONDON, June 12.—Advices from Alexandria late last night state that the disturbances commenced simultaneously at three different points. The object of the rioters in a great measure appears to have been pillage, in which Levantines, as well as Arabs, participated. A regiment of cavalry and a regiment of infantry have been ordered to reinforce the garrison.

SIXTY-SEVEN EUROPEANS KILLED.

A telegram published in London says: The official report of the riot in Alexandria gives the number of Europeans killed as 67. Arabi Pacha and Mahmoud Pachi Saml had separate interviews with Dervisch Pacha yesterday. The result of the interview is not known, but it is generally believed that they submit to Dervisch Pacha's views.

CONTINUED EXCITEMENT IN ALEXANDRIA.

ALEXANDRIA, Monday morning.—Great excitement continues; all the shops are closed.

MORE ABOUT THE RIOTS—THE ENGINEER OF THE SUPERB KILLED.

LONDON, June 12.—The admiralty have received dispatches confirming the report of the murder of the engineer of the Superb. The fighting at Alexandria, expert the deliberate attack upon the consuls when proceeding to the residence of the governor, seems to have been confined to Arabs and Levantines. No English resident is reported to have been wounded.

The Times' correspondent at Cairo lays the responsibility for the riot upon Arabi Pacha. Dervisch Pacha had summoned him to resign, and there seemed to be no alternative but submission or defiance, but since the riots broke out Dervisch Pacha has had to appeal to Arabi Pacha, as commanding the only available force, to restore order.

THE KHEDIVE IN DANGER.

The correspondent of Reuter's Telegram company at Cairo telegraphs that at a meeting of the military leaders it was decided to petition the Khedive to abdicate. It was declared that if he did not he would be massacred. It is rumored that the cavalry and artillery will not join any conspiracy against the Khedive.

THE PROPOSED CONFERENCE.

The Times' correspondent at Berlin says it is proposed, seemingly at the suggestion of France, to hold a conference on the Egyptian question at Paris and not at Constantinople.

General Foreign News.

A DISASTROUS FLOOD.

LONDON, June 12.—A dispatch to the Standard from Pesth states that a disastrous flood has occurred at Versez owing to a sudden rising of the river. A number of houses and two bridges were destroyed. Twelve children and several adults were drowned.

GEN. IGNATIEFF BELIEVED.

St. PETERSBURG, June 12.—A decree is published announcing that Gen. Ignatieff, at his own request, has been relieved of the post of minister of the interior, on the ground of ill-health, and has been appointed president of the academy and a member of the senate. He retains his membership of the council of the empire and his adjutancy. Count Tolstoi, who was formerly president of the academy, has been appointed minister of the interior.

GAMBETTA TO VISIT ENGLAND.

LONDON, June 12.—The Times says M. Gambetta is likely to visit England next week.

ANOTHER EUROPEAN UNPLEASANTNESS.

MADRID, June 12.—The decision of the budget committee of the French chamber of deputies in postponing altogether the question of passing a grant to compensate the Spanish colonies who suffered by attacks of Arabs at Saida has produced considerable impression here. The opposition papers urge the government to obtain from France the fulfilment of her promise.

Trouble Among the Cohoes Strikers.

Cohoes, N.Y., June 12.—Five weavers went to work in the Harmony mill, to-day, under the ten per cent reduction. Great excitement prevails. Three thousand strikers are gathered about the mill gates, and threats are made to kill the seceders. The entire police force have been put on guard.

Stolen Bank Funds Recovered.

St. Louis, Mo., June 12.—A special to the Republican from Kirksville says: The wife of Frank Mason, the leader of the bank robbers, has delivered up $1,600 in gold, stolen from the Brookfield bank. A special grand jury has found indictments against all of the robbers, charging them with robbery and assault with intent to kill.

A Philadelphia Prize Fight.

PHILADELPHIA, June 12.—On Saturday morning, June 3d, a prize fight took place in the suburbs between Wm. Trappe, a grocer, and Wm. Murphy, a peddler, the stakes being $50 a side. It is alleged that the encounter came to a close by Murphy knocking Trappe down, and the latter striking his head against a stone and becoming unconscious. After medical treatment Trappe appears to have recovered, but on Tuesday last he fell on the pavement and hurt his head again. He was treated at the Pennsylvania hospital, but died there on Saturday evening. Murphy was arrested this morning and held to await the action of the coroner.

Ross in Training.

WINNIPEG, Man., June 12.—Ross resumed his training on the Red river to-day. He will claim the championship, as Hanlan fails on his second deposit.

Strike of New York Type Founders.

New York, June 12.—About fifty men, employed in Connor's type foundry, and a number of rubbers, employed by the firm of Farmer, Little & Co., also type founders, quit work this morning. They demand an increase of 15 per cent.

A New York Prize Fight.

TWENTY-ONE ROUNDS FOR $600 STAKES.

New York, June 12.—The prize fight between Benny Greene, of Providence, and Jim Murray, of this city, took place this morning near Fort Hamilton. Twenty-one rounds were fought, nearly all of them being in Murphy for the first time.
Benny Greene, of Providence, and Jim Murray, of this city, took place this morning near Fort Hamilton. Twenty-one rounds were fought, nearly all of them being in Murray's favor. At the last round Greene was carried insensible into his corner, his seconds throwing up the sponge. The stakes were $600.

The Iron Mills Resume Work.
CINCINNATI, OHIO, June 12.—The iron mills in this city, Covington, Newport, and Aurora, are all under headway to-day, under the agreement made on Saturday.

The National Mercantile Travelers' association will begin its session here to-morrow. The chief object of the meeting is to create an influence in favor of legal measures to protect the rights of traveling salesmen in the south and west.

Lynched This Morning.
CHARLESTON, S. C., June 12.—The negro John Johnson, who outraged Miss McDowell, at Rock Hill, yesterday, was lynched this morning.

The New York Horse Shoers' Strike.
NEW YORK, June 12.—The horse shoers, who, on Saturday last, were commanded by the union to quit work, resumed it this morning in the Second and Tenth avenue car stables, matters having been arranged satisfactorily. No additional concessions were reported this morning, and both sides maintain their position with determination.

THE $1,000 BOND PLATE.—Secretary Folger to-day said that he was satisfied that the $1,000 bond plate brought to light by the friends of Doyle, the counterfeiter, is not a genuine plate, but that it will be subjected to further examination by experts.

SECRETARY FOLGER will make no material change in the circular forbidding the carrying of dangerous oils on steamboats.

CHARLES BOOTH, aged 17, was drowned while bathing near Topeka, Kans., June 10.

MRS. MAGGIE LANGO, of Chicago, fell from a third-story window to the sidewalk, a distance of forty feet, June 10, striking on her head and shoulders, and she died on the way to the hospital.

AGILDIUS HOCK, a German, drew a razor from his pocket and cut his throat from ear to ear in St. Mary's Catholic Church, Buffalo, N. Y., June 11, and then rushed for the street, where he hacked himself again, and fell into the gutter and expired. The worshipers were transfixed with horror, women screamed and fainted, and great confusion prevailed.

THE Linn County Bank, at Brookfield, Mo., was entered on the afternoon of the 7th and robbed of nearly $5,000. Five men entered the bank, and while Cashier John Ford turned to make change presented drawn revolvers. The sixth man detained a lady at the front door while the robbery was going on. Cashier Ford and his sister-in-law were the only persons in the bank when the robbers entered. The thieves went out the back door, and left Brookfield in a northerly direction. Immediately after the robbery a posse of men, headed by the Marshal of Brookfield, gave hot pursuit, and after an exciting chase, during which shots were freely exchanged, the robbers were run into a log house, surrounded, and compelled to surrender. They gave their names as Winfield Allen, Frank Mason, Fred Mason, and Burt Ward.

THERE was a triple lynching at Lawrence, Kans., June 10. George Robertson, King, and Peter Vinagar, the negroes who murdered David Bausman, were taken from jail by masked men and hurried to the bridge, where ropes were placed about their necks and they were dropped off.

The envelope factory at Rockville, Conn., owned by White, Corbin & Co., was damaged by fire and water, June 10, to the extent of $100,000.

A powder magazine at Davenport, Iowa., was struck by lightning the other night. Stones were hurled in every direction, one weighing 80 pounds a quarter of a mile. A horse was killed at a distance by another stone. One was thrown into a house, striking a bed where two children slept. Windows were broken a mile away.

A boat containing four persons went over a dam on Fox River, June 11, and Mr. and Mrs. Priest, of Neenah, Wis., were drowned.

A boiler exploded at the Edgar Thompson steel works, Braddock, Pa., June 11. Assistant Superintendent Adair was fatally injured and three workmen were hurt.

Mrs. J. W. Barrett, of Washington, D. C., was killed on the steamer Star of the East, at Bath, Me., June 10, by a collision with a schooner. Several other passengers were seriously injured. The steamer was greatly damaged.

James Freeman, 23 years of age, of Acton, Mass., shot himself through the heart, June 11.

Mary Connors, residing in New York, has been placed in the Tombs on a charge of deliberately starving a small boy.

Two unknown tramps were cremated in a barn at Painesville, Ohio, June 10. The fire is attributed to careless smoking.

At Malden, England, the other day, Sir Claude de Crespigny made an ascension with an aeronaut named Simmonds, intending to cross the Channel. The car struck a house, and De Crespigny fell out and broke his leg. Simmonds was swept onward, and was seen over Calais in the afternoon.

JOHN JOHNSON, a negro who assaulted a little white girl, was taken from jail at Rock Hill, S. C., June 12, and hanged to a tree.

J. H. HARTMAN, aged 15, rushed out of his father's house, near Davenport, Iowa, the other night, and ended his career by plunging into the river. His mind had been affected for some time, presumably by bathing while too warm.

An obstinate cow threw a Baltimore & Ohio train from the track, near Martinsburg, W. Va., June 11, causing a general wreck. Several passengers and a newsboy were injured—none seriously.

PUGILISTS of Providence, named James Murray and Benjamin Green, went to Coney Island to contend for $300 and the light-weight championship of Rhode Island. Three rounds had been fought in a hotel when the metropolitan police captured Murray and his second, the others escaping.

The United States Commissioner at Buffalo, N. Y., held R. Porter Lee and Herman J. Hall for trial in the federal court at Canandaigua for embezzling the funds of the First National Bank. Lee's bail was fixed at $150,000, and he will lie in jail. Hall will be released on giving $10,000 security for his appearance.

A BILL has been introduced in the House of Representatives to grant permission to Fenton Sherwood, George Tenyeck and William Lewis to dig in the Government grounds of West Point for the treasure said to have been buried there by Capt. Kidd. These men claim that they are able to locate the buried wealth, and only want the assurance that when it is found it will be theirs. They had written to the Secretary of War, but were told that, in the absence of legislation, if they succeeded in unearthing the treasure it would belong to the Government. CRIMES AND CRIMINALS.
A masked mob of 100 men burst the doors of the jail at Lawrence, Kan., secured Peter Vinegar, Isaac King and George Robertson, and hung them to the bridge timbers, for the recent murder of Daniel Bausman.

Lynching as a penalty for atrocious crimes is becoming a common occurrence in various parts of the country. Three cases of the kind occurred in one day last week. A negro in South Carolina guilty of outraging a white girl, a negro in Mississippi who had attempted the same crime upon a child, and a half-witted railroad laborer who had killed a fellow-workman at Las Vegas, N. M., were the victims.

At Lawrence, Kan., a public meeting of colored men denounced the lynching of the three negroes who murdered farmer Bausman. Tibbetts, the boy hanged for a double murder at Perham, Minn., is said to have been instigated to the crime by his own mother.

A dispatch from Las Vegas, N. M., says that "four rustlers, who bound and gagged Mason, a store-keeper, near Mesilla recently, robbing his store of all they could carry, were overtaken by a Mexican posse and strangled. All were Americans, but their names are unknown. They belonged to a gang of Arizona cowboys and richly deserved their fate."

In the jail at Geneva, Kane county, Ill., Deputy Sheriff Lawson killed James Irwin for a savage assault upon him and an attempt to release twenty prisoners. The officer was promptly vindicated by a Coroner's inquest.

The Brockfield bank robbers pleaded guilty, and received sentences of twenty-five years each in the Missouri Penitentiary. Their household effects were disposed of at auction at Kirksville, Mo., and brought enormous prices.

George McMillen, of Canton, Ohio, killed his wife with a revolver as she lay in bed, then fired a shot in his own shoulder and called the police, to whom he stated that a strange woman did the shooting.

—A negro named Mitchell was lynched at Mount Sterling, Ky., for a brutal outrage upon the wife of a respectable farmer.

Schumacher fatally shot Policeman Schweimer, who had called to make his arrest; then mortally wounded his wife, who had taken refuge on a neighbor's porch, and then lay down on his bed and killed himself. The Fitz John Porter Case.

WASHINGTON, November 27th. — The bill for the restoration of Fitz John Porter to the army is set for consideration for the first Wednesday in December, and the contest over the case is expected to be renewed at that time. Morrill will undoubtedly antagonize it with his tax bill, which in view of the general clamor of the press to have something done in the way of financial legislation, may cause the regular order to be set aside. Should such contingency not arise, a controversy that will be memorable in the annals of the Senate is expected to ensue. Should the bill for Porter's relief be taken up for consideration, Porter's friends manifest more confidence than they have ever heretofore shown in the result, occasioned by the favorable action of the President some months ago, and the effect of Grant's opinion.

Rich, but Not Yacht Happy.

NEW York, November 27th. — Cramp, who is building Jay Gould's yacht, has been in consultation with the Naval Advisory Board. He says his contract with Gould does not give him any definite number of knots, but to do the best that can be done with a vessel 212 feet long with a fixed breadth of beam. He says Gould cannot bear to be tantalized. A New York silk dealer named Jarrett lives above Gould on the Hudson. He has a yacht 112 feet long, which habitually passes Gould's present yacht on the river. Jarrett, it seems, has a vicious way of coming down and firing a gun as he passes Gould's landing, then when he passes him on the river he beckons to him in a mocking and dreadful way from the deck of his yacht. Gould has no idea of going around the world, but does intend to stop this impertinence. The new yacht will be nearly all boilers and engines, and will probably be the fastest vessel ever built.

**The Railroad War Probably Ended.**

CHICAGO, November 27th.—The *Times* this morning publishes correspondence between Jay Gould and the Presidents of the roads in the Northwest, now engaged in the rate war, which shows that Mr. Gould proposed, and Mr. Riddle and Mr. Mitchell favored, a meeting for arbitration and the restoration of rates to-day, which establishes the genuineness of the dispatch, which had been denied. There is also reason to believe that a plan of adjustment will be agreed upon within twenty-four hours.

**Unloverlike Conduct.**

LANESBORO, November 27th.—Christian Johnson, after fireing what he supposed to be a fatal shot at his afflianced, blew his brains out. The girl was only slightly hurt.

**Nebraska's Vote.**

LINGOLN, November 27th.—Figures show that Dawes' (Rep.) majority for Governor over Morton (Dem.) was 14,936. Average Republican vote on State officers, 44,180; Democrats, 26,847; anti-monopoly, 17,187.

**The Loss of His Cue Causes a Chinaman to Kill Himself.**

CAIRO (Ill.), November 27th.—A Chinaman came ashore from a river steamer yesterday, and in wandering about town had his pig-tail cut off. The loss of it made him so desperate that he beat his head shockingly, and, being stopped by some men, jumped in the river and was drowned.

**The Trial of Frank James.**

KANSAS CITY (Mo.), November 27th.—Frank James was brought here to-day, and will be arraigned at 3 o'clock. His transfer from Independence was effected very quietly.

[SECOND DISPATCH.]

KANSAS CITY, November 27th.—Frank James appeared in Court this afternoon and pleaded not guilty to the indictments for the Independence Bank robbery in 1869 and the murder of detective Wilcher in 1874. His trial on these was fixed for January 22d next, and James was taken back to Independence this evening.

**Archbishop Purcell's Indebtedness.**

CINCINNATI, November 27th.—An article is published to-day, signed "Repudiating Priests," designed to show the creditors of Archbishop Purcell that it will be impossible to do more than temporarily relieve the distress occasioned by his failure, and co-operate in a plan to wipe out the stain upon the Catholic Church caused by it. The Church, they say, is in no manner bound to pay it, as it was purely a private debt.

**Destruction by Fire.**

CARROLLTON (Ill.), November 27th.—Ardinger & Piper's flour mills were burned yesterday. Loss, $18,000; insured for $12,000.

**Death's Doings.**

CHICAGO. November 27th.—General Hamilton N. Eldridge, a distinguished soldier, lawyer and citizen, died this morning, aged 49.

HAMILTON (O.). November 27th.—Lewis D. Campbell, prominent in State politics, for many years Chairman of the Ways and Means Committee in Congress, but lately retired from public life, died yesterday.

NEW YORK, November 27th.—Thomas Le Clare, the artist, died last night.

**Winter Fairly Commenced.**

CHICAGO, November 27th.—Snow was quite general yesterday in the Northwest, four to six inches falling. It is now cool and threatening a further fall to-day. Trains are not much delayed on any roads.

CHEBOYGAN (Mich.). November 27th.—Nine inches of snow fell here last night.

**A Disgusted Clergyman.**

BLOOMINGTON (Ill.), November 27th.—ExRev. Hoffman, expelled from the clergy for unclearly conduct, refuses to attempt an appeal, declaring that spite and malignity, instead of Christian justice, has been awarded him. This ends the ecclesiastical trial, but the criminal case still impends.

**A Family Well Provided For.**

NEW YORK, November 27th.—The will of the late George O. Osgood makes the following bequests: To his wife, $600,000, beside his house furniture; his sister Elizabeth Ann, $200,000; his sister Nancy, $200,000; his sister Pauline, $50,000; his brothers Franklin and William, $100,000 each; to James H. Platt, for the benefit of his brothers and sisters, $200,000.

**Killed While Resisting an Officer.**

CAMPBELLSVILLE (Ky.), November 27th.—Officer Wm. Jones attempted to arrest a colored man, Julius Hart. The latter resisted, when Jones shot and killed Hart, and was himself arrested by the Town Marshal. He had an examination trial and was acquitted.

The Interior Journal wants hogs kept off the streets of Stanford.

In one voting precinct in Todd county, 17 babies were born in three days.

Geo. Ford"and Christian Helm, both young men. suicided in Louisville, last week.

Henry Coleman stepped on John Clark's toe at Lexington, and Clark challenged him to fight a duel. They went to a field near by and fought with pistols, exchanging several shots. Both men were wounded and it is thought Coleman will not recover. Clark who was shot in the leg was arrested.

At a dance at the house of John Mooney, in Indian Territory, on the night of the 10th inst., two young men named Montgomery and Horton got into a quarrel, which ended in both drawing pistols and shooting several times at each other. Montgomery was killed outright and Horton mortally wounded.

Two laborers named Monahan and MacAvoy quarreled at Steubenville, O., on the 11th inst. The latter was fatally stabbed.

At Linkville, Oregon, on the night of the 11th inst., a mob of masked men attempted to take a murderer named H. C. Lewis from the jail. Lewis fired on the mob, who responded with a volley, which killed the deputy sheriff and wounded Justice Wright. The would-be lynchers then retired.

A terrible tragedy was enacted at a school house at Harrisburg, Pernsett County, Ark., on the 7th inst. County Treasurer J. J. Smith remonstrated with the teacher for whipping his child. The conversation became heated and finally led to Smith's striking E. J. Wilmot, the teacher, on the head with a billet of wood, crushing his skull. The injured man died in three hours.

In a drunken quarrel at New Orleans on the night of the 7th inst., Richard Shea was stabbed to death by James Cosgrove.

An aged couple named O'Massey, living near Charlottesville, Va., were found murdered on the morning of the 8th inst., in their house. Money was the object.

A mob took Charles Shelton, John Redmond and Harry French from the jail at Los Lunas, Cal., on the 8th inst., and hung them to a tree.

A courtesan named Mary Sigman and her mother were assassinated at Mount Vernon, Ky., on the 8th inst.

A remarkable story comes from the City of Mexico. The report is that highwaymen attacked a stage full of armed men and that eleven of the outlaws were killed.

It is reported that nine Europeans journeying from Tunis to Gafsa were murdered between Tunis and Kairwan.

Advices from New Mexico are to the effect that Deputy Sheriff Miers and Martinez with a posse were attacked by Pueblo Indians while attempting to arrest some of the Pueblos who had escaped from jail. Miers was killed and Martinez mortally wounded.

A shocking tragedy took place at Boston, Mass., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Harriet Bell while returning from a grocery store near her home was accosted by an unknown man who followed her to the doorstep of her home and then cut her throat. She lived but a short time. The assassin escaped.

A brace of cattle thieves named Arnold Howard and Frank Young, in jail at Del Noter, Col., were visited by a mob on the 7th inst. Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded.

An affray with pistols took place at Arkansas City, on the 5th inst., in which J. W. Hale was killed by John Fuller.

Three negroes—Lewis Smith and Aaron and Ed. Clark—were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia, Ark., on the 6th inst. The shooting was done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

Tax Collector Robert Taylor was shot dead by Dr. Sims at Perryville, Perry County, Ark., on the 4th inst.

squirrels where M. G. & J. Cohen's store now is, and had a turkey blind at the book store corner. He also had something to say about snakes, but it being past our dinner time we excused ourself and withdrew."

Thomaston correspondent Constitution: "Alice McCoy, colored, boarded the train en route to Barnesville from here, and when Conductor Hammond came around he found Alice in the ladies car, and tellin her to get out she refused. Chronicle and Constitutionalist: "Work on King Factory is progressing rapidly. Workmen are busily employed in all directions in breaking, leveling and hauling the ground where it will soon rear itself alongside the Sibley Mills. The foundation of the principal building will soon be completed. There are also in operation two brick molds. They both turn out about 50,000 brick daily. The clay is first wet and fed into the molds on one side as mud and comes out on the other side made into the form of bricks. They are then piled in rows, and after having been thoroughly dried by the sun, are put in the kins and subjected to a great heat for about five days, and then allowed to cool, and are afterwards taken out ready for being used to form the walls of the factory."

Atlanta Post-Appeal: "W. S. Wilson & Bro., coal and lumber dealers on Spring street, exhibited a shattered safe to a reporter this morning which showed the skill of an artist in safe burglary. A hole was drilled near the combination, filled with powder, the fastening blown asunder and the contents of the safe left to the mercy of the depreyders. They riffed the drawers and took the little iron box from its fastening, and going out to the lumber yard tipped it open with a chisel and scooped in its contents, leaving the box and a small drawer contained in it on a lumber pile. The Messrs Wilson are somewhat reticent as to the amount contained in the box, but state that there were fifty dollars in the drawer and a number of checks, which latter were left. The box may have contained one hundred or five hundred dollars. An entrance to the office was effected through the door, which offered little resistance. No cue was left as to who the thief or thieves were. It would be well, while these safe burglars are sojourning with us, for those who have no burglar proof safe to deposit their valuables in a vault for safety."

Monroe Advertiser: "The store of Mr. R. M. Williams, at iceberg, was entered and robbed last Thursday night. The store is set upon a rock foundation. This was broken through and the burglaries thereby got into the cellar and had no difficulty in entering the store therefrom. A large quantity of goods was stolen—value of which cannot well be calculated. Several of the negro workmen on the railroad were arrested on suspicion Friday, and tried before a magistrate, but the proof was not strong enough to warrant their commitment. None of the goods have been found. On Saturday a white man, named A. S. Averitt, was arrested in Macon, as the burglar. He had sold of the stolen goods, and thus he was traced. Mr. Williams being notified of his arrest, sent Mr. Little to Macon after him. He confessed the crime to Mr. Little, and had already confessed to the policeman who arrested him. He was brought to Forsyth and is now in jail. He seems to be a respectable man, and expresses deep regret for his crime, says it is his first offense and shall be his last. He is from Futnam county, and was at work on the railroad, previous to his crime."

Augusta News, 11th: "A young boy was saved from drowning in the canal this morning through the timely arrival and heroic exertions of a gentleman passing near the scene on McKinne street, over the third level of the canal. The little fellow, John Hardman, who lives in that neighborhood, fell into the water while playing with some companions, about a hundred yards from McKinne street. Their exertions to rescue him as he floated down the stream, which is swift at that place, were confined to holding out sticks to him, and while grasping at them he was several times carried under the water. While drifting helplessly along and when about to fail in strength he was seen by Dr. Frank M. Deems, Mr. George Howard and one or two others passing along the street. The two gentlemen named jumped from their vehicles, rushed down the bank, and Dr. Deems, who was first at the water, called to Mr. Howard to stay on the bank and not to jump in unless necessary. Dr. Deems then plunged n the water and swam out to the little fellow, who was about to sink for the last time. With the grasp of a dying man, he seized Dr. Deems as he reached him, and both went under the water. Rising to the surface, the Doctor pushed for the bank with his burden, and was sssisted by Mr. Howard and his colored driver, Eugene. Both were pulled out of the water exhausted. Dr. Deems administered restoratives to the little fellow, and, after sending him home and going across the street to his own residence, nursed him until he was all safe."

There has been less sold so far than for the same period at any time in the last eight years. The price varies in different localities, and in some places standard fertilizers sell as low as four hundred pounds of middling cotton per ton."

Cartersville Free Press: Work on the ore banks at Bartow iron works has been suspended on account of a mortgage of $60,000 being foreclosed. Your Uncle Joseph E. Brown swooped down upon it. We have not as yet learned when operations will again commence. The car factory is working on full time, although without as many hands as before the explosion, the engine not being of sufficient power to work so many. Their new engine will probably arrive within a month.

We learn that the man, Peter Corbin, charged with committing an outrage on a lady in Gilmer county, who was arrested in this place week before last by deputy marshal King and turned over to the sheriff of said county, mention of which was made in this paper, was taken from the Gilmer county jail, the night after the sheriff returned to Ellijay with him, by a party of masked men and was found the next day in a piece of woods near the town with his head completely severed from his body. We are opposed to lynch law under any circumstances, and hope the story is not true.—Dalton Citizen.
munroe-bloom-norcross-1882-03-16.A7:
The dwelling of Mrs. Thomas Macey, near Sulphur Spring, Meriwether county, was destroyed by fire on Wednesday.

A negro named D. Nance was seriously hurt while hauling timber for Mr. J. I. Kemp, near McVille, on Monday last.

The Rome Bulletin learns that twenty-six new engines have been ordered for the Rome extension of the Macon and Brunswick Road. Rogers & Cook's make were ordered, owing to the fact that the Baldwin Works are overrun with orders.

A little son of Mr. A. J. Buchanan, of Americus, was tossed by a vicious cow, one day last week. He was not much hurt, however.

Mr. A. J. Ronder, an old citizen of Heard county, was found recently lying in a gully and greatly exhausted. He had been very feeble for some time, and it is supposed fell down and could not help himself. The exposure was so great that he died shortly after being conveyed home.

Mr. Michael Hartley died recently, in Crawford county, at the age of ninety-seven years.

Mr. David Robinson writes from Albany, under date of Saturday, as follows: "A fine stream of water now flows from our artesian well at a depth of 580 feet. The water commenced to flow to-day at noon. We are still drilling deeper for a stream of more force."

Wiregrass Watchman: "The Darien timber market is very low and we can't for the life of us see why people will persist in cutting it. Timber at the present prices and guano together is fast running this section of Georgia."

Sylvania Telephone: "A very touching scene was witnessed at the Methodist Church in this place on Sunday night last, when the pastor requested the congregation to kneel in prayer for our stricken Representative. There was not one of the large congregation but what knelt without hesitation, and a more sincere and general feeling of sympathy we have never seen."

Americus Recorder: "While the Wide Awakes were throwing water last Thursday the pipemen swung their nozzle around in a half circle, and as the sun shone upon the falling spray a beautiful rainbow appeared, extending the distance of about 200 feet, and making an arch about forty feet high. It was one of the prettiest sights we ever witnessed."

Athens Banner-Watchman: "There are not ordinary and well-behaved set of young
making an arch about forty feet high. It was one of the prettiest sights we ever witnessed."

Athens Banner-Watchman: "There are not a more orderly and well-behaved set of young men in the South than the students at the State University. They are quiet, sober and gentlemanly and attract the attention of strangers by their deportment. We do not know a young man in the University who is addicted to drink or dissipation. They are certainty a credit to the State and to themselves."

Hampton Weekly: "Last Friday night some party or parties forced an entrance into the Arcade saloon and feloniously purloined several packages of choice liquor, six dollars in money and a fine breech-loading shotgun belonging to Mr. E. R. James. Entrance was effected by means of a large rock, with which the door was beaten in, and which was found lying on the three-hold next morning. This occurred in the full glare of a street lamp, which stood not more than twenty feet away."

Cedartown Advertiser: "On Thursday evening last, as the young sons of Dr. Chas. H. Harris were riding his horses to water at Cedar creek and were going at a very rapid pace, Seals, who is about eleven years old, saw the horse he was riding about to go between two trees, and endeavored to rein him so as to avoid them. He was unable to do so, and came in such violent contact with one of the trees that his leg was broken above the knee. He has had the best of attention, and at last accounts was doing well."

Augusta News: "A gentleman from Burke county informs the News this morning that forest fires for several days past have been very destructive to fences, woods, corded wood, and in one instance a residence was destroyed, being that known as the Goff house, some miles from Waynesboro. In the neigh borhood of Green's Cut Dr. Powell and Captain Walton lost large y in fencing, as also did Mr. Pink Thomas and others. Great quantities of corded wood have been destroyed. Mr Keener, living near this city, has lost thirty cords recently."

Cochran Enterprise: "One negro shot and killed another on Tuesday last at Bishop & Co.'s mill, near No. 12 (Chauncey), M. & B. R. R. The two quarreled and one of them started for his gun, which was a short distance away, and the other drew his little pistol and shot at him twice, one ball striking him in the back and coming out just above the navel. He got his gun, but when he got back his antagonist had fled the field. When our informant left, a few hours after, the wounded man was dying. The murderer is still at large. We could not learn the names of the parties."

Meriwether Vindicator: "Charlie, son of Mr. W. P. Findley, has been spending several months at Senoia with his grandfather, Mr. J. R. Heard. Recently the boy ran down to the
Meriwether Vindicator: "Charlie, son of Mr. W. P. Findley, has been spending several months at Senoia with his grandfather, Mr. J. B. Heard. Recently the boy ran down to the train to mail a letter. The letter being mailed, the little boy stepped back to the platform, and overcome by his exertion in running, as it is supposed, he swooped and fell to the ground, a distance of several feet. In falling his breast struck the end of a crosstie. Since that time Charlie has lost all appetite, and is frequently attacked with such paroxysms of pain as to render his screams almost heart-rending. He is carefully attended by Dr Brantley, who pronounced his case a most singular one."

Columbus Times: "Mr. Fred, Little, of Allen's Station, Richmond county, said in his essay at the Georgia Agricultural Convention, in Augusta: 'In his opinion the best land for watermelon culture was a sandy loam, and if possible, a place which had laid out for some time, and had grown up in small pines and broom sedge. He then proceeded to give his method of culture. When the plants are well established they should be thinned down to one plant to a hill if large melons are desired, and this is very requisite if the melons are intended for sale.' The most popular melon in this market the past season was the Mountain Sweet and a long white or gray rhind, and we hope the market gardeners will be prepared to supply the market with fine ones the present season, hence we publish the above."

Rome Bulletin, 24th: "Yesterday afternoon quite a serious accident happened to Mr. J. Monroe Neal, of Cartersville. He had engaged a horse from one of our livery stables for the purpose of going out into the country to see Mr. Mitchell. Just as he got opposite Messrs. King & Bros' store, the horse was moving at a pretty lively speed, when Mr. Neal, not wanting to go so fast, gave the rein a sudden jerk, the horse rearing up and falling backwards, throwing Mr. Neal to the ground. He was assisted into Langey's store and Dr. Hoyt was summoned immediately. After a careful examination it was found that he had sustained a severe sprain in the small of the back. Besides this he suffered from acute pains in his feet, the horse having fallen across them. As good luck would have it, he fell a little to one side, thereby saving his life, as the horse fell directly backward. Mr. Neal is a prominent young attorney from Cartersville."

Jonesboro News: "On Wednesday of last week Munroe Bloom, colored, was killed by Mr. Felix Adamson, L. C., at Morrows Station, in this county. Mr. Adamson had warrants for the arrest of two negroes charged withorgery. He found them at Morrows Station, and required Munroe Bloom to consider himself a prisoner; but Munroe refused to be arrested, draw his pistol and spawn it at Mr. Adamson."

SOUTHERN GLEANINGS.
the swamps of Louisiana, until herds were driven from their fastnesses by the high water of the present season. In the immediate vicinity of Natchez there have been hundreds, and we may probably be speaking within bounds when we say thousands, of these beautiful animals, which have crossed the river within the space of a few miles above and below this city. Worn and exhausted as they have been, after their long swim across the swollen river, they would have fallen an easy prey to the pot-hunters who only hunt for profit, had it not been for the extraordinary exertions of the true sportsmen of the county, and humane people who despise wanton cruelty. On Sunday last, several gentlemen found a number of deer that had fallen into a ravine, from which they found it impossible to get out. With true humanity they went to work and dug a pathway by which the little animals could find their way out of the ravine, helped them to mount to the top of the bank, and sent them on their way rejoicing to the green woods of the country. Instances of the same kind of humane feeling have been, we are glad to say, the rule with the people of this vicinity, while the disposition to capture and kill the deer has been the exception. —Natchez Democrat.

At Burkeville, Newton County, Tex., there is on the premises of Judge M. D. Hines a well of ordinary width and depth, to obtain water from which two buckets are used. These are connected by a rope, which passes over a wheel suspended from a frame above the curbing. The contrivance is a simple one, the arrangements being such that as one bucket is drawn up the other descends. The strange feature about the well is that at irregular periods, and without any visible or known cause, the buckets will change places, the empty one descending to the bottom and the filled one rising to the top of the well.

Mrs. Coker, with her three children, in an ox-cart, was recently returning home from Perry, Ga. The road they traveled passed through very rank wire-grass, which had been set on fire. In trying to get out of the way the cart and oxen became fastened among pine logs, and the fire overtook them. The cart, with the two children inside, was consumed and the oxen were burned to death. The woman attempted to escape with her infant, but her clothing caught fire and she and the other child were so badly burned that they have since died.

A novel suit has been entered by a citizen of Atlanta, Ga. He has been unable, after two years of trial, to get a place in the public schools. He now proposes to resist the payment of the school-tax by law, and has employed an attorney to take the matter in hand. He says: "I do not see why I should be taxed to support the schools when I can not get any representation in them. I have the same right of any other citizen to send my boy, and yet there are hundreds of others who get schooling and I have none. I do not think they can collect a school-tax when they refuse to let me send my son to the school."

The owner of the cave deposits of bat guano in Uvalde County, Texas, says the supply can not be exhausted in a century. An analysis shows over 11 per cent. of ammonia. The caves have recently been reached by railroad tracks, and the first shipment has been made. The product is expected to bring $50 per ton.

For several months says the Conyers (Ga.) Weekly, one of our citizens has been noticing that his butcher invariably let his hand rest on the meat slightly when he weighed it, and he reweighed it at home and found it from a half to a pound short. He kept an account of these deficiencies, and when they aggregated one hundred pounds he took out an attachment for the butcher's hand, claiming that it rightly belonged to him, he having more than paid for it.

The region south of Memphis is swarming with buffalo-gnats, which are killing what little stock was saved from drowning.

The New Orleans Gas-Light Company has been declared by Judge Pardee to have no legal existence.

Out of a total vote of 640, Bryan, Tex., gave a majority of 377 for liquor prohibition.

A convicted horse-thief named Bondy jumped from a train near San Antonio, Tex., last week, and was shot dead by the guards.

Two negroes, who were resisting arrest for forgery, were shot by a constable at Morrow's Station, Ga., a few days ago. Both escaped, but one, named Bloom, was afterward found dead in the woods. The negroes had first shot at the constable.

One hundred families have moved into Birmingham, Ala., since the 1st of December.

Gov. Colquitt, of Georgia, has determined not to call an extra session of the Legislature for the purpose of redistricting the State.

Eighty-five thousand tons of fertilizers were sold in North Carolina for the year 1881.

Silk culture in Louisiana has of late become a thriving industry, and promises an abundant production.

In 1865 Florence, S. C., contained only ten houses. It now has a population of over 2,000, and last year over 100 houses were built.

A Justice of the Peace in Atascosa County, Texas, says that he has assessed but two fines for misdemeanors during eight years.

Watermelons are up and doing well in Georgia. Three hundred acres are planted in Brooks County.

Representative Black, of Georgia, is seriously ill. He is not expected to recover.

Macon, Ga., had a $50,000 fire the other day, and Mr. R. B. Watson, cotton broker, perished in the flames.
Floriada is full of tourists.
During the past week, says the Greenville (N. C.) News, about 140 colored people have left this section for points west and south. It has been developed upon investigation that labor bureaus are in active operation in Texas and Louisiana, which have been organized for the purpose of meeting the large demand made by sugar and cotton planters in those States for laborers.
Isidore Levy, of New Orleans, who was arrested for arson at the instance of the insurance companies and was acquitted, has brought suit against the underwriters for $100,000.
Faber gets the wood for his pencils from Cedar Keys, Fla.
A company proposes to supply the city of Atlanta, Ga., with water by a canal and aqueduct of forty miles from the River Chattahoochee. The cost of the undertaking will be $2,500,000, and the revenue will come from the use of the water by the city and the rent of power to private enterprises. o-neill-dublin-1882-11-23.A1:
RED HANDED CRIME.
A Singular Murder in a Jersey Town.
Hance H. Gant, a wealthy farmer resid

Hance H. Gant, a wealthy farmer residing near Osborneville, New Jersey, was recently found dead in his house with a bullet hole in his body. The ramrod of his gun was lashed to a child's cradle beside the body, but the gun was found in a room below. His wife and children say they did not carry the gun down stairs. Detectives are investigating the matter.

A Murderer Narrowly Escapes Lynching.

The body of Taylor Dunbar, a grocer of Darlington, Iowa, was found in a field near that place on Friday, bearing marks of violence. A young man named Joseph Stout, with whom he had left home, was arrested on suspicion next day, and confessed his guilt, the motive being robbery. The excitement was so great in Darlington that Stout was remanded in Crawfordsville, to avoid mobs desirous of lynching him.

Arrested and Robbed of His Earnings.

Morris Berwald, aged 18 years, while going home, in New York city, early yesterday morning, was followed by two men and importuned for money. After repeated refusals they stabbed and shot him in an obscure street and made off with his week's wages, amounting to $6. It is feared the young man's wounds are fatal.

Riddled With Bullets.

Last Thursday night four men entered the house of a man named O'Neill, near Dublin, Georgina, took him out and riddled his body with bullets. Some negroes who had an old grudge against O'Neill are suspected of the murder.

Fatally Stabbed His Father.

William Donovan, aged 24 years, fatally stabbed his father with a carving knife in Jersey City on Saturday night, because the old man interfered to stop a quarrel between him and a younger brother.
o-neill-dublin-1882-11-23.A4:
Innocent Man Lynched.
MACON, GA., Dec. 4.—Counnell O'Neal, colored, was tied to a tree and riddled with bullets for an alleged assault on a little girl. He is now found to have been innocent of the crime.

The Archbishop's Funeral.
LONDON, Dec. 4.—The funeral of the late Archbishop of Canterbury will take place on Friday. The remains will be interred in Addington Churchyard.

Suicide in Baltimore.
BALTIMORE, MD., Dec. 4.—William H. Butler, aged 21, shot himself in the heart while in a house of ill-fame on North street to-day.

Attempted Suicide.

Attempted Suicide.
AUBURN, N. Y., Dec. 4.—G. H. Van Dyke, aged 49, shot himself through the temple this morning. He still lives.

Another Pasha Exiled.
LONDON, Dec. 4.—A dispatch from Constantinople to the Daily News says that Dervish Pasha is to be exiled.

Paris Under Water.
PARIS, Dec. 4.—The River Selno has so overflowed its banks that a part of this city is inundated.

Another Old Friend Going.
LONDON, Dec. 4.—Anthony Trollope, the novelist, has had a relapse and he is dying.

Shields for English Policemen.

The London Post says: "The Stafford County constabulary are about to be supplied with an ingenious though simple addition to their present means of defense. Mr. Oswell, the deputy chief constable of the county, whose experience of the risks run by the police in hand-to-hand encounters with the rougher elements of a mining and agricultural population extends over upward of twenty years, has invented a light wicker shield to be worn by the police when on night duty, or under circumstances in which they are likely to be brought into conflict with the more desperate characters of the Staffordshire district. The shield is oval in form, and, though very light, is so constructed of carefully-woven willow twigs as to be at once strong and serviceable. The willow work is strengthened by a backbone of quarter-inch ash, running through the centre of the shed and projecting an inch or two at each end. The dimensions of the shed are 23 by 13, and on the inner side there are two semi-circular pieces of rounded leather, so fixed that while the forearm is thrust through one, the other is grasped by the hand. The shield is slung at the back by a strap passing over the shoulder and under the left arm in such a way that it can be instantaneously hitched round to the front. The arm having been put through the leather handles, a single pull detaches the strap supporting the shield, which can then be elevated to cover the head in case of assault with stones and bludgeons. Mr. Oswell thinks that if padded on the inner side with cotton-wool the shield would resist the ordinary gunshot used by poachers at as short a distance as fifteen yards. Two small holes left in the basket work afford the constable, while protecting his head, the opportunity of seeing the movements of his assailants."

It is now clearly established that he did not commit the crime. —Cincinnati Times-Star.

o-neill-dublin-1882-11-23.A8:
THE SOUTHERN STATES.
The Charleston, South Carolina, musical festival was a success.

A colored man is successfully growing bananas at Dublin, Georgia.

Capt. R. B. Rowley has been made chief of the New Orleans police.

An overdose of morphine ended the life of Leon Royer, at New Orleans.

The Alabama legislature will take a recess from December 12 to January 24.

A fire at Bathurst's tannery, Nashville, did $1500 damage Saturday morning.

Pensacola has thrown aside her mourning habiliments, and has given the first hop of the season.

Near Dublin, Georgia, Counce O'Neal, an obnoxious colored man, was taken from his bed by white men and shot to death.

The Savannah, Georgia, News predicts that as much money will be invested in cotton factories and cotton seed oil mills in the south next year as there has been this.

Rice Buckley, who was crippled by a train on the Louisville and Nashville railroad last December, has recovered $700 damages against the road at Bartlett, Tennessee.

Near Camden, South Carolina, F. M. McDowell, a prominent citizen, was killed with an ax by Joe Wilson, colored, who threw the body of his victim in a ditch and covered it with brush. The murderer escaped, and will probably be lynched if caught.

Conyers, Georgia, is greatly excited over the elopement of an old, gray-headed school teacher named Dowdy, a married man, with a fourteen-year-old girl pupil named Ragsdale. They went to South Carolina, but were overtaken, and the girl carried back home.

The Savannah News says Georgia gave thanks for a corn crop, the largest since 1872, which will reach 30,000,000 bushels; an oat crop of 8,000,000 bushels; a wheat crop of 2,500,000 bushels and a cotton crop of 1,000,000 bales. Added to this, plenty of space for your own text.
o-neill-dublin-1882-11-23.A9:
SOUTHERN GLEANINGS.
ber of votes cast for the candidates for Governor was 87,877. This is considerably less than one-half of the entire vote at the State, which, according to the census of 1889, was 205,789. At the election of 1876 the total vote cast was 182,682. In 1889 the total vote for President was 170,976.

Col. W. C. Young is starting a ranch in Gaza County, Texas, which olt in that country is looked upon as rather a small-sized affair. He begins with only 125,000 acres and $225,000 worth of cattle.

A Tennessee law prohibits the sale of loose cotton between sunset and sunrise, the object being to protect planters from the theft of their cotton by night. Under this law thirty indictments were returned against G. N. Trust, doing business near Memphis, who had been buying loose cotton at night from colored men whom he knew had stolen it. Six negroes who testified in the cases were held for perjury.

The jailer at Louisville, Ky., ascertained that a life prisoner, named George M. Alsop, who had been kept heavily fhoneed, had filed his shackles apart and secured a model key with which to escape, the other day. He is a shrewd, educated man, very desperate. This is his second almost successful effort to escape. He is now confined in a close cell, with sixteen-pound shackles on his limbs.

The grand jury at New Orleans found indictments against the following persons for election fraud: Edmond J. Dupaquier, Butholomew Thaines, Jr., R. Urrich, Dan Rees, Prosper Grand, Jr., Charles Cune, Gustave Buder, Jr., William Lyons, James Daigman, Louis Kathman, William H. Buckley, John A. Brennan, John Vigers. Rees and Dupaquier gave bail in $5,000 each. The remainder filed bonds of $1,000 each.

Just prior to his death an Elberton, Ga., man hid a large amount of money in a secret place in his house, known only to him. All efforts to discover the treasure have, so far, proved futile.

The scene of the Dade massacre, in Florida, historic field, is being plowed for cultivation. Cannon and musket balls, muskets and other broken weapons are found in great numbers.

The Governor of Alabama has ordered an election for Tuesday, Jan. 2, 1883, in the Eighth District, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of William M. Lowe, who had been seated in the place of Gen. Joseph Wheeler.

The Kentucky Public Elevator, owned and operated by a stock company of Louisville, the first of the kind erected there, opened the other day, and is ready to receive grain of all descriptions. The capacity is half a million bushels. There are half a dozen other elevators in the city, owned by private parties, but this one will issue grain certificates, as is the custom in other cities.

Admiral Strong, retired, died at Columbin, S. C., the other day, from hemorrhage of the lungs. For some time he had been confined to a wheel chair with rheumatism.

Mrs. Sullers, of Chattanooga, has become a maniac over the sentence of her son to the penitentiary for horse-stealing.

In Coffee County, Georgia, the other day, a hawk fell to the ground, and upon investigation was found to have a black snake wound around its neck.

The St. Louis & Texas Narrow-gauge, when completed, will reduce passenger rates in Arkansas to 3 cents a mile.

It is alleged that a gold mine in Forsyth County, Georgia, was recently sold for $1,000,000, the purchasers being a syndicate of English capitalists. The claim is made that the mine is richer in ore than any of the California mines.

There are hundreds of acres of cotton between Austin and San Antonia, Texas, on the International line, which will not be picked, owing to the scarcity of labor. Hundreds of thousands of dollars will be lost in the State this season on this account.

The North Carolina peanut crop will this year reach 149,000 bushels.

Moses Lockhardt, colored, was hanged at Edgefield, S. C., on the 1st, for the murder of Moses Blairock last April. The cause of the murder was jealousy.

At Mayersville, Miss., recently, Joe Thomas was found guilty of the murder of Charles M. Murphy, editor of the Rolling Fork Review. Sentence was fixed at life imprisonment.

John W. Dorsey, a young man widely known in the social circles of Baltimore, having sunk a large inheritance in the grain business, took his life recently with a revolver.

Burglars the other day raided the post-office and three stores at Ringgold, Ga., obtaining nearly $2,000 in goods and stamps.

Near Maplewood, La., a few evenings ago John Morgan (white) killed two colored men. The parties had a difficulty about a beef just slaughtered. Morgan fled. A large posse was in pursuit.

Mayor Johnston, of Daeville, Va., has been acquitted of the killing of the Chief of Police.

Eli McConnell, a drunken carpenter, residing at Weatherford, Texas, recently took his wife and his two-year-old child out in a buggy. As soon as they were out of town he began abusing her, and finally fell to beating her with a pistol, and accidently struck the child on the head with the weapon, killing it instantly. To cover the crime, he told his wife if she did not tell that the child was killed by the buggy turning over on it he would kill her, but on reaching home McConnell became frightened, and, mounting a horse, fled. Mrs. McConnell then went before the Grand Jury and told the truth about the matter.

The total expense to the State of Kentucky arising from the Neal, Craft and Ellis trials will amount to $60,000.
Georgians are seeking homes in Texas.

The Virginia State Board of Canvassers throw out the vote of Gloucester County and gave a certificate of election to Mayo, Coalition. The Congressional delegation stands, six Coalition, four Democrat.

While workmen were engaged in tearing down the walls of a building at Louisville, Ky., a few days ago, Patrick Burke fell into the cellar of the same without the knowledge of the others. The wall was thrown down, burying Burke under the ruins. He was taken out an hour afterwards dead, but, singular enough, no bones were broken.

The Texas corn crop is three hundred per cent. above last year.

A negro man named Couch O'Neal, living five miles from Dublin Lawn, Gai., was taken from his house the other night and shot to death, his body being riddled with buckshot. The killing was done by negroes because several days before O'Neal had committed a criminal offense.

riley-virgins-el-paso-1882-08.A1:
A Former Dallas Hotel Waiter in Trouble for Killing at El Paso.
Information comes from El Paso that a few days ago in the Mexican section of that city, a colored man by the name of Riley Wiggins, known to many of the Grand-Windsor hotel boarders as Sam, Smiling Sam, something of a musician, killed two Mexicans there this week. The circumstances appear to be these: Sam was an assistant cook in one of the hotels, and had a difficulty with some of his fellows. Pistols were drawn on him when he started to run and escape, when the Mexican boys fired upon him wounding him in the head. He fired some shots and killed two of them. Sam is now in jail at El Paso, and they have tried to lynch him, though he is duly cared for by the officials in charge. A letter from one of his colored friends there, John McCutcheon, to Sam's former fellow-waiters at the Windsor here, says that inasmuch as he has to be tried in the Mexican limits, where the killing was done, he fears full justice will not be done, and he asks for some assistance from here. Sam, it seems, has a family or relatives in Mansfield, Louisiana.

schmidt-red-bluff-1882-06.A4:
Serious Accident.

ALTA, June 28th.—J. Henderson and J. P. Pollard, of Grass Valley, were thrown from a buggy while crossing the railroad here at 1 o'clock this afternoon. Henderson was badly bruised about the left temple, and sustained some serious flash wounds about the body. Pollard escaped without serious injury. Henderson at 8 P.M. is still unconscious, but his physician thinks the wounds not necessarily fatal. The accident was caused by the fractional team becoming frightened at a locomotive standing on the side track. The buggy is a wreck, and one horse was badly cut.

Fire—The Fraudulent Certificate Case.

NEVADA CITY, June 28th.—A fire yesterday on Aristocracy Hill, in this city, destroyed a barn and its contents belonging to Frank Guild, and some outhouses belonging to John Hook. The loss was about $650. There was no insurance.

The County Board of Education met yesterday for final action upon the case against Mary McAuliffe, Maggie Ryan and Ada Deacon, of Grass Valley, recently tried for unprofessional conduct by asking for and receiving information while writing for teachers' certificates. County Superintendent Hickes and Mr. Preston voted to revoke their certificates, while Messrs. Power, Byrne and Potter opposed the motion. Unprejudged outsiders, who heard the testimony, are surprised at the result. The subject will be revived in some shape when the County Supervisors meet.

Impressive Funeral Ceremonies.

NEVADA, June 28th.—The funeral ceremonies of George S. Powers, the deceased mining Superintendent, were held here today, under the auspices of the Nevada Commandery, Knights Templar, and were of a very impressive nature. Sir Knights were present from all parts of this Sierra, Placer and other counties. The remains were taken to the train and escorted to Colfax by a large delegation of Knights. Business generally was suspended during the progress of the ceremonies.

The Chico Wife Murderer Held to Answer.

OROVILLE, June 28th.—The preliminary examination of the Chico wife murderer, Schmidt, took place to-day at this place before Justice Leonard. The evidence disclosed an unprovoked and brutal killing, without any notice or warning whatever. He was held to answer without bonds on a charge of murder. He offered no evidence in his defense, and appeared for examination without counsel.

The Stranded Ship.

BODEGA, June 28th.—There are no reliable details from the wreck. The ship is hard and fast on the reef. The tide rises on her deck at high water, leaving her pretty well forward at low water. Portions of the top sail and top-gallant sails are still set. The steamer Santa Cruz took the Captain, officers and all hands to San Francisco this morning.

Body Recovered.

SAN RAPAEL, June 28th.—The body of George Reinfeld, the boy who was drowned with his two sisters by the upsetting of a boat near Saucelito last Sunday, was recovered to-day.

Death from Natural Causes—A 200-Foot Fall.

SAN JOSE, June 28th.—The inquest this evening on the body of Mrs. Isabella Dillon, found dead yesterday in her house on the Alameda, resulted in a verdict of death from natural causes.

At half-past 5 last evening Santiago Ordines, a Chilean miner, attempted to climb upon a hoisting cage while in motion in the Randal shaft of the Almaden quicksilver mine, and fell from the 1600 to the 1800 foot level, being instantly killed. The Coroner's jury to-day found a verdict of accidental death, attributable to his disobeying orders.

Report Corrected.

SAN JUAN SOUTH, June 28th.—The telegram from Holliister in regard to the shooting of Julius Breithbarth is not correct in some particulars. He has had no difficulty, domestic or otherwise, to lead to an attempt at suicide. The matter was entirely accidental, and he is now in a fair way of recovery.

A Faithless Wife.

LOS ANGELES, June 28th.—Ever since the Sumeret-Shayer affair of a few weeks ago, Mr. and Mrs. Thayer have been living harmoniously as man and wife, but the friends of Mr. Thayer have constantly told him that his wife was still running with Sumeret, and was still untrue to him. This Thayer has refused to believe until yesterday, when Mrs. Thayer was seen entering Sumeret's room. Matters were allowed to proceed for a time, and Mr. Thayer was brought to the scene of action. The room was entered by force, and Billy Sumeret and Mrs. Thayer were found just preparing to indulge in an opium debauch. Mr. Thayer flew at his wife in a rage, and would have done her violence, but was prevented from so doing and taken from the place. No arrests have been made. Thayer will now leave his wife, and a divorce suit will soon follow.
