Disastrous Fire at Berkeley—The Olive Branch Hotel Burned.

OAKLAND, July 6th.—One of the most disastrous fires ever known in Berkeley occurred early this morning. The large hotel known as the "Olive Branch," situated on Choate street, at the terminus of the Oakland dummy railroad, was totally destroyed. The fire was discovered about 3 o'clock by some of the members of the Mackin family, living directly opposite on Choate street. The entire upper portion of the building was then in flames, and it was evident that it was doomed to destruction. The neighborhood was quickly aroused and a dozen or two men soon gathered and did all that was possible to prevent the spread of the flames. The building containing the Postoffice, Dr. Merrill's drug store and the Chinese school-room are within twenty feet of the hotel, and it was thought at one time that these, too, would be destroyed. It was only by persevering efforts that they were saved. The fire burned fiercely, and by 7 o'clock this morning the hotel was in ruins. The building and furniture were valued at about $5,000, and were partially insured, but the exact amount is not known. Mr. Jackson, the lessee, estimates his loss at $2,500. He has $1,800 insurance, but owing to a delinquency in paying the premium he is fearful that it will not be of any benefit to him.

Destruction of the Famous Lick Mills by Fire.

SAN JOSE, July 6th.—The famous Lick mills, seven miles from this city, on the Alviso road, caught fire about 2 o'clock this afternoon, and were destroyed. The round-house, originally built for a granary, which hard fighting had preserved intact up to 5 o'clock, is also now gone. The buildings were erected some twenty-five or thirty years ago at an immense cost by the late James Lick, who intended to make this the model grist mill of the world. The inside woodwork was of mahogany and other costly wood. In 1878 the property passed into the hands of A. D. Remington, the noted paper manufacturer of New York, who carried on the manufacture of manila paper until June, 1880, when the Lick Paper Company was organized, with F. H. McCormick, of San Francisco, as President. About $100,000 was invested in the business. The loss is not known. A fire engine was telegraphed for, and if the ground floor can be kept from burning through, so that the machinery does not fall through into the basement, it may not be a total loss. The round-house, which was used as a warehouse, was full of finished stock, which was saved, except some $4,000.

The Napa County Assessment Roll

NAPA, July 8th.—The assessment of Napa county for the fiscal year has just been completed. The total value of property is over $9,000,000. The increase in value for the year is over $120,000. The railroad assessment in the county is $143,000 less than last year.

Crushed to Death.

NEVADA CITY, July 6th.—Hiram Mariner, an employee of the V flume sawmill, about eight miles from this city, was crushed to death yesterday afternoon by being caught between a huge bowler and a log. He was digging around the bowler, in order to get it out of the way, when it suddenly rolled from its place and pinned him against a large sawlog. He was afterwards found by some of his fellow-workmen, who, with the aid of crowbars moved the bowler to one side and extricated the unfortunate man. Deceased was 31 years of age, a native of Maine, and unmarried. He will be buried by the Masons.

The Annual Cornish Wrestling Match.

GRASS VALLEY, July 6th.—The annual Cornish wrestling match at this place was concluded this evening. The prizes were as follows: First, $100; second, $70; third, $50; fourth, $30; fifth, $20; sixth, $10. The meeting lasted two days, resulting in James Pascoe, of Bodie, taking the first prize; Charles Kelly, of Grass Valley, the second; Edward Hoskin, of Nevada City, the third; James Rodda, of Nevada City, the fourth; Samuel Rodda, of Nevada City, the sixth. The matches were witnessed by large crowds on both days.

Killed by Lightning.

SUSANVILLE, July 6th.—Near Buntingville Monday, during a heavy thunder-shower, William Leith, Jr., was struck by lightning and instantly killed.

MARSVILLE, July 6th.—L. N. Breed, D. Fairfield and R. E. Ross were to-day appointed delegates to the Republican State Convention.

Sentenced to be Hanged—Remarkably

Rapid Judicial Proceedings.
OROVILLE, July 6th.—The Chico wife murderer Schmidt was to day sentenced by Judge Hundley to be hanged. The promptness of action displayed in this case is in remarkable contrast to the usual procedure of our Courts in the disposition of criminal cases. The murder was committed on Saturday night, June 24th. He was examined on Wednesday following. On Thursday an information was filed in the Superior Court, and the defendant was arraigned, had able counsel assigned him by the Court, pleaded not guilty, and on Saturday, July 1st, he was tried and found guilty of murder in the first degree—all in less than a week from the commission of the deed—and to-day he has received the sentence of death. He displayed but little feeling or emotion when the sentence was pronounced.

 Death from Heart Disease.
SAN JOSE, July 6th.—D. Sullivan, a native of Ireland, aged 30 years, fell dead from heart disease at Aguirre's ranch, in the Santa Clara hills, Tuesday.

 Work of the Flames.
STOCKTON, July 6th.—Tuesday afternoon two barns were burned on the ranch of Lewis Tubert, about six miles northeast from Lockeford, south of the Mokelumne river. The origin of the fire is a mystery. The loss is about $2,000, with no insurance. The barns contained about thirty-six tons of hay, some machinery, etc.

 The Central Pacific Railroad bridge over Walker slough, two miles south of this city, was burned yesterday.

LOS ANGELES, July 6th.—A three-year-old child of J. S. Breen, who resides on the corner of Fourth and Charity streets, was poisoned yesterday by eating cheese that had been charged with arsenic for killing rats. The child died in less than an hour.

THE FIRE DEPARTMENT. Chief Engineer Galligan Turns Over the Keys to His Successor.
Chief Engineer J. J. Galligan, who for seven years conducted the affairs of the fire department of this city, once for a term of three years and again for four and a half, yesterday surrendered his office, keys and mantle of authority to Capt. John H. Butler, who was nominated by the mayor and confirmed by the council Tuesday night as chief.

The appointment was in many respects unsatisfactory to the boys, it being admitted that the election of April 13th, which saw Mr. Edward Welsh chosen to the office, was a legal one, and the protest made being decidedly mild. Capt. Butler may be a number one man, and prove a good chief, but he will have hard work to fill the place Jack Galligan has occupied for so long. There probably never was a better fireman in Omaha; he was always on time, foremost in fighting the fire and ready to brave any danger however great. He never asked a man to go where he wouldn't go, and many a time has gone where others dared not. After the catastrophe of September 5th 1878, when the city got a serious lesson on the subject of appointing men whose skill was to be tested and was not already proven, it would seem that that would have been enough and it was asserted yesterday by firemen and others that the first emergency will see another transfer of the office like the one in 1878.

The boys of No. 2 are indignant at the rejection of their candidate, Mr. Welsh, and called a meeting for yesterday at which there was a prospect of a lively time. Some are for disbanding and retiring from the service, and it may be that the business will end in the total disorganization of the department. Certainly the effort to harmonize the two factions in the department is by no means successful and harmony seems farther off than ever. It is said that the mayor merely wishes to keep up his reputation for doing what nobody else would think of doing.

THE FIREMEN'S MEETING.

At 8 o'clock last evening there was quite a large gathering at Firemen's Hall, and the meeting was called to order by the president of No. 2, F. J. McShane, who stated the object of the meeting.

It appears that a company meeting was held in the morning, at which steps were taken to ascertain the amount of funds in the company treasury, and also in the department treasury, the idea being to pay Mr. Edward Welch the amount in which he was the loser in the campaign for the position of chief engineer of the department.

It was, in accordance with the determination of this meeting, moved, that the secretary be instructed to draw a warrant for $50 on the treasurer, to be paid over to Mr. Welch, and this motion was carried.

Messrs. O'Byrne, Ryan and Ed Kosters were appointed a committee to hand

handsome secretary's desk to the now in progress at Creighton hall, this representing their part of the furniture in Firemen's Hall. There was a number of old members present at the meeting who did not grasp the drift of things and could not understand what this move meant. The boys explained that the other companies had desks in the hall that they could use and they wanted to contribute to the fair, as there was no telling when one of them might be sent to the hospital.

The motion carried, and Messrs. Ed Kosters, Morris Hengen and Barney Shannon were appointed a committee to deliver the desk to the officers of the fair, and they did so on the adjournment of the meeting.

On motion the president was requested to appoint a committee of five to request the president of the department to call a general meeting as soon as possible, and the following were appointed as such committee: Barney Shannon, Jas. Teahon, I. W. Miner, Fred Lowe and Theo. Grebe.

The company then adjourned for two weeks.

National Associated Press.

MAYSVILLE, Mo., April 19.—An unknown crazy tramp who imagines himself one of the James boys has been prowling around here some weeks, living in the woods and stopping people in the highway. Western Mobs.—More than one dozen men have been hanged by mobs at the North and West during the past month. The average is one every other day. Our latest report is, O. W. Garrett taken from jail and hanged in the yard at Greensburg, Indiana, by 50 masked men. The victims had helped a negro to murder a white man.

At Minneapolis, a Boston scallawag named Tim Crawley, who had served a term in prison for outraging a couple of negro girls, coaxed the 4 year old daughter of Jason Spear, a prominent citizen, into the bushes, and left her in such condition that she has since died. Sixty men broke open the jail, and seized the wretch who showed not a particle of fear. He was marched to the house of Mr. Spear and fully identified the agonized mother exclaiming: "It is the man; take him away." While this scene was going on the victim of the villain lay dying in an adjoining room. He was placed under an oak tree, and a noose was prepared. While this was being done he was asked if he had anything to say. He said that he had a mother named Nancy Ann Crawley, living in South Boston. He then took a member of the vigilance committee aside and had a few moments private conversation, reposing in him something to be delivered to his mother at some future time.

The nerve of the wretch remained unshaken. When asked how he came to perpetrate the crime he said it was done while he was drunk."

Cairo, Ill., August 7.—The steamer Gold Dust blew up, and burnt to the water's edge and sank two hundred yards north of Hickman, Kentucky. Seventeen are known to be killed and seven wounded. The captain was wounded slightly. A tug with physicians loft here at 8 p. m. for the scene af the disaster.

Attempted Lynching.

Pomroy, Ohio, August 7.—A mob of one hundred men last night surrounded the jail to get Holmes, the negro charged with outraging a little girl near Rutland. Extradited.

Montreal, August 7.—The Belgian broker, Duchaire, charged with embezzling $300,000 from the Belgian government has been extradited.

WIFE MURDER AND SUICIDE.

NEW YORK, July 12th.—The strike of the freight handlers still continues. The piers and depots are still crowded with freight, which the inexperienced men employed in the place of the strikers cannot handle, and as a consequence deliveries are very slow.

WILMINGTON (Del.), July 12th.—William H. Chadwick, head chemist of the powder manufacturing firm of Dupont & Company, was killed this afternoon by an explosion of chemicals.

Eastern Weather.

The Henderson (Ky.) Reporter, of Friday, gives the following particulars of the first lynching that ever occurred in that county, brief mention of which was made in our dispatches of that date. On Wednesday last nearly a hundred men went to the jail, forcibly took possession of the keys. William Ritter was taken from his cell and bound, then carried a mile off and hung on a sassafras tree. He was let down three times to make him confess, but nothing could be got from him. A continual stream of people like a fair poured out to the spot where he hung until the coroner took charge of the body. The man had committed a nameless outrage on a respectable colored girl, and the mob was about equally black and white. The Reporter remarks: "It should be a source of satisfaction to the colored people to note how their white friends are determined to protect them also from outrage and rapine."

Lynching in Henderson.
HENDERSON, July 12, 1882.

Henderson county is now to the front with a horrible tile of outrage and murder, and the now, in Kentucky, almost inevitable lynching. A week ago last Monday the friends of Helen Brewster, a colored girl about fourteen years of age, who lives in the Bellefield neighborhood, about six miles from this city, were greatly disturbed over her sudden and mysterious disappearance, and for several days could learn nothing that would furnish a clew to her whereabouts. On the morning of the day of her disappearance she was seen in company with William Ritter, a negro who farmed in a small way about a mile from the residence of Mr. Junius Taylor, where the Brewster girl worked, but his answers to all inquiries threw no light on her whereabouts. The search, however, availed nothing until last Sunday morning when Ritter, whose crime seemed to weigh heavily on his mind, announced the finding of a bonnet near a field in which he had been plowing, and this proved to be the one worn by the girl when last seen. Ritter's actions, coupled with several questions he asked, led to the belief that he knew more of the girl than he cared about telling, and after a search for and the finding of her body, he was arrested.

The body was found in the woods, not more than a hundred yards from the field, and was badly decomposed, yet still recognizable. The inquest held by Esquire Jordan developed very strong evidence against Ritter, and a verdict charging him with the murder was returned. It was proven that he had asked if buzzards ever ate human flesh, and that he had once told his wife, soon after the girl's disappearance, that he was afraid some one had ravished and murdered her. Beside this evidence it was found that a piece of rope which had been used in strangling the girl, was cut from a piece found in Ritter's house after his arrest, and footsteps found in the soft earth near the place where the murder was committed were exactly the size of those his shoes would make.

After the inquest, Sunday, Ritter was brought here and placed in jail. Frequent threats to lynch him were made by the people, both white and black, who live in the neighborhood where the crime was committed, and ever since his arrest the question of summary vengeance has been freely discussed. The colored portion of the murdered girl's friends were especially indignant at the crime and the storm that for three days has been brewing, broke suddenly, yet quietly, this morning and the human fiend was made to suffer the penalty of his hellish crime.

About 1 o'clock, while the Jailer, Elliott Johnson, and his deputy were soundly sleeping, they were awakened by a rapping at the jail door, and on inquiring what was wanted were informed by parties on the outside that they had a prisoner whom they wished taken care of. The Jailer at once opened the door, only to find himself seized

and held by the powerful grasp of several determined men, who presented pistols and guns at his head, saying, however, they did not wish to hurt him, but wanted the murderer, Ritter. Leaving a guard over the Jailer the deputy was seized, the keys taken from him and the door to the guard-room opened. Finding the cell occupied by Ritter, he was dragged forth and taken outside the jail. Arriving at the gate of the jail-yard the Jailer, his deputy and Judge J. C. Averitt and Joseph Adams, who had also been captured by the mob, were released. Mr. Elliott seemed anxious to do his duty and prevent the mob from lynching Ritter, if possible, but in response to his inquiry Judge Averett informed him that he could do nothing, the mob was too strong and seemed capable of carrying out the plans they had laid.

The mob was very quiet, indulged in little talking, and successfully prevented a general alarm by capturing the Marshal and policemen before the jail was visited. Marshal Galloway was held under guard at the Baptist church, and the other officers at the station-house.

After releasing the Jailer and others, the mob, which was composed of between fifty and sixty masked men, took up their march, and leaving the city about a mile behind, found a convenient sassafras tree, and without waste of time the negro fiend was launched into eternity. The crowd then quietly dispersed, leaving the dead body swinging to the tree, a ghastly warning to all that outrage and murder would not be tolerated in Henderson county. Most of the lynchers were negroes, but the number of whites were sufficient to show that others than the murdered girl's race were determined to see her cruel murder avenged.

The body was cut down this morning and an inquest held, and a verdict returned in accordance with the facts. None of the lynchers are known, and the lynching meets with such general approval among all classes that no special effort will be made to discover them. Ritter was about thirty years of age, and leaves a wife, who it is said he frequently threatened to murder.

A mob attempted to take H. C. Brown, a murderer, from the jail at Las Vegas on the night of the 11th, for the purpose of initiating him into trapeze performing. The jailor spoiled their plans somewhat by filling four of the lynchers with shot. Two will die.

Jack Harris, a noted gambler of San Antonio, Texas, was shot and instantly killed by Marshal Ben Thompson on the 11th inst. Thompson vacated the country immediately.

Near Sanford, O., on the 11th inst., Andrew Fugna and Alex. Bandy quarreled, owing to domestic scandal. Fugna killed his opponent and escaped.

Williard Adams killed Milton Schalter near St. Joseph, Mo., on the 11th inst., in a quarrel about a pasture ground.

Charles Stiles, a well-known Chicago sporting character, was murdered at the Palmer House on the morning of the 10th inst., by his mistress, known as Madeline Stiles. Deceased at the time of his taking off was caller at the board of trade, and was well-liked by all his associates. The murderess states that Stiles seduced her from the path of virtue and lately had abused her to such an extent that she became desperate, and intended to leave him. She says that she called at Stiles' room to bid him good bye when he assaulted her so fiercely that she shot him.

A young man named Cobb cut his brother's throat in Kalamazoo County, Mich., on the 10th inst.
william-ritter-henderson-1882-07-11.A19: William Ritter murdered a girl at Henderson, Ky., and buried the body. Nobody suspected him, and, indeed, it was not thought that she had been killed, her disappearance not causing much stir. Actuated by some singular motive, he produced her hat, saying that he had found it in a field near his house. Then a search revealed the deed, and circumstantial evidence fixed it upon him.
